00e8ccf8-737d-5f57-8f34-61ad77978a5f.name: Vase
00e8ccf8-737d-5f57-8f34-61ad77978a5f.short_description: This vase is one of the most impressive examples of Mamluk glass in known existence. Made of blown cobalt blue glass, this pear-shaped vase — with a cylindrical neck flaring to a rounded thickened rim and resting on a low splayed foot — is entirely painted with polychrome enamel and gilt decoration consisting of horizontal registers of vegetal motifs, calligraphy, and birds. The elegant *naskhi* script encircling the neck translates as, “Glory to our Lord the King, the holy solider, the defender, Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, tamer of unbelievers, possessor of justice in the world”; with the verse around the middle of the body reading, “Glory to our lord the Sultan, the King, the learned, the doer, the holy soldier, the defender, the King, the learned, the just, the holy soldier, the defender, the pious, the victorious, trusting in God, the triumphant, Sultan of Islam, the doer, the just, the holy soldier, the defender, the pious, trusting in God, the triumphant, Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, tamer of unbelievers and polytheists, possessor of justice in the world.” These inscriptions carry the heroic and pious attributes of an unnamed sultan, a form of eulogistic titling commonly found on objects from early seventh century AH / thirteenth century AD Ayyubid Syria, and later continuing into the Mamluk period. Three exotic birds also decorate the vase, which reflect the influence of luxury central Asian textiles (Mongol in particular) arriving into Egypt in the mid-eighth century AH / mid-fourteenth century AD. The birds may also relate to the famous phoenix from the 572 AH / 1177 AD Persian literary work, *Conference of the Birds*, and represent symbols of immortality and hope. The precision and detail of the vase’s decoration suggest that it was made in an accomplished workshop in either Egypt or Syria, both established centres of enamelled glass making during the Mamluk period.

01297cdc-9e31-571a-af09-f3c97533e3f8.name: Cup with Handle
01297cdc-9e31-571a-af09-f3c97533e3f8.description: With its squat globular body on a disk-like base and a high, flaring neck nearly as tall as its body, this object shares key features with a small group of vessels. Such vessels have been called drinking cups or pouring jars because their shape differs from typical Islamic ewers or pitchers with globular bodies and cylindrical necks. Some related examples are plain or have moulded decoration, while others—like this piece—have wheel-cut designs in a linear style. All seem to have been produced in the Iranian region. Apart from the typical grayish colourless glass and the decoration, a strong argument for an Iranian origin is the fact that two vessels of this shape have been excavated from a tomb in Inner Mongolia with finds dated to 1018.

materials: Glass, colourless, matte white weathering; blown, wheel-cut, applied, tooled, worked on the pontil

012a86aa-50ab-584f-aaec-cc16d09de613.name: Oval amulet with Arabic script
012a86aa-50ab-584f-aaec-cc16d09de613.short_description:
An oval amulet of rock crystal, with *naskhi* epigraphy in the centre reading: “There is no God but Allah the king the manifest truth”.  
In the background there are crossing and parallel lines forming rhombus shapes, while the external frame is formed by two lines.

015a0932-63f4-51f9-8b86-46619809c4df.name: Bottle
015a0932-63f4-51f9-8b86-46619809c4df.description:
The absence of decoration on this bottle suggests that it belongs to the large group of utilitarian vessels which were made for everyday use in glass workshops throughout the Islamic world. Fragments of such vessels found during archaeological excavations tell us that they were blown in great quantities and in very different shapes and sizes. However, because very few vessels like this one actually survived, little is known about this group. Several features point to its origins in Egypt: its colourless glass with a greenish tinge; its short, rounded mouth; its rim that folds inwards; and the fact that this bottle has obviously been buried in a dry climate which has hardly destroyed its surface. It is thus very likely that it was blown in Egypt during the period of the Fatimid caliphs (909–1171), a time when many varieties of glass vessels were produced.  
A bottle with a related thick rounded mouth is said to be in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo. For a utilitarian bottle from 17th-century Iran with a rim that folds inward.
015a0932-63f4-51f9-8b86-46619809c4df.bibliography: Carboni, Stefano, *Glass from Islamic Lands, The Al-Sabah Collection*, New York: Thames & Hudson, 2001: 372, no. 102a.
materials: Glass, colourless, greenish tinge; free-blown, tooled, worked on the pontil

017b29ae-c148-5a7b-9dd5-4d1116a32454.name: Book of the Sea
017b29ae-c148-5a7b-9dd5-4d1116a32454.short_description: The multimedia artist Anne Petters, has a growing reputation for creating technically innovative and creatively complex works in glass that reflect her interest in controlling and displaying moments of our fleeting, vulnerable existence. Her work ‘Book of the Sea’ is influenced by the history of Caithness in the far North of Scotland, and its coastal communities which grew and fell with the Herring trade.  The text glimpsed on the pages is composed in a variety of languages, written in reverse—a product of Petters’ process—often illegible, the words or phrases are symbols, for her perspective of the stories we create about a place. Anne utilises a specific kiln casting and pate de verre glass technique that she developed herself, pushing the boundaries of traditional craft processes to create sculptures that have a unique physicality and aesthetic, giving life to the pages as if they have been caught by a breeze.
017b29ae-c148-5a7b-9dd5-4d1116a32454.obtention: Donated by Bullseye Projects, the commissioner of the artwork in 2021. The piece was originally created by the artist for their 2019 exhibition 'Field Notes', at the Byre, Latherwheel, Caithness, Scotland which was on show between 12 August, 2019 -  31 March, 2021

01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.name: Cup and a stand
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.short_description: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) was a distinguished Macedonian intellectual who lived and worked in Russia. Being the President of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society in St. Petersburg, he contributed to the publishing of historical memorandums and other official acts that presented the national ideology and objectives for unity and liberation of Macedonia. He also published numerous articles drawing attention to the partitioning of Macedonia after the Balkan Wars. In his struggle for preserving the integrity of Macedonia he wrote various memoranda to governments of western countries on many occasions.
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
keywords: Political and diplomatic engagement; cup; stand; metalwork; domestic vessels

01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.name: Mosque lamp.
01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.description:
A hanging mosque lamp, with a fat body and a long neck, that widens towards the top. Six loops are attached for hanging up the lamp from chains. The entire surface of the lamp's body, which is painted green on the inside, is decorated with compositions in dark-blue, white, red, and gilding which form inscription bands and geometric and floral designs. Since the decoration is enamelled, its raised appearance gives the lamp's body a sense of depth.  
  
The body features floral decoration in red and white medallions with pendants, while the neck has a border of arabesques and bears verses from the 'Light' chapter of the Qur'an (*sura* 24). Amid the inscription bands are round medallions showing polo sticks depicted in white on a dark-blue ground, a characteristic motif of the Mamluk period.
01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.short_description: Hanging glass lamps were produced for lighting the holy areas and they were a divine symbol of the light. The glass lamps of the Mamluk period are decorated with the blazons of the rulers, which symbolise the power of the state.
01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.initial_owner: Sayf al-Din Ilmalak, Jaukandar (polo-chief) of Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad (his third reign: 709-740 /1310-1340).
01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.dates: first half of hegira 8th century / AD 14th century.
01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.method_for_datation: The polo sticks, painted in white on a dark-blue background within round medallions, are characteristic of the Mamluk period. The inscriptions on the neck also indicate that the lamp was made for the Jaukandar Sayf al-Din Ilmalak, who served the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, and who built a *madrasa* in Cairo in 1319. Therefore, the lamp is dated to the first half of the 14th century.
01b9cadc-1da9-5e4c-8402-8fb4c0c6b2b9.obtention: The item was brought from the Mevlana Tomb in Konya to the Tiled Pavilion (Çinili Köşk), Istanbul, in 1898 and then transferred to the Museum in 1911.

0249f767-5443-57bb-8d12-7736dfa82a7b.name: Sugar bowl
0249f767-5443-57bb-8d12-7736dfa82a7b.description:
Opaline sugar bowl with annular foot; rounded lower body and thick-rimmed, conical lid with prominent knob. Multicoloured enamel decoration encompassing body and lid, depicting a leafy garland, strung with rose blooms and small flowers. A golden thread encircles the upper rim.  
  
The technique and decoration of this piece would likely place it in the Classical Period (1787-1810), with the Real Fábrica de Cristales de La Granja (La Granja Royal Crystal Factory) as the place of production. As Paloma Pastor notes, the secret of firing glass to adhere colour to its surface was rediscovered in 1791. This enamelling technique, of Bohemian influence, was often applied to white glass made to resemble Chinese porcelain, and was accompanied by fired, gilded decorations. The featured flower garland was one of the most common motifs of the era.

02634558-6e36-5e79-a40f-cb165e871136.name: Bottle
02634558-6e36-5e79-a40f-cb165e871136.short_description: Colourless glass vessels with a wheel-cut, slant-cut style design were extremely popular in the late second, third and fourth centuries AH / ninth and tenth centuries AD. This type of bottle was also created by glassmakers in an even more expensive material such as rock crystal. This cylindrical glass bottle with a flat base, rounded shoulders and a narrow neck is decorated with a row of four camels facing left. The vessel has an inscription in *kufic* calligraphy around its neck that reads: “wa liman baraka" (blessing to the owner). Decorations were applied using a wheel-cut relief-cut technique which applies design by grinding into the thick glass with rotating wheels of varying sizes and materials, leaving the glass only a few millimetres thick in some areas. Stylistic details such as the deep grooves at the base of the bottle and the special treatment of the flattened rim indicate that this object may have originated from Iran. Vessels with this specific design and technique were found among archaeological finds in the medieval Iranian cities of Nishapur, Sirjan, Rayy, Siraf and Qasr-I Abu Nasr.

02c4ddb9-06e7-5947-9482-34080e873481.short_description: Woman's waistband of cotton threaded with glass beads of red, pink, blue, white and black in geometric patterns with cotton ties at each end: Africa, Eastern Africa, Malawi, probably Yao people, late 19th century. 03230889-be25-54ae-8f0c-3c53dc52f596.name: Bottle
03230889-be25-54ae-8f0c-3c53dc52f596.short_description: Typical Iranian glass bottles from the fourth and fifth centuries AH / eleventh and twelfth centuries AD usually have a specific decoration on the entire surface except for the neck. These motifs include various designs such as the honeycomb, the rosette, or the curly vegetal pattern. This free-blown pale green glass bottle has a bulbous body, a long tubular neck with a flared opening, and a splayed trumpet foot. Its body is decorated with a moulded band of scrolled motifs, raised dots and a plain band with applied manganese trails around the shoulder.

03a27e68-fae1-5950-a3b8-9e7fa5eb103e.name: Goblet.
03a27e68-fae1-5950-a3b8-9e7fa5eb103e.description:
A goblet that was found during archaeological excavations at Palace B, a building which bears an inscription on plaster associating it with the Caliph al-Mu'tasim Billah (r. AH 218–27 / AD 833–42). The goblet has a simple circular base and an inverted bell-shaped body; a twisted stem connects the two parts.  
The application of metallic lustre to decorate vessels is a quintessentially Islamic technique that first appeared in glasswork before becoming, famously, applied to pottery. The body of this goblet is decorated with vertical and horizontal lines of metallic lustre, that take the shape of sequential dots forming stylised vegetal motifs and bands of circular geometric patterns. The rim is articulated with line of cobalt-blue.  
Raqqa, a region that lies between the Euphrates and Balikh rivers, flourished during the Abbasid period. A group of Abbasid palaces, parts of which were excavated during the 1950s and labelled with the letters A, B, C and D, are found in the region.
03a27e68-fae1-5950-a3b8-9e7fa5eb103e.short_description: This elegant blue-rimmed chalice with metallic-lustre and painted decoration is a masterpiece of royal glasswork. It was found in the Raqqa region during excavation of the palace of the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tasim Billah who reigned AH 218–27 / AD 833–41.
03a27e68-fae1-5950-a3b8-9e7fa5eb103e.method_for_datation: The object is believed to be contemporary to Palace B, which has been dated to the period of al-Mu'tasim's reign (218–27 / 833–41).
03a27e68-fae1-5950-a3b8-9e7fa5eb103e.method_for_provenance: The goblet was found during an archaeological excavation at Raqqa. There is no way of establishing whether it was made locally or imported, as similar glass production flourished in both Baghdad and Damascus.
03a27e68-fae1-5950-a3b8-9e7fa5eb103e.obtention: The object was obtained during archaeological excavations undertaken in the 1950s by the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities under the direction of Nasib Salibi.

03ff2c55-3119-5277-81c8-9df402166831.name: Two-handled Bottle
03ff2c55-3119-5277-81c8-9df402166831.description:
*Amphoriskos*. Boulbous bottle.  
This little *amphoriskos* is a fine sample of the use of the mould-blown glass forming technique. After the free-blowing technique has been found, possibly around in the first quarter of the 1st century BC, the mould-blowing technique has developed and the desired glass forms and patterns were obtained by blowing into glass, terracotta, stone, metal or wood moulds. The use of angular and patterned moulds has usually made it unnecessary to apply additional ornaments. With this technique, mass production of glasses with the same form, measurement, and decoration can be produced by using a single mould. Additionally, the use of the free-blowing technique allowed thinning of the walls and the construction of larger and transparent closed forms.  
This *amphoriskos* (meaning small amphora) was made of free blown glass. The handles have been made separately and attached later to the bottle. This type of bottles first appears in the 1st c. AD and continues until the 4th c. AD. The *amphoriskos* has a reddish-brown body, dark brown rim, and a very short cylindrical neck. Its rim is broad and flaring; folded over, in and flattened with cut-out underneath. The rod handles were most possibly applied to the upper part of the body, curved up and round, and then pressed on the neck. There are deep tooling impressions on the pads at the base of handles and smaller flattened pads under the handles at the top. It has a globular body and a pushed-in bottom. Its globular body is in an intact situation. The body is partly covered with enamel-like black weathering which partly flaked off and left iridescence and faint pitting on the surface.

056771ef-9af4-5927-8bf2-f6d5fff85ebd.name: *Victoire* or *Spirit of the Wind*
056771ef-9af4-5927-8bf2-f6d5fff85ebd.short_description:
René Lalique (1860-1945) was the foremost proponent of the Art Deco style in glass. Having trained as a jeweller, at the end of the 19th century Lalique began to produce glassware and by the 1920s opened a factory in Wingen-sur-Moder in the Alsace region of France. His output was defined by its inventive approach to surface, using contrasting patterns, patinas and colours.  
  
Throughout the late 1920s and early 1930s, Lalique also designed a number of car mascots. The forerunner of modern hood ornaments, the car mascot was a small decorative item, often mounted on a car's radiator cap. His 'Victoire' or 'Spirit of the Wind' is a small cast glass head with hair and a facial expression that implies travelling at a great velocity, an appropriate summation of the advances in motor car technology in the early decades of the twentieth century.

059dc6e6-50b6-57db-9d8b-cf35da18b989.name: Pitcher
059dc6e6-50b6-57db-9d8b-cf35da18b989.description:
A massive pitcher made of blue cast glass with handle. The entire object is covered with decoration made according to designs of Czech artist Vladislav Titelbah (1847-1925). The image of a Serbian medieval ruler from the Nemanjić dynasty, Stefan the First Crowned, is centred under the pitcher's pour spout. Ornamentation designed by Vladislav Titelbah, a Czech born artist encircles the open rim and base.  
Vladislav Titelbah's opus contains over 9,000 watercolours, drawings, sketches and graphics inspired by Serbian folklore, national and mythology themes. He depicted rural interiors, persons, and scenes. During the 19th century, at the time of Serbian national awakening, his work had an important role. Today, his works are classified as first-class sources for the interpretation of Serbian visual culture and art of the 19th and the beginning of the 20th century.

0684364e-3c9c-540b-bc81-35b48166dcc0.short_description: Vase of opaque blown glass with calligraphy reading Heiwa (Peace), made in response to the destruction of the World Trade Center, New York on 11 September 2001: by Mitsushima Kazuko, Japan, 2001. Mitsushima has captured the fluidity of brush strokes by pouring the blue glass as if writing with ink to add the calligraphy for ‘peace’ to this vase. In recent years, there has been a move away from the traditional male-dominated apprentice-based system alongside a broadening of material types, including glass, in Japanese art and craft. This has enabled many women makers such as Mitsushima to pursue creative careers in glassmaking. This piece is on display in the Japanese Contemporary Design exhibition at National Museums Scotland from 6 May 2022 – 5 March 2023.

07c20ff9-23db-5b2a-9931-ea2c87d1566c.name: Flask
07c20ff9-23db-5b2a-9931-ea2c87d1566c.short_description: Small glass bottles with animal figurines were popular vessels in the pre-Islamic and early Islamic world and have been discovered in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Egypt. These bottles were likely produced in Syria or Egypt sometime from the 1st-2nd century AH / 6th-8th century AD. This free-blown animal flask in the shape of a fish is made of colourless glass with mouth, eyes and fins decorated with applied blue glass. Such an object would have been used as a container for perfume, balsam or kohl or as a decorative element attached to the outside of a glass bowl to give it the appearance of swimming when the vessel was filled with liquid.

0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.name: Jar with enamel decoration
0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century and as a training school for specializing artisans. The idea was part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history passed down from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic traditions in the Middle Ages. In the 19th century there was also a rebirth of the Murano glass for different reasons. The jar with enamelled decorations, white flowers and green leaves was made in Murano and dates from the beginning of the 20th century. It shows evolution of forms and techniques through the new ideas coming from Art Nouveau and the diffusion of polychrome enamels.

0ada34d4-4f85-58d3-9785-a8c3da166b40.name: Vase
0ada34d4-4f85-58d3-9785-a8c3da166b40.description:
Vase designed by Josef Hoffmann and produced in the Lötz Witwe factory. It was ordered from the Austrian Werkbund as part of a large 1914 German Werkbund exhibition in Cologne. The Viennese pieces displayed at the exhibition were often inscribed under their bases with the artist’s signature and occasionally the factory mark. This piece, a case in point, bears the inscription “PROF. HOFFMANN” at its base.  
  
An image of this example, pictured on display in a cabinet at the Cologne Werkbund exhibit, was published in volume 34 of the Darmstadt journal *Deutsche Kunst und Dekoration*, in 1914. Evidently, the piece was number 31 on the Lötz factory dispatch list (archived at the factory) for the event. The list includes two of Hoffmann’s vases, numbers 31 and 39, priced at 20 and 26 kronen, respectively.  
  
The piece is a clear example of the preference in Viennese glasswork for round, geometric forms and architecturally inspired design. Hoffmann helped to spread new principles of design in Vienna through his teaching work at the Vienna School of Decorative Arts. For its part, the great 1914 exhibition in Cologne won recognition for Viennese modernism and represented a landmark in the collaboration between art and industry.

0ada34d4-4f85-58d3-9785-a8c3da166b40.method_for_provenance: Analysis of style and technique and review of published material

0ae2df3d-d412-5e2f-976a-66ccdd8f1b53.name: Jar
0ae2df3d-d412-5e2f-976a-66ccdd8f1b53.short_description: This jar is a rare example of early Islamic glasswork with Arabic inscription. Around its base runs a wide horizontal inscription, moulded in *kufic* form, bearing the name of its owner: “Amal Muhammad" (Work of Muhammad). Moulded in a sphero-conical shape, the jar tapers downwards to a narrowing point which presumably once held a splayed foot upon which the jar stood, now missing. The jar has also been heavily weathered over time leaving rich iridescent coloration on its surface. Moulded glass vessels with inscriptions such as this have been attributed to Mesopotamia and northeast Iran and were made for elite members of the society as containers of khol or precious ointments.
0ae2df3d-d412-5e2f-976a-66ccdd8f1b53.bibliography: Walton, Michelle, *Imperfect Perfection - Early Islamic Glass*, Doha: Bloomsbury Qatar Foundation Publishing, 2012: 82.
keywords: Glass; Jar; Free-blown; Abbasid

0b050562-2abf-56e5-90ae-a301939db660.name: Bowl
0b050562-2abf-56e5-90ae-a301939db660.short_description: Made of opacified turquoise blue glass, this Chinese bowl bears two finely carved Arabic inscriptions, each set within a polylobed medallion. While inscriptions may appear on Chinese ceramics from the Qing dynasty (AH 769-1053 / AD 1368-1644) onwards, they are less commonly found on glass. The shape of the present bowl is reminiscent of early eighth century AH / fourteenth century AD Damascus and Shiraz metalwork with the stippled ground seemingly imitating the hammered metal of its precursors. While the earliest archaeological evidence of glass manufacture in China comes from the Warring States period (475-221 BC) – as found in burial tombs along the ancient Silk Road – glass blowing was reintroduced into China in the early modern period by European Jesuit missionaries. In AH 1107 / AD 1696 the Qianlong Emperor of the Qing dynasty appointed Jesuits to run the imperial glass workshops in the Yuanming Yuan, also known as the Imperial Gardens, in Beijing. This workshop was located in the confines of the Imperial city next to the Jesuits’ church. Glassware became one of the most popular crafts during the Qing dynasty, with Beijing and Boshan of Shandong representing the most famous places for glass production. However, it was those pieces made in Beijing, such as this bowl, that were deemed the finest examples.
keywords: Glass; Bowl; Free- blown; Qing
materials: Glass; free-blown with etched and tooled decoration

0bc685fb-9104-5b6d-bc52-01f271a8884b.name: Bowl
0bc685fb-9104-5b6d-bc52-01f271a8884b.short_description: This bowl belongs to a large group of early Islamic vessels decorated by pinching or stamping the surface with tongs or stamps most often made of iron. This mould-blown deep sea-blue bowl presents a rounded shape with an inverted base and a stepped gilded rim. The decoration of this bowl consists of impressed and repeated geometric motifs. These simple roundels, each containing six circles, can be seen on the sides of the bowl. Additional circles are positioned in the interstices above and below, with a band with ovals just below the stepped rim. This kind of decoration was very popular during the early Islamic period and is found on several surviving examples attributed to Egypt.
0bc685fb-9104-5b6d-bc52-01f271a8884b.bibliography: Walton, Michelle, *Imperfect Perfection -Early Islamic Glass*, Doha: Bloomsbury Qatar Foundation Publishing, 2012: 96.
keywords: Glass; Bowl; Free-blown; Fatimid

0c019886-fbcb-57c7-b12c-71cc27dd35d7.name: Panel
0c019886-fbcb-57c7-b12c-71cc27dd35d7.short_description:
Casper Lehmann is the earliest glass engraver about who anything is known. Born in the 1560s, he was trained in Munich, where there was a tradition of engraving hardstones, and glass was being engraved by the 1580s. By 1588 he was associated with the court of Emperor Rudolph II in Prague and in 1608 was styled 'Imperial Gem Engraver and Glass Engraver'. Lehmann's work is usually found on flat panels such as this one, and often contains symbolic allusions to contemporary political events.  
  
This panel's imagery remains obscure. The date - 1619 - is surmounted by the electoral hat of Saxony, and the intertwined numbers '3' an '8' reference the third and eighth letters of the alphabet 'C' and 'H' for Christian II of Saxony and Princess Hedwig of Denmark.
0c019886-fbcb-57c7-b12c-71cc27dd35d7.obtention: Given by Albert, Prince Consort in 1860
0c019886-fbcb-57c7-b12c-71cc27dd35d7.bibliography: Kappel, Jutta, "Der kaiserliche Glas- und Edelsteinschneider Caspar Lehman (Uelzen 1563/65-Prag 1622)", *Jahrbuch der Staatlichen Kunstsammlungen Dresden*, 24 (1993): 37-38 & fig. 7.
0c019886-fbcb-57c7-b12c-71cc27dd35d7.author: Simon Spier

0c47494e-2c63-56e7-970e-4a2773e44e7b.name: Amen' glass
0c47494e-2c63-56e7-970e-4a2773e44e7b.short_description: ‘Amen’ wine glass comprised of a trumpet-shaped bowl and plain drawn stem enclosing a tear, with a folded, circular foot. The bowl is engraved with a crown surmounting a mirrored monogram ‘JR’, intertwined with the number ‘8’, alluding to James VIII, together with two verses of the Jacobite anthem ending with the word AMEN. The verses of the anthem are as follows: God Save the King I pray / God Bless the King I pray / God Save The King / Send Him Victorious Happy and Glorious / Soon to Reign Over Us / God Save The King / God Bless The Prince of Wales / The True Born Prince of Wales / Sent to Us by Thee / Grant us one Favour more / The King for to Restore / As Thou hath done before / The Familie. On the foot, engraved in diamond point are the words: A Bumper To The Prosperity of The Family of Lochiell. The engraving on the glass informs that the object is associated with James Francis Edward Stuart. James was born in 1688 to the Catholic monarch James VII of Scotland and II of England, and his wife Mary of Modena. His birth was viewed as a threat to the established Protestant Parliaments and Churches of both Scotland and England and as a result, his family were forced into exile. The followers of the exiled Stuarts became known as the Jacobites, the Latin for James. Although James was never crowned king, to his supporters he was King James VIII and III. Cameron of Lochiel and his family were staunch Jacobite supporters throughout the Jacobite period.
0c47494e-2c63-56e7-970e-4a2773e44e7b.method_for_datation: By comparison with other 'Amen' and Jacobite glasses.
0c47494e-2c63-56e7-970e-4a2773e44e7b.method_for_provenance: The original owner’s name is engraved on the glass and it is believed that the production of the glass and the engraving is contemporaneous. Furthermore, the ‘Amen’ glasses are known to be associated with the Scottish landowning elite and Lochiel was a known Jacobite.
0c47494e-2c63-56e7-970e-4a2773e44e7b.provenance: Glass - probably England; Engraving - probably Scotland
0c47494e-2c63-56e7-970e-4a2773e44e7b.bibliography: Seddon, G.B., *The Jacobites and their Drinking Glasses*, Woodbridge: Antique Collectors' Club, 1995.
keywords: Glass; Amen; Jacobites; Lochiell

0cd521af-ef45-5fa5-b4d8-956732ab4af1.name: Two-handled Bottle
0cd521af-ef45-5fa5-b4d8-956732ab4af1.description:
*Amphoriskos*. Boulbous bottle.  
This little *amphoriskos* is a fine sample of the use of the mould-blown glass forming technique. After the free-blowing technique has been found, possibly around in the first quarter of the 1st century BC, the mould-blowing technique has developed and the desired glass forms and patterns were obtained by blowing into glass, terracotta, stone, metal or wood moulds. The use of angular and patterned moulds has usually made it unnecessary to apply additional ornaments. With this technique, mass production of glasses with the same form, measurement, and decoration can be produced by using a single mould. Additionally, the use of the free-blowing technique allowed thinning of the walls and the construction of larger and transparent closed forms.  
This *amphoriskos* (meaning small amphora) was made of transparent blown glass. The handles have been made separately and attached later to the bottle. This type of bottles first appears in the 1st c. AD and continues until the 4th c. AD. The *amphoriskos* has a brown body in colour, and has a short cylindrical neck. Its rim is broad and flaring; folded over, in and flattened with cut-out underneath. The rod handles were most possibly applied to the upper part of the body, curved up and round, and then pressed on the neck. There are deep tooling impressions on the pads at the base of handles and smaller flattened pads under the handles at the top. It has a globular body and a pushed-in bottom. Its globular body is in an intact situation. The body is partly covered with enamel-like brownish weathering which partly flaked off and left iridescence and faint pitting on the surface.
0cd521af-ef45-5fa5-b4d8-956732ab4af1.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and material dating

0e020cb4-5b0e-5b53-9a97-0e2adfd0f102.name: Large Red Line
0e020cb4-5b0e-5b53-9a97-0e2adfd0f102.description:
Ira Sapir (1995) specialised in glass and sculpture, obtaining his BFA from the California College of Arts and Crafts in 1978.  
He opened his own glass studio in 1979 in Oakland, California. During the 80s, he worked with blown glass as if it were a canvas to be painted, developing his well-known elliptical shape in minimalist colours. It was at this point that Torres Esteban contacted him in order to participated in the VICOINTER, 83 project.  
In 1985, he decided to take a break in his career. He later began to work with steel and copper, developing a weaving method using both materials. In 2003 he began to carry out installations dominated by steel as a sculptural material.

0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.name: Mosque lamp.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.description: A mosque lamp of typical size and shape for Mamluk lamps, with flaring neck, wide body and high foot. Thick glass loops are attached for the suspension cords. It is decorated with enamelling, mostly in blue and red, with some highlights added in green, white and gold. The majority of the decoration is calligraphic. A prominent inscription states that 'This is one of the objects made for His High Excellency, our lord the great Amir, Sayf al-Din Aqbugha 'Abd al-Wahid \[officer of\] al-Malik al-Nasir'. The areas in and around the calligraphy are decorated with floral motifs and arabesques. Sayf al-Din Aqbugha's blazon, a diamond (napkin) on a rectangular field, appears in roundels on the neck. Aqbugha built an important *madrasa* at the Mosque of al-Azhar in Cairo (the Madrasa al-Aqbughawiyya) in AH 740 / AD 1340, and this lamp was probably suspended from the ceiling in that building, possibly with the very cords that are still attached to it.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.short_description: A lamp of typical Mamluk shape, decorated with enamelled glass forming inscriptions, floral decoration, and blazons. The patron, Sayf al-Din Aqbugha, founded a *madrasa* (religious school) at the Azhar mosque complex in Cairo in AH 740 / AD 1340, and this lamp may originally have hung there.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.method_for_datation: It is likely that the lamp was made for the Madrasa al-Aqbughawiyya, built by Sayf al-Din Aqbugha in 740 / 1340.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that glass lamps like this were made in Cairo, as it would have been easier and safer than making them elsewhere and then transporting them.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.obtention: Purchased by the Museum in 1869 from the collection of Dr Meymar.

0ebbd11a-afd1-5df4-98f9-79409500ae91.name: Bottle
0ebbd11a-afd1-5df4-98f9-79409500ae91.short_description: This unusual bottle—formed as an elongated oval with flat sides—seems to have survived without a counterpart. It may have been a utilitarian vessel which glass artisans produced for daily needs. Its rounded oval footring, made by folding, is slightly irregular and has a pontil mark in its centre created by a metal rod with glass added to it. Above its two applied handles, a constricted neck leads to a short, rounded mouth and a rim that folds inwards.

0ef0c4e8-1ce1-5a5d-808a-4f620baf1364.name: Roemer
0ef0c4e8-1ce1-5a5d-808a-4f620baf1364.short_description:
A 'Roemer' is a glass for white wine used throughout Germany and the Netherlands in the 17th century. Roemers are perhaps the most well-known type of forest-glass, which was the dominant glass industry in the northern and central parts of Europe. Forest glass is characterised by a green-yellow colour and was produced overwhelmingly for domestic use from the early Medieval period, often to quite crude designs.  
  
Nevertheless this roemer displays ornate and sophisticated diamond-point engraving signed by Willem Mooleyser, one of the most accomplished engravers working in the Netherlands in the late 17th century.
0ef0c4e8-1ce1-5a5d-808a-4f620baf1364.author: Simon Spier

100c3cd0-799a-5feb-ac7f-8516c0d5b098.name: *Saint Catherine of Alexandria*
100c3cd0-799a-5feb-ac7f-8516c0d5b098.short_description:
Under a Renaissance arch with leafy garlands and ornamented pillars, St Catherine stands on a brown tiled floor in front of a balustrade, next to a broken torture wheel. In accordance with her position as a king’s daughter, she wears a fashionable Burgundian Low Country dress with a high-girded, ermine-trimmed cloak and a crown on her long, blond tresses. In her role as a martyr, she carries the sword of justice. As a symbol of her exaltation, two *putti* hold up a draped cloth behind her, concealing part of the hilly, wooded, castle-studded landscape in the background. On the frieze of the entablature there is an inscription that reads “S katherina”, and affixed to the pillars are little frames with the date (1523) in both Arabic numerals (left) and Roman numerals (right). So far, no drawing or print has been produced that might have served as a model for this reverse glass painting.  
  
The date must be connected to an event that sparked the commission for this magnificent small painting, but there are no inscriptions nor heraldic clues as to whether it was commissioned for personal use, as a gift to a private individual, or as a donation to a private or public building. The quality of the glass support, the careful painting technique with generous application of gold leaf, and the meticulous, delicate etching as well as the high artistic merit identify it as a precious reverse glass painting that could only have been created in the context of rich patronage.

10d27bf1-4cdc-582d-8b10-97a58ec4e602.name: Vase
10d27bf1-4cdc-582d-8b10-97a58ec4e602.description: The great history of Austrian Art Nouveau owes a large debt to the female artists who participated in its creation, development, and flourishing. The participation of women in the Wiener Werkstätte was omnipresent – not only were women attendant in the workshops, they were also present in management. These creative women took part in almost all fields of decorative arts within the Wiener Werkstätte, simultaneously co-creating and collaborating with many of their male colleagues. One of the many female artists that took part in creating the long tradition and large inventory of the Viennese workshops was Karoline Lotte Fink, a graduate of the Kunstgewerbeschule. Developing a new technique with the glassworks of Carl Drobnik and Sons in Haida, Fink implemented her neoclassical designs, resulting in beautiful and colourful creations. This bucket-shaped glass from the MAK collection is an ideal representation of the amalgam of Fink’s many talents and skills. Depicting four female figures (three on the one side and one on the other) and two leafy shrubs, the composition presents a beautiful contrast to its blue background. The forms and lines of Fink’s work in enamel are in line with the contemporary tendencies of the co-occurring movements, further indicating the importance of such examples and, of course, such figures as Lotte Fink and her colleagues.

12a71572-fcf3-5304-88eb-7860dea1698c.name: Sugar bowl
12a71572-fcf3-5304-88eb-7860dea1698c.short_description:
Pressed glass is produced by placing a batch of hot glass in a metal mould, usually made up of several parts, and pressing the glass into this mould with a plunger. It is an invention dating back to the early 19th century. The technique used in this process makes it possible to produce glass of exactly the same shape in large numbers and to decorate the surfaces in a way that would not be possible with other techniques, or only with a great deal of work. The sharply detailed decoration, evident in this piece, could otherwise only be achieved with glass-cutting and carving techniques.  
  
The 1840 and 1841 catalogues from Launay Hautin & Cie., a company with its headquarters on the renowned Rue de Paradis in Paris, provide an invaluable resource for the identification and dating of early French examples of pressed glass. Launay Hautin distributed products from several glassworks, notably those of Baccarat and Saint-Louis. The glassware items listed in the company’s catalogues are reproduced as meticulously executed lithographs, all of which are to a consistent scale for each piece.

140a4693-dab1-58ff-bebc-612e7b9ac1a6.name: Sweetmeat dish
140a4693-dab1-58ff-bebc-612e7b9ac1a6.short_description: This sweetmeat dish was probably created in the Hirschberger Valley. The design is evidence of the highest mastery of glass engraving, using a combination of intaglio engraving and relief carving. On the base, the rim of the foot and the stem, there are ground and brightly polished sections. The bowl is oval in cross-section and has raised palmettes on three sides, which are also polished. The dish is largely covered with wheel engraving, which is mainly left matte. Both the smooth walls and the palmette leaves are covered in detailed ornaments and motifs, ranging from foliate scrolls and ribbon work to scalloped or dotted ornaments and miniature landscapes. On the one narrow side of the cup is a hitherto uninterpreted coat of arms with a crest and the initials “R H G V D”. The curved edge of the bowl is cut and polished; the form follows the outline of the palmette scroll.

14d06b46-f0d5-5b98-9b91-7af2422052d9.name: Centerpiece
14d06b46-f0d5-5b98-9b91-7af2422052d9.description: This piece is colourless cut crystal glass with a tall stem and oval-shaped, shallow, polygonal-cut bowl with a slightly corrugated wall. It is from the Series Strnad, AD 1910: In AD 1909, the architect Oskar Strnad started teaching at the School of Arts and Crafts. After 1910, he also worked for Lobmeyr (a pioneering glass manufacturing house in Austrian /Bohemian crystal production), with whom he remained in close contact until his death. This colourless cut crystal glass is one of the first designs Strnad created for Lobmeyr, using thick-walled crystal glass. The designs are simple and created by means of sharply cut edges. For the jars especially he sketched out variations of painting or cutting surface designs. These artworks by Strnad were part of a series applying “rock crystal-like cutting”. Some of them were presented at the Exhibition of Works from the Austrian Arts Industry in the Museum of Art and Industry in AD 1910/11. According to Fischel, "New paths have been broken in crystal cutting. Mr. F. Alber, O. Hofner, P. Philipp, A. Horvath and Professor Strnad were active here. They succeeded in combining elegant lines and delicate modelling in such a way that an extremely noble effect was achieved on some beautiful pieces. the high gloss of the water-bright, polished crystal comes into its own best when the softly curved surface supports it." see: H. Fischel in KKH.

1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.name: Mosque lamp.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.description: A glass mosque lamp with a rounded body, flared neck and attached splayed foot. The lamp is almost intact apart from the neck which has been repaired. Attached to the body of the lamp are six loops used to suspend the lamp from the ceiling. The lamp is covered in peonies outlined in red against a blue background. On the neck and underside of the body are three circular medallions of a composite vegetal design. This is a fine example of the more unusual type of Mamluk mosque lamps without inscriptions. The small numbers of similar lamps that survive are all associated with buildings constructed under Sultan Hasan ibn Muhammad. Rows of these lamps, lit up, illuminating the floral designs against a blue background would have been a spectacular sight in a mosque interior.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.short_description: An enamelled glass mosque lamp with rounded body, flared neck and attached splayed foot. Although typical of Mamluk mosque lamps in shape and technique, this lampis unusual as it has purely floral or vegetal decoration and no inscriptions.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.method_for_datation: This lamp is one of a group of lamps without inscriptions, decorated with purely floral motifs, produced in about the mid-7th / 14th century. They are associated with buildings commissioned by Sultan Hasan ibn Muhammad (r. between 747–51 / 1347–51 and again in 754–62 / 1354–61). Two similar lamps, now in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo, were found in the Madrasa of Sultan Hasan built in 756 / 1356. Another lamp in the same museum in Cairo is inscribed with the name of Sultan Hasan.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.method_for_provenance: This lamp bears close resemblance to others produced for buildings in Egypt that were commissioned by Sultan Hasan.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by Sir Augustus Wollaston Franks in 1881.

170c8cf5-b614-5435-ab40-7ff0326cc97f.name: Bottle.
170c8cf5-b614-5435-ab40-7ff0326cc97f.description:
Small glass bottle, gilded and translucent, with greenish-brown tones. The flattened spherical form of the body, the tall truncated cone neck and the concave base give it stability and a formal coherence of great quality. The fragility of the material is thus combined with a solidity of form. The refined decoration of the body consists of oval-shaped motifs which become denser in the upper part, around where the neck rises up.  
Its shape and refined decoration suggest that it was probably used to contain perfume.  
It was found with other luxury objects in the inside of a system of channels, where it is presumed to have been hidden at the end of the Muslim administration of the town, a very turbulent period which resulted in valuable objects being hidden away. This is probably the reason for its having survived intact over the centuries.  
This object has unique characteristics in the context of Islamic archaeology in Portugal.
170c8cf5-b614-5435-ab40-7ff0326cc97f.short_description: Small gilded glass bottle with green-brown hues. Its shape and decoration suggest that it was used to hold perfume. It was found alongside other luxury Almohad items in a drain, where it must have been hidden just before the town was taken by the Christians.

174a686d-d71c-5900-ac66-c2dba02914eb.name: Jug
174a686d-d71c-5900-ac66-c2dba02914eb.short_description: It is known that there were workshops producing glass vessels around Beykoz in Istanbul in the 19th century. The first glass workshop was founded by Mevlevi Dervish Mehmed Dede during the reign of Selim III (1789–1807). There were European glass craftsmen working in those workshops as well. Cups, bottles, jugs etc. made of colourful, colourless and opal glass were among Beykoz's productions. *Çeşm-i bulbul* is the name of the technique used to make this glass jug. In this technique, the glass bars are immerged into transparent glass. On the body of the jug we see spirally placed opaque white, opaque purple and blue glass bars immerged into colourless ground. It is of pear-shaped with a short neck and a lid. The handle was attached later. The lid handle is in the shape of a *Mevlevi sikke* (Mevlevi Sufi headwear).

183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.name: Goblet.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.description:
A goblet in the shape of a truncated cone. The upper part is undecorated and spreads out slightly into a chalice shape. The base is concave (for stability) and retains the navel-like mark where the glass-blower's pipe broke away.  
The glass is transparent, slightly smoky and has very few air-bubbles. It has an iridescent and pearly appearance. The lower part is decorated with a grid of incised lines forming two rows of seven diamond shapes and two rows of seven triangles. Topped by a double circumferential band, the upper rows are decorated with oblique tapering grooves whereas the lower rows have opposing lobes. This grid is decorated at each intersection with an ellipsoidal groove shaped like a segment of a circle. Around the base are more notches, linked to the wall of the goblet with quarter-circle shapes. This goblet is similar to some found at Fustat, Raqqa and Damascus, and to others discovered in the cargo of the wreck discovered off the Turkish coast during the Serce Limani seabed excavations. The goblet's straight profile reminds us of those drinking vessels held by the *caliph*s and high dignitaries shown on the Fatimid wood carvings in Cairo.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.short_description: This goblet in the shape of a truncated cone has a concave base, and its slightly tinted transparent glass contains some air bubbles. The goblet is comparable to similar objects found during submarine excavations along the Turkish coast.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.dates: Hegira, second half of the 4th–first half of the 5th centuries / AD 10th–11th centuries.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.dimensions: Height 11 cm, diameter 4 cm to 6 cm, thickness of glass at rim 0.1 to 0.15 cm.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.method_for_datation: Although this object is similar to articles found at Raqqa dating from the 3rd / 10th century, it was, however, discovered at the Sabra al-Mansuriyya site. This capital city of the Fatimids was founded in the mid-4th / 9th century. As for the likeness of the goblet to the above-mentioned Serce Limani wreck cargo, we know that the ship sank in the second quarter of the 5th / 11th century. Sabra was completely abandoned after the Hilalian invasions in 449 / 1057. We can therefore date this goblet with assurance between the second-half of the 4th / 10th and the beginning of the 5th / 11th centuries.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.method_for_provenance: This goblet was discovered by chance in 1992 at the Sabra al-Mansuriyya site. Brick pickers broke open a large jar with a pick-axe and found contents of priceless value: carafes, goblets, flasks and cups. The shape and decoration of other similar objects found in the Sabra excavations suggest that this object was either produced at the Sabra glass-works, which were highly reputed at that time, or at those of Kairouan, the nearest economic capital.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.obtention: After its discovery in 1992 this piece was kept at the Bardo Museum. It was then acquired by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada, on its inauguration. It is currently on display there.

18a05606-6682-56be-addb-1dd84f122347.name: Self-portrait Dreaming of Portavadie
18a05606-6682-56be-addb-1dd84f122347.short_description: Scottish stained-glass artist Pinkie Maclure, creates works of art that are social commentaries on today’s society and the toll humanity has upon our environment. 'Self-portrait Dreaming of Portavadie' explores the artist’s memories, connection with place, and sense of loss around her childhood holiday cottage at Portavadie, on the west coast of Scotland, following the destruction of the Loch after the government sold the surrounding land to a company to build oil platforms who dynamited the shallow bay, killing the delicate eco-system within. The piece layers surrealism and historic symbolism in a poetic manner, sensitively combining imagery of her family within the landscape in happier times, with the brutality of the concrete building, razor-wired, and symbols of occupation of the land. Maclure does not shy away from themes of this nature, challenging us the viewer to take responsibility for our impact upon the landscape, whilst commemorating a forgotten area of outstanding natural beauty whose destruction has been covered up by the passage of time.
18a05606-6682-56be-addb-1dd84f122347.author: Sarah Rothwell
keywords: Contemporary Glass; Studio Glass; Art Glass
materials: Stained glass; sandblasted, painted, fired and layered, with glass beads

19309244-d3ba-5328-b6af-d77395f59e8e.name: Mosque Lamp
19309244-d3ba-5328-b6af-d77395f59e8e.short_description: This mosque lamp was almost certainly made for the monumental mosque and madrasa complex of the Mamluk Sultan Al-Malik Al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Barquq (AH r. 783-791 and 792-801 / AD 1382-1389 and 1390-1399) in Cairo, completed in 788 AH / 1386 AD. It presents a typical decoration for glass lamps produced in that period with inscriptions in blue enamel, gilding on the neck, and in reserve on blue background with a floral interlacing motif on the globular body. Al-Malik Al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Barquq is mentioned twice in the inscriptions on the body and in the circular medallions on the neck. The blue inscription on the neck is verse 35 from the Sura of Light (Qur’an 24), “Allahu nur al-samawati wa al-ardhi mathalu nurihi kamishkatin fiha misbahun al-misbahu fi zujajatin" (God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The Parable of His Light is as if there were a Niche and within it a Lamp: the Lamp enclosed in Glass). This quotation is often used for lamp decoration and emphasizes the sensorial, luminous aspect of the Qur’anic text. The large spaces of the mosques and madrasa founded by the Mamluks during the eighth century AH / fourteenth century AD required ample lighting. This need prompted the production of hanging lamps in Egypt and Syria and explains the relatively high number of surviving examples today.

19609cec-21c6-592e-ae9e-0f91416d8114.name: Vase
19609cec-21c6-592e-ae9e-0f91416d8114.short_description:
'Clutha' glass was a type of 'art glass' designed by the industrial designer Dr Christopher Dresser (1834-1904) for production at James Couper & Sons, Glasgow. Named after the mythical name for the river Clyde, on the banks of which James Couper & Sons' glassworks stood, it was characterised by its organic colouring and shapes that drew inspiration from early Roman and Venetian prototypes.  
  
This vase is of an elongated form that resembles the organic shapes that would typify art noveau glassware around 1900. The glass is also flecked with aventurine inclusions, giving the surface its distinct textured effect, and very much borrowed from earlier glassmaking techniques. With an approach to historic styles that somehow seem to pre-empt the modern, this vase exemplifies the design ethos of Dresser.

1a4406cc-c297-5034-9d30-5ee7a58f491a.name: Plaque
1a4406cc-c297-5034-9d30-5ee7a58f491a.short_description: This glass plaque, made with a stamp or mould, bears the figure of a mounted huntsman.  It depicts a central hunter wearing a peaked toque-like hat, a belted caftan, and boots riding a heavily caparisoned horse depicted in mid-stride. The delicate, pearl-like edgings of clothes, reins, and trappings are marked with dots of glass. Other careful details noted are the feathers on the birds’ wings, the plaiting of the horse’s tail, and the curve of the huntsman’s hand. A falcon is perched on the left hand of the rider while another bird hovers at his right shoulder. Below the hunter's mount a hunting dog, presumably a type of saluki, attacks a leaping hare. Plaques of this type can be dated with some certainty following the discovery of a group of similar objects during excavations of the fifth or sixth century AH / eleventh or twelfth century AD at Ghaznavid palace at Termez (Tirmidh), in modern-day Uzbekistan. The colours of the excavated plaques include rich purple, vivid blue, pale yellow and green. Judging from architectural elements found at the site, it seems probable that those objects may have been inset into windows as decorative elements.

1a9e5630-70cb-5d3f-a3ff-92564b210c02.name: Lamp
1a9e5630-70cb-5d3f-a3ff-92564b210c02.short_description: The Mamluks were prodigious patrons of the arts who took a special interest in building religious foundations, which they supplied with all manner of beautiful furnishings, including lamps such as this. According to the inscriptions on the lower part of the lamp, it was commissioned "By order of the most noble authority, the Exalted, the Lordly, the Masterful, holder of the sword, Shaykhu al-Nasiri", a former mamluk of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. On the upper and lower sections of the lamp is Shaykhu’s heraldic device or blazon in the form of a circular medallion bearing a red cup set between a red and a black bar. He is known to have built a mosque and a *khanqa* in Cairo in the mid-eighth/mid-fourteenth century, and this lamp was most likely made for one of these structures.

1b3ce880-1b98-56ec-b2e1-893acaafef9c.name: Flask.
1b3ce880-1b98-56ec-b2e1-893acaafef9c.description:
The rectangular flask of translucent colourless glass consists of three sections – neck, body and base. The slightly flared, six-sided neck is faceted and has a rimless opening. The decoration of the body is composed of plain geometric shapes. The shoulder is angular with a V-shaped element at each corner. Triangles of different sizes, incised with large linear cuts, divide the four sides forming a complex aesthetic design. A deep horizontal groove separates the body from the flat base with its four short pyramidal feet.  
Because of their shape, these small solid flasks, distinguished by a platform-like base and four short feet, constitute a discrete group. However, their decoration is of such great variety that it is difficult to find similar examples.  
These flasks were articles for everyday use and intended to contain perfume, extracts or powders. The great number of surviving flasks is evidence of the extensive use of glass during this time.
1b3ce880-1b98-56ec-b2e1-893acaafef9c.short_description: Small rectangular flask of translucent colourless glass with a six-sided neck, a body and a base with four short pyramidal feet. Plain geometric shapes form the decoration of the body. Articles of every day use, these flasks were probably used to contain perfumes or other essences.

1beb457a-4a0a-5fa1-808d-bfbe3828bb08.name: Plaque
1beb457a-4a0a-5fa1-808d-bfbe3828bb08.description:
Plaque of pyramid-shaped composition, depicting the triumph of Hercules upon firing a poison arrow at the centaur Nessus to rescue his wife Deianira from the monster’s clutches. A floral border with four coats of arms frames the scene.  
  
This work was one of the tests that Antonio Juan underwent to earn the title of Master Engraver. The position was left unfilled when his father, Félix Juan, died in 1788. As Paloma Pastor indicates, a passing exam required engraving a figure on flat glass and another figure or image on a vessel. The candidates for the exam were Manuel Calleja, Manuel Pérez, Joseph Lagrú and Antonio Juan. Juan won the contest while Lagrú became Second Master.  
  
In 1799, Carlos IV appointed Antonio Juan as Court Engraver and granted him the right to wear the engraver’s uniform, in honour of his teaching service and work at Casa del Labrador de San Lorenzo de El Escorial.

1caa0741-193b-5ce9-9a9c-423846c3eeff.name: Small bucket
1caa0741-193b-5ce9-9a9c-423846c3eeff.short_description: M.A.I. was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The small bucket in glass cobalt-blue is decorated with crystal animal-shaped applications and gold leaves recalling ancient eastern motifs. The object was made according to the 18th century taste and recalls 15th century models of aspersoriums, or holy water basins, from Venice dating from the 16th and 17th centuries. These objects were depicted in paintings by Veronese and Carpaccio.
1caa0741-193b-5ce9-9a9c-423846c3eeff.holder: Museo Artistico Industriale, National Gallery of Ancient Art in Palazzo Barberini

1d8b1dbb-7b5e-5007-a0ce-c3f6d73adf31.name: Cup
1d8b1dbb-7b5e-5007-a0ce-c3f6d73adf31.short_description: This refined cup made of greenish tinged glass, with slightly curved sides, was initially blown as a thick vessel. Its flowing decoration was then masterfully wheel-cut in relief. This work was carried out in the so-called bevelled technique, where the slanted profile of the decoration blurs the distinction between the pattern and the background. Cut glass was the most luxurious of all, requiring separate skills of hot glass working, and then wheel-cutting the finished products.

201e230b-e913-5349-b14d-69a729ecf657.name: Disk
201e230b-e913-5349-b14d-69a729ecf657.short_description: The disk in green glass with a golden square foil is considered of remarkable interest because of its label, attributed to Ippolito Rosellini, which proves that the relic was found inside a tomb in Thebes. Rosellini, one of the main figures of the Franco-Tuscan expedition in Egypt, wrote on it "Disco di vetro con entro una lamina d'oro. Trovato in una tomba a Tebe, Egitto, da I. Rosellini 1824 -dono di Elenina Ox Sicard, dicembre 1902". The relic was later acquired by Enrico Hillyer Giglioli. As a result of the excavations by W. Petrie and J. De Morgan, who documented the existence of an era preceding the 1st dynasty, Luigi Pigorini decided to expand the Egyptian archaeological collection in the "Museo Preistorico Etnografico e Kircheriano" which he directed at that time. In 1878 he began to acquire important groups, with the main body of the collection donated by David Randall-MacIver in 1901, after the excavations he carried out on the behalf of the Egypt Exploration Fund in the town of el-Amrah, Upper Egypt. Another major purchase — from the Italian Archaeological Mission in Egypt (excavations of Hammamiye) led by Ernesto Schiaparelli, director of the Egyptian Museum in Turin — followed in 1905. The last main acquisition took place in 1913 when the Egyptian objects from the Enrico Hillyer Giglioli’s collection entered the museum collection.

208acb08-f9ab-592b-b800-800ffe643ab6.name: She the fresh
208acb08-f9ab-592b-b800-800ffe643ab6.description: In 2014, Rostislav Materka (1982) presented this piece as an entry into the competition organised by the European Glass Experience. According to the artist, the concept that governs the creation of this piece was following “the basics of craftmanship”. Specifically, it drew on the technical abilities of the craftspeople in workshops in the Czech Republic. The challenge was to create the piece without moulds or other external aids, in search of the shape created as a result of the physical properties of the glass itself. Once this shape was achieved, the artist managed to reshape it by sculpting, redefining its visual appearance. It can be said that he upturned the initial idea.

20b2d682-82b3-52ba-ad46-c7e5bc9647a3.name: Alabastron
20b2d682-82b3-52ba-ad46-c7e5bc9647a3.description: The alabastron has an everted flat rim, long slender body and rounded base. There is a small lug on either side of the neck. The bottle is made of dark blue opaque glass and the body is decorated with yellow and blue zigzags and lines. There is a yellow band around the rim. Broken pieces have been restored. Most of these types of core-formed glass bottle used for ointments and cosmetics, were produced in the eastern Mediterranean between the 6th and 1st centuries BC. Formerly in the collection of Hüseyin Kocabaş.

214be064-96bb-55b5-a13e-9888c7b4d009.name: Cup of early-Christian inspiration
214be064-96bb-55b5-a13e-9888c7b4d009.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century. In the second half of the 19th century the tradition of Murano glass experienced a revival and a museum in Murano was created with an archive to offer models to artisans to copy. Objects included archaeological glasses of Phoenician, Egyptian, Alexandrian, Roman and Byzantine origin. Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. In Venice, one of the most popular glass factories was the Salviati Society, which was awarded with several prizes at National and International Exhibitions. The Venice-Murano Company made the smoked glass cup with gold leaf and biblical scenes (Inv. n.3046) recalling Early Christian tradition dating to the second half of the 19th century. Aquamarine glass and gold leaf medals are applied on the cup.

2151f95d-a3ae-59cd-a7b6-bb8e993e8b1f.name: Bottle
2151f95d-a3ae-59cd-a7b6-bb8e993e8b1f.short_description: Glass vessels embellished using the relief-cut technique hold a special place in the history of Islamic glasswork. Though many such vessels were produced, only a few exceptional examples with complex cutting patterns survive today. One such example is this bottle in the Aga Khan Museum Collection. It can be dated to the 9th or 10th century, for outstanding examples of geometrical relief-cut decoration only emerged during this relatively brief period. Iranian glasshouses seem to have specialized in these patterns.

21c93aba-2215-59ef-bc15-90da134f4749.name: Glass Model
21c93aba-2215-59ef-bc15-90da134f4749.short_description: In 1863, the Bohemian-based glassmaker Leopold Blaschka started making models of sea invertebrates at the instigation of an admirer of his glass botanicals. These initial models were based on the illustrations of Philip Henry Gosse published in his treaty ‘A History of the British Sea-Anemones and Corals’, later observations were taken from live specimens shipped directly to the studio and kept in aquariums on site. Around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and over the years they produced models of anemones, cephalopods, mollusca, nudibranchs, and protozoans as well as the vast collection of botanicals held by Harvard University. In 1866, the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art was one of the first UK institutions to order invertebrate models from Leopold Blaschka after its Director Thomas Archer had viewed the then Natural History section of the British Museum’s collection. A set of actinia arrived in 1866, followed by a batch of 58 medusae and mollusks in 1868. In 1910, Ewen Kennedy, a private collector, donated his collection of 123 Blaschka models. The Blaschka models are now highly regarded for their beauty and realism and are still considered ‘an artistic marvel in the field of science and a scientific marvel in the field of art’.
21c93aba-2215-59ef-bc15-90da134f4749.method_for_datation: In the mid-1860s Leopold started selling models, around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and then in 1890 the Blaschkas signed an exclusive contract to produce glass flowers for Harvard University, and stopped producing any other zoological models.

22f76b8b-02d4-572f-a730-9fa0910f176e.name: Vuelos I
22f76b8b-02d4-572f-a730-9fa0910f176e.description:
It is one of the greatest exponents of contemporary glass sculpture in Spain. Self-taught, Javier Gómez took his first steps in the world of glass in 1971, when he began working in the family workshop, which he would leave behind shortly later to focus exclusively on his art.  
Javier Gómez has worked with sculpture for more than 30 years, during which he has never stopped experimenting with sheet glass, using simple, overlapping sheets that are cut, polished and bonded. He sometimes includes expressive elements, such as cracking, sandblasting, or small trapped air bubbles, in addition to cold cuts, in order to achieve eroded and degraded surfaces, where light intentionally condenses causing unexpected plastic effects.  
His main source of inspiration has always been nature. He needs the calm of the surroundings in his hometown, Pedro Bernardo (Ávila), home to his studio, in order to work. His sculpture is forever in distant conversation with the orographic beauty of Valle del Tiétar, the landscapes and the birds that surround him. His art can be classified within the abstract genre, however certain organic resonances appear to belong to a distant universe that he has created himself.  
Not only a sculptor, Javier Gómez has been committed to driving and promoting contemporary glasswork in Spain. His most ambitious project was the 1997 creation of the Museo de Arte en Vidrio de Alcorcón, MAVA, thanks to the legacy of Takako Sano (+2006) and the support of the Local Council.  
The piece, Vuelos I, corresponds to the second stage of his work, from 1999 until the present day, when he moved away from the dynamic appearance of the first phase, in search of a new means of expression. He gravitated closer and closer to block sculpture, with a solid and resistant appearance in which the sheets of “floating” glass are held and the colour is incorporated into the pieces, based on shades of black, red, pink, blue, etc. Perfectly polished pieces with a translucent finish, colour scheme tinged by the light. The edges have a more translucent appearance, compared to the more intense central areas.

23cd7a48-e1a8-5e39-b2d1-eca8c5619bcb.name: Emmett Till
23cd7a48-e1a8-5e39-b2d1-eca8c5619bcb.short_description: 'Emmett Till', named after the 14 year-old African-American who was lynched in Mississippi, USA in 1955, is a mixed-media sculptural work by the glass blower Chris Day (b. 1968). It incorporates a large blown and sculpted glass form, reminiscent of a human heart, bound by copper wire to a found remnant of a tree - a composition that is brutally evocative of the fate of Till, who was abducted and severely beaten before being shot. Day's work is consciously confronting the viewer with difficult subject matter that derives from his own experience as a mixed-race artist living and working in the UK and within a predominantly white industry.

materials: Handblown and sculpted glass with terracotta, found tree branch and copper wire

245dd249-e73a-50a0-b669-6f6e972f8337.name: Çeşmibülbül jug
245dd249-e73a-50a0-b669-6f6e972f8337.description:
The rippling effect created by the design of parallel spiral threads when turned against the light and moved backwards and forwards was compared to the eye of a nightingale and so gave rise to the name çeşmibülbül. The jug has an elliptical body and pedestal foot. It is made of white opaque and purple opaque glass with one handle, painted under a transparent glaze in cobalt blue. The lid has a stopper in the shape of Mevlevi cap. The handle is attached later.  
In this type of glass making, an iron rod is plunged into the molten glass and turned to gather the glass. The glass, called a gather, is removed from the crucible, shaped and partially cooled outside the furnace. The gather is dipped into a mould prepared with thin coloured glass rods. It is blown into a bulb over the rods and fuses to them while still hot. The form is returned to the crucible to case the rods completely in glass. The vessel is given a last shaping in the mould, during which a twist is given to the filigree by hand. The finished form is cooled and severed from the rod. The skill in this technique lies in ensuring that the glass rods are identical remain equidistant and parallel during the twisting of the vessel.

24a1ef30-391f-5de1-b0c3-ac5c96034a3d.name: Sketch
24a1ef30-391f-5de1-b0c3-ac5c96034a3d.description:
Sketch for a rectangular stained-glass window, comprised of three panels – the outer two narrow and the middle wider. Likely due to this symmetry in design, only the left half of the sketch was completed; thus, the right-hand panel and right half of the middle panel appear empty. The decoration consists of an outer border and rocaille detail in the corners and centre of the design. The centrally positioned main panel features a coat of arms bearing the image of a building. Surrounding this blazon is a medallion with a circular inscription reading “Banco Hispano de Edificación Madrid” (Spanish Bank of Construction, Madrid). The medallion is adorned with a wreath (perhaps of laurel and oak) and construction tools; culminating in a central rosette; surrounded by a frame of trimmed leather and crowned with a scallop shell.  
  
As its inscription indicates, the sketch was made for a stained-glass window to be placed in the Banco Hispano de Edificación. The building that originally housed the bank exists to this day, at 60 Calle Gran Villa in Madrid. The bottom of the sketch bears the workshop registry number and scale of the drawing. As Paloma Pastor notes, in stained-glass window production, the sketch serves as the proposed design. Traditionally, it was offered to the client as a model before carrying out the work. Colour, applied with ink and watercolour pigment, is a fundamental element of these sketches.  
  
Casa Maumejean was a French family business with several branches in Spain, the most renowned of these being the Madrid office. While the company created works for export to diverse locations, the bulk of its production occurred on national soil. Many early-century buildings in Madrid continue to preserve the magnificent stained-glass windows made by the Maumejean company.

25c0e794-1eb1-5442-a5fb-745b80a3d212.name: Beaker
25c0e794-1eb1-5442-a5fb-745b80a3d212.short_description:
This enamelled glass beaker was made in Egypt or Syria around the 13th or 14th century. In this region lustre painted decoration gave way to enamelled glass, where brightly coloured glass in reds, blues, blacks, greens, whites and yellows was ground with oil and painted on to the glass surface. Once refired this mixture would fuse to the surface creating elaborate patterned decoration.  
  
The beaker arrived in Europe from Syria soon after it was made, possibly in the possession of a knight returning from the crusades. A protective leather case was made for it and it was preserved in the country seat of the Musgrave family, Edenhall in north-west England. By the 18th century the beaker had attained a mythic status, where it was thought to have been left behind by a group of revelling fairies. Supposedly, upon being disturbed in their reveries, the fairies placed a charm on the beaker, stating 'If this cup should break or fall, farewell the luck of Edenhall!', giving the beaker its familiar title.
25c0e794-1eb1-5442-a5fb-745b80a3d212.obtention: Recorded as in the possession of the Musgrave family of Edenhall, Cumberland from the 18th century, but it may have been with them for a number of centuries beforehand. It was acquired by the V&A in 1959 after being on long-term loan since 1926.

2686bfec-8eb0-5ef5-b318-9e3c7c3c966a.name: Fragment of a glass vessel.
2686bfec-8eb0-5ef5-b318-9e3c7c3c966a.description: Half a glass vessel with a brim that slightly widens outwards. It is decorated on the outside by a layer of blue glass mounted onto a base layer of uncoloured glass. Decorations are cut into the upper layer of glass creating in high-relief the outlines of two confronting animals. Above them is a band of epigraphic decoration in *kufic* script, which reads: 'delight to its owner'.The bodies of the animals are ornamented with tiny circles cut into the uncoloured lower layer of the vessel itself. This method of production and decoration on a vessel with two layers of glass is considered to have a special value, for it is an extremely rare example of a style that was not prolific either in the arts of the Middle East or during the Middle Ages.
2686bfec-8eb0-5ef5-b318-9e3c7c3c966a.short_description: This is one half of a vessel formed of two layers of glass, an extremely rare example of a style of glass decoration little known in the Orient.
2686bfec-8eb0-5ef5-b318-9e3c7c3c966a.method_for_datation: The fragment is dated based on its decorative style, known to be prevalent during this period, and also by comparison with other contemporary pieces of carved rock-crystal. Furthermore Egypt acquired considerable fame for the production of this type of glass during the Fatimid period. There are also pieces extant that closely resemble this piece, some of which are still preserved in the Museum of Islamic Art, Cairo (registered nos. 3885 and 5/7023).
2686bfec-8eb0-5ef5-b318-9e3c7c3c966a.method_for_provenance: This style of cut high-relief decoration reached the height of its development in Egypt during the Fatimid period when glassmakers resorted to producing decorative thick-glass vessels in an attempt to imitate contemporary rock-crystal pieces, which were extremely costly.
2686bfec-8eb0-5ef5-b318-9e3c7c3c966a.obtention: This glass fragment was bought in 1955 from a dealer of antiquities, Bentazi.

28258903-e228-56c1-a917-a44c2886b42c.name: Flask
28258903-e228-56c1-a917-a44c2886b42c.short_description: Since Roman times the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly Syria, has been the centre of a vibrant flowering of glassmaking technology. Syrian craftsmen further developed techniques of glass colouring and decoration and expanded the variety products. This flask, mould-blown of a clear green glass, featuring a cylindrical body and a narrow neck with two convexities, represents a well-known type of Syrian production of late 11th–12th centuries. The flask is decorated with several thin trails of red-brown glass, applied in parallel horizontal lines at the top and the bottom of walls and in a large zig-zag pattern in between. The Khanenko Museum Syrian glass collection highlights another flask very similar in shape, size and material but different in décor (applied small blobs), dated to the late 11th century.

294f1d81-e3a5-5cce-9338-19bc02cc739e.name: Ánfora
294f1d81-e3a5-5cce-9338-19bc02cc739e.description:
Glass jug with two handles, mould blown and puntil worked. In terms of the shape of the piece, although it appears Oriental-inspired, as it reminds us of Islamic jugs with multiple handles, its classification follows that of two-handled jugs very typical of Hispanic ceramics, more specifically the contemporary factories of Talavera or Alcora. The shape of this piece, with a globular vessel, wide cylindrical neck, two ribbed handles and a dome cover was used in many products at the Real Fábrica de Cristales during all stages.  
It has mixed wheel-engraved, gilded and cold-painted decoration with floral bouquets, a decoration widely used during the reign of Carlos III and which can be seen in the Real Fábrica de Cristales. Scattered on the surface of the piece are cutted geometric facets.

2a8712ba-8b88-5ee9-9129-b2c6ecca6096.name: Rectangular Composition
2a8712ba-8b88-5ee9-9129-b2c6ecca6096.description:
David Magán (1979) trains at the Escuela de Artes y Oficios de Madrid, where he specialises in both woodwork and steelwork. His relationship with glass began in 2003, after having attended a stained glass course, in addition to other glass courses at the Escuela de la Real Fábrica de Cristales. He has since experimented with multiple techniques born of a profound artistic investigation.  
He has collaborated in exhibitions and fairs around the world, including Korea, London, Colombia, Belgium or Denmark. His work has also been selected for various Visual Arts exhibitions and competitions, the most recent being the “European Glass Experience”, headed by the City of Venice, in collaboration with the Museo Vetratio di Murano, the Museo Tecnológico del Vidrio de la Granja and the Glass Museum of Riihimaki in Finland.  
His work is defined as a geometric abstraction, developed using translucent sheets of coloured glass, suspended in the air, where movement and light fuses the colours. Light is what truly drives his work, with its ability to modify the sculpture and the space that surrounds it, creating an atmosphere filled with colour, shadows and reflections.

2ab6702d-e98a-5a0c-b186-a06db03e02cc.name: Animal flask
2ab6702d-e98a-5a0c-b186-a06db03e02cc.short_description: During Roman and early Islamic times, animal‑shaped vessels were made using intricately decorated double or quadruple glass tubes. Draped with trailed glass threads that imitate protective cages, the tubes are carried on the backs of domestic animals. The uppermost portion of the cage in this example supports four projecting animal heads. Vessels like this one were probably used as containers for kohl or perfume.
