2bafe7c5-903e-5972-ac9f-b5290eb8ead0.name: Sprinkler
2bafe7c5-903e-5972-ac9f-b5290eb8ead0.short_description: Perfume sprinklers or *qamaqim* (plural of *qumqum*) with enamelled and gilded decoration were characteristic of Mamluk glass production. This free-blown glass sprinkler presents a globular shaped body with a pronounced kicked-in base, and a long neck that gradually narrows to a pin-sized opening. The body of the sprinkler is decorated in blue enamel and gilding, outlined in red with a broad frieze of interlaced palmettes and four gilded fish encircling the shoulder. The fish motif became a popular decorative feature of early Mamluk enamelled glass and is often associated with prosperity. These long-necked glass sprinklers were used as perfume or rose water containers by elite members of Mamluk society.

materials: Glass; free-blown with enamelled and gilded decoration

2c61e46e-3c33-5e1e-acf0-98b19112c300.name: Mosque Lamp
2c61e46e-3c33-5e1e-acf0-98b19112c300.short_description:
The Mamluk glassmakers invented mosque lamps gilded and enamelled in vibrant colours between the 13th and 14th centuries. Production centres in Egypt and Syria became prominent for these mosque lamps with innovative Islamic enamelling techniques.  
  
During the 13th century, extensive trade occurred between Venice and the Mamluks, influencing the glass lamp techniques and styles. Hematite and cassiterite pigments created the pink tint in Mamluk glassware.  
  
This mosque lamp embodies an example of the vase-shaped enamelled lamps gaining popularity in Europe in the 19th century as exotic and luxurious medieval Islamic art pieces.  
  
The pink lamp reads the year 1867 along with the signature Philippe-Joseph Brocard, a renowned French craftsman fascinated with reviving, preserving and reproducing Mamluk lamps. The *kufic* calligraphy is reminiscent of the style used during the Mamluk era.

2d62bc1c-0c3f-50f2-b292-e9b923adbeef.name: Hebron glasses
2d62bc1c-0c3f-50f2-b292-e9b923adbeef.short_description:
Since the Middle Ages, the people of Hebron have manufactured glass which has been characterised by its elegance. Around 1840, glass factories began supplying the households of Palestine with bottles and other glass wares for every day use. For Christian pilgrims, colourful and inexpensive jewellery was produced, which they take back home, either to Western Asia or to Europe.  
At the beginning of the 1990s, the "Hebron glasses" still find rapid turnover amongst tourists and pilgrims. The forms of the hand-blown bottles, cups and little jugs are simple. Their colours are based on precious stones: cobalt blue, bottle green, turquoise, amber yellow, or rose. In the meantime, most of the shops are barricaded, the doors of the houses sealed. A large area of the old city is closed off to Palestinians, and Hebron is divided into a Jewish and a Palestinian zone. The flow of pilgrims and tourists has dried up, and the old "Hebron glasses" have become the trademark of Palestinian identity.

2e604f97-ef84-59bd-9748-88044e01631f.name: Mug with Lid
2e604f97-ef84-59bd-9748-88044e01631f.description:
The mug is made of transparent mould-blown glass with a glass handle and a tin lid. The tin lid is attached to top of the handle. The front of the mug is decorated with a printed reproduction of the painting by Jaroslav Čermak, a 19th-century Czech painter famous for his themes inspired by the history of the Slavic peoples.  
Glass made locally with ornaments in the form of printed or hand-painted national motifs was quite popular with the Serbian bourgeoisie in the 19th and early 20th centuries. This type of glass was supplied primarily to Vojvodina, but also to the rest of Serbia by Uroš Čavić, who had a shop in Velika Kikinda and held a workshop for decorating glass and ceramic. He would add prints or manually refined individual compositions to premade, simple forms of glass. The prints and compositions were simply made decorations inspired by the national themes and cult works of the celebrated artists, such as the Herzegovina Slaves by Jaroslav Čermak.

312bf674-239f-5b4a-9e5f-5a7110044d90.name: Ewer and Wine Glass
312bf674-239f-5b4a-9e5f-5a7110044d90.description:
Part of the set that is kept in the Museum of Applied Art collection, these items were created at the end of the 19th century in one of the Czech glasshouses, the Gebrüder Feix Brothers, of Albrechtsdorf (Bohemia). The items are made of colourless glass, with ground decoration at the bottom in the form of stylized leaves. Each part of the set has a silver coating along the rim and filling the engraved emblem of the Obrenović dynasty with the motto, Tempus et Meum Jus – (translation from Latin: "Time and My Right").  
The Museum of Applied Art collections contain items from the legacy of the Obrenović dynasty, which with minor interruption reigned in Serbia from 1815 to 1903. The part of the set with a dynastic monogram comes from the last period of this dynasty's reign. A large part of the procurement for the Obrenović court came from Austro-Hungary, particularly utility items and sets primarily intended for formal banquets. Thus, in addition to German, French and Austrian glass, the Feix glass, known for its high quality and various decorative models, was also purchased for the Obrenović court. This factory's specialty was a type of crystal decorating, created by fine galvanic grinding technique, which filled the ground fields with enamel or, as with the coat of arms of the Obrenović dynasty on the Obrenović court set, by silvering.

32db9874-813f-566f-afe8-d3adcab6c80a.name: Saint Georges
32db9874-813f-566f-afe8-d3adcab6c80a.short_description:
This stained glass was commissioned from the artist Yoki by the Association “Semper Fidelis” to commemorate the entry of the canton of Fribourg into the Swiss Confederation in 1481. Although officially presented to the Fribourg cantonal authorities, this piece of glass art was designed for the Musée du Vitrail (now Vitromusée Romont), which opened in 1981 as part of the celebrations for the 500th anniversary of the canton joining the Swiss Confederation. For a long time it was exhibited in the attic of the museum, where a special opening was created to display it.  
  
This glass in concrete depicts St. George in armor and nimbus, riding a white horse, holding a spear in both hands and piercing the mouth of the dragon lying at his feet, which turns its head to look at him.

32f51c73-db81-5e08-a00e-f89af413a9e1.name: Monetary weight (*sandja*).
32f51c73-db81-5e08-a00e-f89af413a9e1.description:
A token that is round in form and of a green colour. One side has been pressed with a stamp whose cursive characters could be translated to mean: 'The supreme power belongs to God Abdesslam'. The seal sits within a circle that has not been well centred, whose left edge shows signs of having been milled.  
Researchers differ as to the exact use of these discs. Some interpret them to be standards of monetary weights and measures, while others believe that these pieces of pâte de verre substituted for copper coins or even commercial weights. Laily (see Bibliography) considers this disc to be a controlling standard that is equivalent in weight to two *dirham*.
32f51c73-db81-5e08-a00e-f89af413a9e1.short_description: A round, greenish token with one face stamped with cursive characters expressing the omnipotence of God and an off-centre seal with granulations on its left edge. This may be a master weight for measuring coins or goods, or even a substitute for copper coins.

33919ff9-2350-55d3-9e18-73ae206b029a.name: Head V with square eye
33919ff9-2350-55d3-9e18-73ae206b029a.description:
Stanislav Libenský (1921-2002) and Jaroslava Brychtová (1924-2020) are key figures in the Czech Art Glass Movement, which drew the kiln casting technique (glass casted in a mould) to the forefront, in which geometric and monochrome pieces prevailed.  
Brychtová learned the techniques of cast, moulded and molten glass alongside his father, sculptor and founder of the Železný Brod Glass School, Jaroslav Brychta, in the 40s. In 1950 he led the architectonic glass department at the same school, where he met the director, Stanislav Libeský. Together they developed and perfected the glass fusion moulding technique, inspired by Czech cubism from the early 20th Century and metaphysical philosophy, within the purest abstraction where the light creates a fourth dimension to the sculptural work.  
Their work was highly valued by studio glass artists from the United States and Europe at international exhibitions, where their exhibited their work in the 60s and 70s. However, it wasn’t until the 80s that their work was recognised internationally as true pioneering works in the glass sculpting field.

343b4b0c-f914-5030-83b1-c3fc4c54d86f.name: Microscopic photo-jewel, containing a microscopic photograph of Napoleon III
343b4b0c-f914-5030-83b1-c3fc4c54d86f.short_description: Stanhopes are an optical device that integrate a powerful magnifying lens and image to enable the viewing of microphotographs without additional tools. They first became popular following their launch at the 1859 International Fair in Paris by René Dagron. He mounted these into optical jewellery and novelties, including miniature binoculars.  One very rare variety of these stanhopes is those where the glass lens is also facetted as an artificial gem. This example held by National Museums Scotland is one of a selection in the Museum’s collections that are the only known surviving examples of these gemstones still in their original settings. The stone is in fact the glass lens and a viewing hole in the reverse of the setting allows the viewer to see the portrait.

357ca8d6-2298-55eb-bb2f-89b87f66112d.name: Back to Black
357ca8d6-2298-55eb-bb2f-89b87f66112d.short_description: Christopher Day is a glass artist based in the UK, who uses his craft to navigate the complexities of internalised racism. Creating works of glass art that explore the cultural segregation, repression, and death of black individuals during not only our colonial past but our most recent history. His work ‘Back to Black’ discusses the development of the BLK Art Group. Formed in Wolverhampton in 1980, amidst growing racial tension towards the black community. Especially from the British National Front. And perceived racist discrimination, due to the stop and search policy from the police. The BLK Art Group endeavoured to confront aspects of racism and expose it in a different light. Empowering and encouraging black voices and resources within Britain through art. Whilst also drawing our attention to the fact, that four decades on these same voices are still fighting to be heard. And embedded institutional inequality still needs addressing.

35e2f7b3-c55b-5331-9438-fc9c203c87c2.name: Cosmetic Vessel
35e2f7b3-c55b-5331-9438-fc9c203c87c2.short_description: This free-blown cosmetic vessel is of pale-green colour with a sky-blue turquoise applied basket handle. It has two tubular compartments with an everted rim and a sky-blue turquoise basket handle applied on its sides. This type of cosmetic flacon was used as a toiletry item made to hold kohl, a dark powder for eye make-up. Cosmetic glass vessels were widespread in the eastern Roman Empire and were produced in large quantities until the early Islamic period.

362b7d19-842a-53d3-8072-b5f3cff26a98.name: Glass Model
362b7d19-842a-53d3-8072-b5f3cff26a98.short_description: In 1863, the Bohemian-based glassmaker Leopold Blaschka started making models of sea invertebrates at the instigation of an admirer of his glass botanicals. These initial models were based on the illustrations of Philip Henry Gosse published in his treaty ‘A History of the British Sea-Anemones and Corals’, later observations were taken from live specimens shipped directly to the studio and kept in aquariums on site. Around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and over the years they produced models of anemones, cephalopods, mollusca, nudibranchs, and protozoans as well as the vast collection of botanicals held by Harvard University. In 1866, the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art was one of the first UK institutions to order invertebrate models from Leopold Blaschka after its Director Thomas Archer had viewed the then Natural History section of the British Museum’s collection. A set of actinia arrived in 1866, followed by a batch of 58 medusae and mollusks in 1868. In 1910, Ewen Kennedy, a private collector, donated his collection of 123 Blaschka models. The Blaschka models are now highly regarded for their beauty and realism and are still considered ‘an artistic marvel in the field of science and a scientific marvel in the field of art’.
362b7d19-842a-53d3-8072-b5f3cff26a98.initial_owner: Edinburgh Museum of Science and Arts
362b7d19-842a-53d3-8072-b5f3cff26a98.bibliography: Swinney, G.N., "Enchanted invertebrates: Blaschka models and other simulacra in National Museums Scotland", *Historical Biology*, 20 : 1 (2008): 39-50.
362b7d19-842a-53d3-8072-b5f3cff26a98.author: Sarah Rothwell
keywords: Blaschka; lampworked glass; glass models

367baec2-64a1-55c4-9099-925663518d96.name: Beaker.
367baec2-64a1-55c4-9099-925663518d96.description: A glass beaker with thick walls and slanted relief cut decoration of figures and hatched detail. Covering the body of the beaker is a highly skilled rendering of an eagle, griffon and a lion against a background of palmettes. This is one of a group of relief cut-glass beakers known as the 'Hedwig' beakers. They range in height from 8.3 cm to 14.6 cm; this vase is one of the tallest. The name derives from the association of the beakers with Saint Hedwig of Silesia (AD 1174–1245). Henry I 'the Bearded' was alarmed at Hedwig's abstention from wine, believing it to be essential for maintaining good health. However, one day as she lifted her glass to drink he saw the water inside turn into wine. The story of Hedwig and her glasses became legendary in later centuries, causing a number of glass vessels in Germany to be associated with her, and have miraculous properties attributed to them.
367baec2-64a1-55c4-9099-925663518d96.short_description: One of a distinctive group of thick-walled glass beakers with an intricate relief-cut decoration of figures. It is difficult to place the exact date and place of production. There are no equivalent dated or signed medieval cut-glass objects.
367baec2-64a1-55c4-9099-925663518d96.dates: Hegira 5th or 6th century / AD 11th or 12th century.
367baec2-64a1-55c4-9099-925663518d96.method_for_datation: It is difficult to provide a precise date for this group of beakers. However, two of them are recorded as gifts of Jacques de Vitry, who was Bishop of Acre from 1216 to 1226, to the Church of Saint Nicolas d'Oignies aux Soeurs de Notre-Dame in Namur, Belgium. Therefore, they must have been made before about 1200. It seems likely that they were produced under the Fatimids in the 5th or 6th / 11th or 12th century.
367baec2-64a1-55c4-9099-925663518d96.method_for_provenance: The Hedwig glasses are a puzzling group because they are difficult to relate to any other type of medieval cut-glass. The Islamic world, Byzantium or southern Italy have all been conjectured by scholars as possible places of production. However, there was a strong tradition of relief-cutting in Egypt. The eagle, lion and griffon were frequently reproduced in Fatimid and Ayyubid art in various media; they also appear in Christian art.
367baec2-64a1-55c4-9099-925663518d96.obtention: Donated to the British Museum by P. T. Brooke Sewell in 1959.

36a35ce8-0f8d-522b-8ff1-593fcf2e3c64.name: Fragments of a flask.
36a35ce8-0f8d-522b-8ff1-593fcf2e3c64.description: Fragments of a gilded-glass flask upon which gold dust has been applied in suspension with an adhesive. The flask has then been lightly fired to fix the gold to the surface of the glass and the decoration scratched through the gold with a needle. This technique seems to have replaced lustre-painted glass after the 11th century. Figural designs fill the upper and lower bands. In the upper section there are two dancing women playing the harp and a castanet, and standing between pomegranate trees. In the lower register are eagles with wings outstretched, also between pomegranate trees. A band around the centre of the flask has a cursive inscription with the name of the Mosul ruler, Imad al-Din Zangi, (r. AH 512–41 / AD 1128–46), who was appointed Atabeg (Turkish, 'father-lord'), a guardian or governor that served a young Seljuq prince. The Atabeg/Zangid dynasty continued to grow in power until Nur al-Din bin Zangi took Damascus in AH 549 / AD 1154 and established independent sovereignty.
36a35ce8-0f8d-522b-8ff1-593fcf2e3c64.short_description: Fragments of a flask decorated in gold with dancing figures and eagles. An inscription, also in gold, tells us that this flask was made for the Mosul ruler, Imad al-Din Zangi.
36a35ce8-0f8d-522b-8ff1-593fcf2e3c64.method_for_datation: Imad al-Din Zangi is mentioned in the inscription indicating that the flask would have been made while he was ruler of Mosul in AH 512–41 / AD 1128–46.
36a35ce8-0f8d-522b-8ff1-593fcf2e3c64.method_for_provenance: The ruler of Mosul, Imad al-Din Zangi, is mentioned in the inscription: the flask would therefore have been made in the vicinity of Mosul.
36a35ce8-0f8d-522b-8ff1-593fcf2e3c64.bibliography: Brend, B., Islamic Art, London, 1991, pp.112–3.
36a35ce8-0f8d-522b-8ff1-593fcf2e3c64.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Figurative decoration; Zangids; inscription; calligraphy; cursive script; glass; gold; women; dance; music; musician; animal decoration; bird

398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.name: Ewer
398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.description:
This delicate mouth-blown transparent glass ewer has a very tall neck ending in a spout. An elegant handle attaches to the base of the spout and extends to the body. The base is decorated with a ring of yellow paint. The same yellow colour is used to create a floral pattern. However, the upper edge of the bottle and the top of the spout are covered with a purple paint.  
  
Such ewers were used by women to hold rose water, perfume or scented oil. In Arabic, this object is known as an *abriq*.
398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.obtention: Object has been in the National Museum's permanent collection since 1975.
398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.author: Tania Abdulmonem Al Majid

3b172d1e-51c5-5182-81bb-c45aa0927ca2.name: Stemmed beaker with abbot's coat of arms
3b172d1e-51c5-5182-81bb-c45aa0927ca2.short_description: The significant element of this glass is the coat of arms of the abbey of St. Gallen. The abbey of St. Gallen (bear), the abbey of St. John in Thurtal (lamb of God) and the county of Toggenburg (black mastiff against gold background) have all been united under the mitre with the abbot’s staffs. The cockerel is the personal coat of arms of the reigning abbot. Coats of arms for abbots had only been used since 1565. The year 1676 attributes the coat of arms and the glass to the 67th Prince Abbot Gallus II Alt from Oberriet (1654–1687). The glass was purchased for the Swiss National Museums in London in 2006.

3b3c5a47-4329-5629-bd23-31d6ccb2b1dd.name: Guild panel, butchers' guild of St. Gallen, Switzerland
3b3c5a47-4329-5629-bd23-31d6ccb2b1dd.short_description: The central image depicts a butcher wielding his axe towards a bull's head while his wife brings a bowl to catch its blood. The donor names appear above the coats of arms.
3b3c5a47-4329-5629-bd23-31d6ccb2b1dd.obtention: Purchased in 1891 from the Vincent Collection Constance, Germany

3bc7d695-d9fb-5921-bdf7-7e279b62862d.name: Garrafilla
3bc7d695-d9fb-5921-bdf7-7e279b62862d.description:
Milk glass carafe with pronounced shoulders, cylindrical neck and flat, circular lid. Enamelled decoration with floral garlans, with the inscription “Viva la Constancia”. Small, enamelled bouquets of flowers and golden stars can be seen scattered on the surface of this deposit. Golden contours cast silhouettes on each profile.  
The most common enamelled repertoire during the reign of Carlos IV are naturalist floral decorations, floral garland with inscriptions and landscapes with pastoral images. These bouquets of flowers are inspired by the German floral bouquets of Meissen, which were in vogue in Europe during this period.  
As is the case with porcelain, the enamel on the glass is combined with gold decoration on the edging and contours in order to enhance the contours and give the piece both greater elegance and sumptuousness.  
The Real Fábrica de Cristales de San Ildefonso employed numerous components in order to obtain the milk glass:  
1.- In accordance with Venetian formulae, with lead and tin.  
2.- Or mixing calcined animal bones: a formula written by Johan Kunckel, in the well-known “Art Vetraria” of the 18th Century, by Antonio Neri.  
The discovery of this enamel technique in the Real Fábrica de Cristales dates back to 1791, when Patricio Sanz, thanks to the contributions of the famous book on the Art of Glassmaking by Neri, and the book on the art of enamel painting by Monsieur Montany, discovered the secret of fixing the colours to the surface of white glass using fire, in imitation “from China".  
The enamel used to decorated glass are very similar to those used on ceramic. They should be vitrifiable, consisting of colouring agents, generally metal oxides and fluxing agents. In other words, vitrifiable compounds which function both as a vehicle and setter for the colourants to the glass. They require annealing in a furnace at a temperature of 400ºC.

3c18dfa3-8e52-5116-bf41-c9550b769ba0.name: Cup with a curved stem
3c18dfa3-8e52-5116-bf41-c9550b769ba0.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, and was part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The Crystal cup with curved stem and appliqued aquamarine glass flowers and leaves dates from the second half of the 19th century. Baroque repertory inspired its form and use of floral decoration. A tendency toward abstract form is noticeable.
3c18dfa3-8e52-5116-bf41-c9550b769ba0.holder: Museo Artistico Industriale, National Gallery of Ancient Art in Palazzo Barberini

3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.name: Two mosque lamps.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.description:
Two glass mosque lamps with globular body and flared neck, decorated with enamel and gilt. Around the body is a bold inscription, while roundels exhibiting a cup emblem alternating with calligraphy surround the neck. The inscriptions around the body of both these lamps state that they were made for Sayf al-Din Shaykhu al-‘Umari, a prominent amir for Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. Shaykhu achieved the status of commander-in-chief of the palace and then Great Amir before being assassinated in AH 759 / AD 1357. The roundels around the neck and the underside of body contain a cup motif, the blazon of Shaykhu, indicating that he held the post of cup-bearer. The neck is inscribed with the Qur’anic verse 24:35, known as the ‘Light’ verse: ‘God is the Light of heavens and the earth; the likeness of His Light is a niche, wherein is a light, the light in a glass, the glass as it were a glittering star’.  
Mamluk lamps with their non-figurative decoration, and inscriptions of Qur’anic verses, were mostly intended for religious buildings, hence the term ‘mosque lamp’. However, there are some lamps of the same shape from this period that would have been used in a secular setting. These lamps are part of a group of extant lamps probably made for the mosque Shaykhu commissioned in AH 750/ AD 1349, or for the sufi hostel (*khanqa*) he had built soon after in AH 756/ AD 1355, situated at the foot of the Citadel in Cairo.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.short_description: A pair of glass mosque lamps decorated with enamel and gilt. Around the body are medallions containing the cup emblem, the heraldic symbol belonging to the patron Sayf al-Din Shaykhu al-‘Umari, who was cup-bearer for Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.dates: Hegira mid-7th century/ AD mid-14th century.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.dimensions: Height 53 cm, diameter (at base) 14 cm, diameter (at top) 26 cm.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.method_for_datation: Embellished with the blazon of Shaykhu these lamps were probably made for one of the religious buildings he commissioned; a mosque in 750/ 1349 and a *khanqa* in 756/ 1355. Shaykhu rose to prominence in the 740s / 1340s, and helped re-instate Sultan al-Nasir Hasan on the throne in 754 / 1354. Thenceforth Shaykhu effectively ruled the Mamluk Empire until he was assassinated in 758/ 1357. These mosque lamps probably date to the mid-7th / mid-14th century when he was at the height of his powers.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.method_for_provenance: The objects are embellished with the blazon of Shaykhu (amir of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad in Cairo, Egypt), and inscribed with his name, it is probable, therefore, that these lamps were made for one of the religious buildings that Shaykhu commissioned.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.obtention: One of the lamps (OA+521) was bequeathed by Felix Slade in 1868; the other (G.497) was part of the Godman Bequest of 1983.

3c5e07e3-62f5-59e4-93ad-271d31b1d7b7.name: Bottle
3c5e07e3-62f5-59e4-93ad-271d31b1d7b7.description: On its a globular body, this bottle features a honeycomb pattern that was common to glass vessels produced in the Near East throughout late antiquity and the Islamic period until the end of the 13th century. Numerous examples of patterned bottles can be found in all major collections of Islamic glass. They can be distinguished by the details of their pattern, their necks, and their applied parts as well as by their measurements and the glass colours used. The deep blue colour of this bottle is quite unique, as surviving bottles of this type are most often colourless, light green, or yellow.

3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.name: Window.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.description:
A window made of stucco, which contains pierced decoration filled with coloured glass. The decorations of the window are placed in two rectangular sections: one, larger, at the bottom and the other, smaller, at the top. The decoration in the lower section is composed of a pointed arch, within which are vegetal motifs including cypress trees, and decorative architectural components such as domes and minarets, which bear a strong Ottoman imprint. The upper section is composed of an inscription in *naskhi* script, which reads: 'Oh Muhammad'.This inscription is written against a background of geometric decoration and stylised-coloured flowers distinguished by their simplicity.  
Stucco windows appeared in buildings in the early Islamic era and were used in Amr ibn al-'As Mosque and in al-Azhar Mosque, during the Fatimid period. In the Mamluk and Ottoman periods stucco coloured-glass windows were used more generally. The Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo has a number of stucco coloured-glass windows in the collection that are embellished with a variety of decorations, which invests in them a special beauty particularly when the sun shines through them or when they are exposed to artificial light. Among the most beautiful is that with the registry number 9886.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.short_description: Stucco windows were known in different Islamic periods and were used in different buildings to filter the sunshine and soften its glare. When their pierced patterns were covered with coloured glass, the aesthetic effect was exquisite.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.method_for_datation: The window is dated based on the decorative architectural components, which have a definite Ottoman stamp. The window is also associated with construction of the Sariyat al-Jabal (Mosque of Suleyman Pasha) which was built in 935 / 1528.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.method_for_provenance: This window is associated with the Mosque of Suleyman Pasha, built in 935 / 1528 in the Citadel of Cairo and was probably made in Cairo, Egypt.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.obtention: This object was transferred to the museum from the Mosque of Sariyat al-Jabal (Mosque of Suleyman Pasha).

3cce65e9-b5bd-5b53-9b90-2b8d522d809b.name: Cup with serpentine stem
3cce65e9-b5bd-5b53-9b90-2b8d522d809b.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The motif of glass filaments worked with pincers to look like crests, typical of the 17th century objects is used also in the ruby-red glass cup with snake-shaped stem of neo-baroque inspiration and dating from the second half of the 19th century. Its form is inspired by snake goblets common in Venice and Germany in the 17th century.

3d1e0397-a4ea-57c6-9cac-9bda792a5ff2.name: Crystalware
3d1e0397-a4ea-57c6-9cac-9bda792a5ff2.description:
Prism-shaped travel trunk of varnished wood with metal trim. Housed in its two overlapping compartments is a collection of 44 blown glass, engraved and gilded pieces, decorated with floral motifs. The upper part of the set includes six stemmed glasses; two small bottles with lids; two small, lidded jars; two small glasses and a funnel. The middle portion features four medium-sized glasses, two large ones and two vinegar cruets with lids. Below these are two small stemmed glasses, two oil cruets, two flat-panelled salt cellars, a lidded jam jar and a tower salt cellar with a screw top. A total of 29 pieces are arranged on a tray lined with red fabric and moulded to fit each piece, an arrangement that has perfectly preserved the condition of both the glass and the gold that overlays the engraved decoration. Beneath the tray and within the lower compartment are 15 engraved but ungilded, square foot goblets. Originally there must have been 20 of these.  
  
All of these pieces, in their careful engraving and gilt finish, bear the influences of the foreign masters. The collection may be traced to the most prolific and highest-quality production period of the Royal Factory.  
  
Paloma Pastor Rey de Viñas identifies the set as a carrying case or travel glassware tote:  
  
…although rare, the so-called “carrying cases” were also made during this period. All the essentials for making an impromptu stop along the road were contained in these cases, including square foot goblets, glasses, dishes, vinegar bottles and even mugs. Pastor Rey de Viñas, Paloma, *La Real Fábrica de Cristales de La Granja. Historia, Repertorios decorativos y tipologías formales*, Madrid: Arte Segovia S.L., 1988: 70.)

3d771def-d6a2-5f0a-b177-14c17fa46ee3.name: Bottle
3d771def-d6a2-5f0a-b177-14c17fa46ee3.short_description: This square cobalt blue glass bottle with a rounded shoulder and cylindrical neck is composed of four swelling bands of glass. Made by a glassmaking process called marvering, taken from the French word, *marbre*, meaning "marble", this bottle presents fine white lines made with melted glass rods woven seamlessly into harmonious lines across the body. This glassmaking technique was particularly popular during the early Islamic period in Egypt, as evidenced by numerous examples of similarly decorated bottles excavated from Fustat, Egypt. Fustat, a centre of glass production during the early Islamic period, also served as the first capital of Egypt. Bottles like this were possibly made for the courtly elite to store precious ointments and perfumes.
keywords: Glass; Vessel; Mould-blown; Marvered; Abbasid; Umayyad

3fa02df5-d795-5f9f-b7e5-30c092cc2de3.name: One-handled Jug
3fa02df5-d795-5f9f-b7e5-30c092cc2de3.description:
This one handled jug is a fine example of free-blown glassware. In the middle of the 1st century BC, glass-makers along the Syro-Palestinian coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated with air through a hollow blow-pipe. This invention of ‘free-blowing’ revolutionized the glass industry. It allowed vessels to be mass-produced thus rendering them less expensive and available to a wider market so that by the end of the 1st century AD free blown glass vessels were used widely throughout the Roman Empire. The majority were undecorated utilitarian pieces, used for storage and transport, and tablewares, like beakers and plates, but others were embellished with applied decoration. While still hot their bodies were rolled over loose glass chips of contrasting colours and then marvered flush with the wall of the vessel. Next, the pieces where reheated and further inflated and manipulated, so that when their necks were pulled out of their bodies the splashes also became elongated.  
The jug is light green in colour; its neck is flaring downwards and its shoulder is sloping. Strap handle is applied at the shoulder with a large downward claw to either side, drawn up vertically, then turned in at an acute angle and trailed onto neck below the rim. It is in an intact situation, but some soil-encrusted weathering, blowing striations, pinprick bubbles, partly flaked off dulling and a jagged pontil scars are also seen on the surface.
3fa02df5-d795-5f9f-b7e5-30c092cc2de3.dates: AD Third or early fourth century
3fa02df5-d795-5f9f-b7e5-30c092cc2de3.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and material dating

3fa155c2-eba9-5b9f-af9b-ebd2b6db0840.name: Cup
3fa155c2-eba9-5b9f-af9b-ebd2b6db0840.short_description: This pale green glass cup belongs to a very small and rare group of lobed glass vessels with high-relief vegetal decoration. It is mould-blown and of a rounded form with a lobed rim, a short foot and an applied handle. It is decorated at the rim with flutes, giving it a flower shape when viewed from above. A band of alternating vegetal palmette motifs in moulded high relief wraps around its body. A manganese-purple ring handle topped with a flattened thumb-rest is applied to the body. Lobed bowls were most often made by Iranian potters and metalworkers using moulds to produce vessels of other shapes with similar vegetal decoration in relief. High-relief vegetal decoration and lobed rims were also created in glass and pottery prior to the fifth century AH / eleventh century AD using methods other than moulding, especially relief cutting. In view of its relationship to ceramic production, this glass cup was probably made during the Ghaznavid or Seljuk era (late fifth or the early sixth century AH / late eleventh or the early twelfth century AD).
3fa155c2-eba9-5b9f-af9b-ebd2b6db0840.bibliography: Walton, Michelle, *Imperfect Perfection - Early Islamic Glass*, Doha: Bloomsbury Qatar Foundation Publishing, 2012: 133.
keywords: Glass; Cup; Mould-blown; Ghaznavid; Saljuk
materials: Glass; mould-blown with applied and tooled decoration

3fcd8100-afd3-57c4-a509-8022500866f3.name: Goblet
3fcd8100-afd3-57c4-a509-8022500866f3.short_description: Cut glass goblet engraved with crown and thistles. This goblet is thought to have been used at a banquet in honour of King George IV's visit to Edinburgh in August 1822. During the late-eighteenth and early-nineteenth centuries, both the Caledonian Glass Works (Holyrood) and the Edinburgh Glasshouse Company (Leith) were known for producing decorative cut glass tableware. The crown and thistle would have been appropriate designs to welcome the British king to the Scottish capital. During this visit, various pageants, balls and banquets were organised with Sir Walter Scott leading the planning. Scott wanted to present a distinctive, loyal, Scottish population to the king. He encouraged the use of materials and motifs associated with Scotland, such as the thistle and tartan.
3fcd8100-afd3-57c4-a509-8022500866f3.method_for_provenance: By consultation of Turnbull's book, which discusses the Edinburgh glassworks and their products, including reference to design books, which evidence similar patterns being produced by the Caledonian Glass Works.
3fcd8100-afd3-57c4-a509-8022500866f3.provenance: Leith or Holyrood Glass Works, Edinburgh
3fcd8100-afd3-57c4-a509-8022500866f3.bibliography:
Prebble, J., *The King's Jaunt : George IV in Scotland, August 1822 : 'one and Twenty Daft Days'*, London: Collins, 1988.

keywords: glass; Scottish George IV

4045d849-3e52-5808-ad72-f0d7d187f640.name: Vase
4045d849-3e52-5808-ad72-f0d7d187f640.description:
This is a design by Marie Kirschner, a painter, architect, decorator and designer of textiles, glass and ceramics, born in the present-day Czech Republic. This example was personally signed by Kirschner (with the monogram “MK”), which she apparently only did for pieces she sold herself.  
  
Educated in Paris and Berlin, Kirschner began specializing in home accessory design around 1880. In 1900, she began working as an interior decorator in Berlin. She focused primarily on glasswork between 1902 and 1914, producing around 270 examples of vases, containers and figures, all varied in form and organic in nature.  
  
Kirschner worked as a glass designer for the Johann Lötz Witwe factory in Klostermühle, Bohemia (modern-day Czech Republic). The factory had become the most renowned glass manufacturer around the turn of the twentieth century, thanks to its boldly coloured and iridescent designs, which were called *Phänomen* (phenomenon). Kirschner made her first contribution to the company between 1897 and 1898, and served as its director of design from 1900 to 1904.
4045d849-3e52-5808-ad72-f0d7d187f640.obtention: Dation in payment of taxes, 1999. From the Torsten Bröhan collection.
4045d849-3e52-5808-ad72-f0d7d187f640.bibliography: Bröhan, Torsten and Eidelberg, Martin, *Glass of the Avant-Garde, from Vienna Secession to Bauhaus (Cristal de vanguardia, de la Secesión Vienesa a la Bauhaus)*, Munich: Prestel, 2001.
4045d849-3e52-5808-ad72-f0d7d187f640.author: Celia Diego Generoso, María Villalba Salvador
keywords: Glasfabrik Lötz Witwe; Phänomen

4131e0e1-b6d0-5f71-b742-8d240cc5a7bd.name: Glass Model
4131e0e1-b6d0-5f71-b742-8d240cc5a7bd.short_description: In 1863, the Bohemian-based glassmaker Leopold Blaschka started making models of sea invertebrates at the instigation of an admirer of his glass botanicals. These initial models were based on the illustrations of Philip Henry Gosse published in his treaty ‘A History of the British Sea-Anemones and Corals’, later observations were taken from live specimens shipped directly to the studio and kept in aquariums on site. Around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and over the years they produced models of anemones, cephalopods, mollusca, nudibranchs, and protozoans as well as the vast collection of botanicals held by Harvard University. In 1866, the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art was one of the first UK institutions to order invertebrate models from Leopold Blaschka after its Director Thomas Archer had viewed the then Natural History section of the British Museum’s collection. A set of actinia arrived in 1866, followed by a batch of 58 medusae and mollusks in 1868. In 1910, Ewen Kennedy, a private collector, donated his collection of 123 Blaschka models. The Blaschka models are now highly regarded for their beauty and realism and are still considered ‘an artistic marvel in the field of science and a scientific marvel in the field of art’.
4131e0e1-b6d0-5f71-b742-8d240cc5a7bd.initial_owner: Edinburgh Museum of Science and Arts
4131e0e1-b6d0-5f71-b742-8d240cc5a7bd.bibliography: Swinney, G.N., "Enchanted invertebrates: Blaschka models and other simulacra in National Museums Scotland", *Historical Biology*, 20 : 1 (2008): 39-50.
4131e0e1-b6d0-5f71-b742-8d240cc5a7bd.author: Sarah Rothwell
keywords: Blaschka; lampworked glass; glass models

41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.name: Bottle.
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.description: Bottle with globular-shaped body, a cylindrical neck and convex foot-ring. It has an inscription with a dedication to the Mamluk sultan, 'Glory be to our master, Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf, the wise, the industrious', in cursive script with ornamental ascending characters (*thuluth* script), in blue on a background of arabesques of pink and green leaves separated by two medallions. This inscription continues around the neck, repeating the word *al-alim* (the wise). The upper section of the globular body is filled with delicate stems outlined in red, interspersed with counter-curved cartouches containing trefoil motifs in bright colours, and six circular medallions, each with a phoenix in gilding on a blue background.
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.short_description: Bottle made in Syria or Egypt. The upper part of the belly is covered with plant motifs and six circular medallions with phoenixes. The inscription, which reads ‘Glory to our master, Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf, the wise, the industrious’, dates this piece to the Mamluk era (AH 8th / AD 14th century).
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.initial_owner: Made for Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf or possibly Sultan al-Ashraf ‘Ala’ al-Din Kayk (r. AH 742–3 / AD 1341–2) or Sultan al-Ashraf Sha’ban (r. AH 764–78 / AD 1363–77).
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.dates: Hegira mid-8th century / AD mid-14th century.
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.dimensions: Height 42.5 cm, diameter (of rim) 6.5 cm, max. diameter 30 cm, diameter (of base) 30 cm.
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.method_for_datation: The inscription with a dedication to Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf enables us to date the piece to the Mamluk period. This dating is confirmed by stylistic analysis and comparison with works from the same period.
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.method_for_provenance: By expert examination complemented by archive documents which verify the object's authenticity. For example, the expert's report carried out by Dr Otto von Falke states that: 'After detailed examination of its characteristics, technique and style, this bottle should be considered as an undoubtedly authentic and perfectly intact work of art from the period of the Mamluk sultans of Egypt, from the 14th century to the 15th  century AD'.
41e2c44a-687b-5a33-a465-b90fb6356433.obtention: The object belonged to the Rothschild collection, London, and was acquired through Hans Stiebel (S. & R. Rosenberg, London) at the Rothschild Sale at Sotheby's in London in April 1937.

421e9ac1-d58d-520b-ad76-09fc22723e4a.name: Part of Drinking Service
421e9ac1-d58d-520b-ad76-09fc22723e4a.description:
This decanter with two glasses is part of a set that originated in the First Serbian Glass Factory around 1910. It is a colourless blown glass that is lavishly decorated with engraving in the form of stylized leaves extending up from the base of the decanter and each wine glass with the Art Nouveau Cyrillic initials, "B.D.".  
At the beginning of the 20th century the glass stove in Jagodina was shut down and the factory of Nacko Jankovic & Son ceased to operate. After that, glass was imported into Serbia in large quantities and at a high price. The need for a domestic glass factory resulted in the construction of a new factory in the immediate vicinity. Production modernization and the struggle for the new glass market marked the beginning of the work of the First Serbian Glass Factory, the only one that still, in limited circumstances, operates in Serbia today.  
The First Serbian Glass Factory was established in Paraćin in 1907. Government benefits granted the owners Sava M. Savić and Milivoje Popović certain tax deductions and exemption from trade taxes for the import of machinery, materials and chemicals for processing. The initial craftsmen were Czechoslovakian and German, who subsequently trained local craftsmen. With few interruptions during wartime and significant transformation of the factory after the Second World War, it became one of the leading glass manufactories in the Balkans.  
The First Serbian Glass Factory followed European production style during the first period of its work, 1907–1913, when this set was created. The design and decoration relied on the Central European centres. With slim shapes in design and fine Art Nouveau decorations, this type of utility glass resembles the production of large Czech glasshouses around 1900.

42a5b8d3-d3e6-5f66-b30c-e0e42cc2177e.name: Portrait of Dalí
42a5b8d3-d3e6-5f66-b30c-e0e42cc2177e.description:
Harcuba was born in Harrachov, Czech Republic, in 1928, at the heart of a glassmaking family. He was educated at the Glass Art School in Nový Bor and the Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (previously known as the School of Applied Arts in Prague). During this period, Jiří Harcuba began to feel a profound sense of admiration for engraved glass. Today, he is considered one of the best engravers, not only in his country but also globally.  
Years later and upon completion of his training, he joined the professionals at the Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague as a member of teaching staff, where he later became Associate Professor. During his time at this School, Harcuba was particularly influenced by one of his teachers, Kaplicky, who helped him to solidify his creative foundations, an aspect that determined his future work.  
The prime exponent of Harcuba’s work are his magnificent portraits. His technique is more than just engraving; he paints. He sculptures faces whose features reflect nuances of a life captured in time, using glass.  
From 1960 onwards, Harcuba changed his realist view for a much more personal perspective. This facilitated his exploration of faces which he would later engrave, in search of their innermost and most profound sense, thus achieving works that can never go unnoticed to the observer. This piece was created during one of the monographic courses he gave at the Escuela del Vidrio at the Real Fábrica de Cristales.

42cdbd1e-9c50-5291-82a1-23a7f03ab55c.name: Bowlegarnitur
42cdbd1e-9c50-5291-82a1-23a7f03ab55c.description: An essential association for the foundation and development of Czech modern art was the one of Artěl – an initiative that was founded by two men: Alois Dyk, an art enthusiast, and banker. and Vilem Štech, an art theoretician and art historian also responsible for endorsing young Czech modernism. Several artists joined in the beginning, such as Pavel Janak, Jan Konupek and Helena Johnova. The name of the association was taken from Tolstoy’s novel *Anna Karenina* and meant a merely verbally agreed-upon community of people who work together and jointly vouch for each other, as well as have an equal share of the income. Since they lacked the finances, the Artěl could not afford their own workshop, and therefore performed manufacturing in different factories, such as the Rydl and Thon Company in Svijany-Podoli in Northern Bohemia for ceramics and porcelain, and the Pryl glass factory in Růženin in Central Bohemia for glass. Among the various artists that participated in Artěl, Josef Rosipal, even though he was an architect, was of particular importance for the implementation of the association’s ideas in the medium of glass. Rosipal’s most famous pieces are his cut services, created in simple shapes, commonly overlayed in red or blue with cut geometric decorative motifs. Additionally, since the sentiment of the Artěl association was oriented more towards expressionism, and, even more, cubism, these tendencies can be seen most clearly in the decorative motifs of the glass. This particular punch bowl, together with a lid and spoon, presents an ideal example of Rosipal’s experiments with the material and a standard case of the cubist, geometric patterns in red overlay.

436f4699-37fd-544f-bb71-8f51ac527b09.name: Beatrice elevated by love
436f4699-37fd-544f-bb71-8f51ac527b09.short_description:
Alexandre Cingria made this stained glass window, with a counterpart, for the Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes held in Paris from April to October 1925.  
  
This leaded stained glass window depicts Love (angel) carrying Beatrice. Love, represented in the foreground with eyes closed, holds Beatrice by her left ankle and her head. The woman, lying down, draped in dark green and red, wears a bracelet on each wrist. On either side, a bluish figure observes the scene. In the centre below the figures there is an inscription engraved in grisaille “Amore/e'l cor gentil/ sono una Cosa”, taken from a sonnet by Dante Alighieri. To the right of the inscription are the artist’s signature and his monogram. The scene is distributed on seven panels (a central rhombus, two lateral triangles and four quadrilaterals) inserted in a metal frame, with supports for stabilisation.

437746a9-6e03-54b3-96cc-81c10acfd104.name: *Chanterelle* or *Kanterelli*
437746a9-6e03-54b3-96cc-81c10acfd104.short_description: Tappio Wirkkala (1915-1985) was a designer across many different types of media - glass, metalwork, wood and ceramics - but all his designs reflect his preoccupation with the natural features found in homeland of Finland. The 'Kanterelli' vase takes its name from the chanterelle mushroom variety, which it resembles in appearance. The design, produced in 1946 for the Iittala glassworks started his relationship with the factory, which would endure for several decades and saw a number of design icons produced such as the Finlandia vodka bottle. The vase was exhibited at the Milan Triennial exhibition in 1951 and won the prestigious Grand Prix. The V&A's vase is from the first of two series of 50 numbered vases produced, being number 25/50, and was purchased in 1953. Later unnumbered vases were produced by Iittala, as well as variations on the 'Kanterelli' design.
437746a9-6e03-54b3-96cc-81c10acfd104.bibliography: Opie, J., *Scandinavia: Ceramics and Glass in the Twentieth Century*, London: V&A Publications, 1989.

45e59ca3-7cc0-5d4c-9c4d-65c4f1800f30.name: *Gorgons* vase
45e59ca3-7cc0-5d4c-9c4d-65c4f1800f30.short_description: A vase in lost-wax moulded clear glass with an amber patina. The decoration is of four metal gorgons in whose hair nude figures are tangled. At the turn of the century, Lalique frequently employed lost-wax casting, a technique derived from an ancient process for casting objects in bronze, which he adapted to his more elaborate glass creations.

4630ad06-c537-5e33-97c0-fd099cff5b57.name: Resurrection of the Dead – The Last Judgement
4630ad06-c537-5e33-97c0-fd099cff5b57.short_description:
Characteristic of the Romanesque period, this panel was probably part of a rose window representing the Last Judgement. The western façades of 13th-century cathedrals, particularly in France, often included a representation of the Last Judgement in their iconographic program. This is the case, for example, on the west façade of Chartres Cathedral, dating from 1200-20. Typically, Christ as judge occupies the central panel of the rose window.  
  
In this medallion, a young man about to emerge from an open green sarcophagus is depicted on a blue background. The body of the figure is oriented towards the right. This posture indicates that he is directing his attention to the centre of the image, where the Christ of the Judgement is enthroned. He is thus to the right of Christ, the place reserved for saved souls. He is naked, except for a mauve shroud that drapes his shoulders. His bent left arm is raised upwards, while his right arm, also slightly bent, leans on the back edge of the tomb. His bent left knee is sticking out of the sarcophagus, while his right leg is hidden. The face and gaze are directed upwards. Below the sarcophagus, the brown ground is decorated with a few herbs and flowers. A border of red glass frames the medallion.
4630ad06-c537-5e33-97c0-fd099cff5b57.method_for_datation: According to an analysis of the intensity of the colours and the refined draping of the shroud depicted on the medallion, which reflect the characteristics of the style around 1200.
4630ad06-c537-5e33-97c0-fd099cff5b57.method_for_provenance: The provenance remains vague because this medallion is marked by two different artistic styles, from Soissons and from Braine. The current state of research does not allow us to determine the work’s place of origin with certainty.
4630ad06-c537-5e33-97c0-fd099cff5b57.obtention: Purchased from the Collection Bucher-Sarasin in 1993

485104a2-c65b-5c03-9552-8fe4f6bc4b16.name: Narcissus
485104a2-c65b-5c03-9552-8fe4f6bc4b16.short_description:
Erwin Eisch (1927-2022) was instrumental in founding the studio glass movement, which sought to make artistic statements with glass and move away from the functional and decorative uses that had previously constrained glass-making.  
  
This sculptural form of 'Narcissus' is one of a number of works that Eisch based around the mythological story of Narcissus, as told in several ancient sources. In all accounts the protagonist Narcissus falls in love with his own reflection and unable to pull himself away from the allure of it he eventually passes away to be replaced by a flower that now bears the same name. Eisch's 'Narcissus' sculptures are larger-than-life multi-part figural pieces in which the glass material acts as both human and mirror. the first version was displayed as part of a complex installation in a domestic interior featuring other mixed-media components by Eisch. The V&A's version is the third 'Narcissus' produced by Eisch, and was displayed in a mirrored glass box. This component no longer exists, but at the museum the figure is instead displayed in a showcase with a mirrored surface on which Narcissus lays.
485104a2-c65b-5c03-9552-8fe4f6bc4b16.author: Simon Spier

4a08dfe7-ca45-5627-83cf-f527f59c053e.short_description: A miniature round bowl with a smooth rim. 4ad5424f-dc5c-51b8-ae7b-00f62d3a6860.name: Fragment of a glass floor tile with a plaster base.
4ad5424f-dc5c-51b8-ae7b-00f62d3a6860.description:
A fragment of a glass floor tile that was found amongst a group of glass tiles in the southern wing of the palace, in the formal reception hall no. 9, which was paved with glass tiles. The floor of the hall was first covered with a thick layer of plaster and then green glass tiles were placed on top. The bottom surface of the glass tiles is toothed to allow the glass to be embedded into the plaster. The upper face of the glass tiles is smooth but also wavy to prevent those walking on it from slipping.  
The Abbasid period is distinguished by prosperity and extravagance. Historical sources contain references to luxurious palaces, the floors of which were paved with glass tiles. Palace B, located in the Raqqa region, extending to the east of the Euphrates River and bordered by its tributary the Balikh River, is one such palace.
4ad5424f-dc5c-51b8-ae7b-00f62d3a6860.short_description: The use of glass floor tiles, reminiscent of the glass floor in King Solomon's legendary meeting with Queen Sheba as described in the Holy Qur'an, is here found at the 'Abbasid palaces of Raqqa.
4ad5424f-dc5c-51b8-ae7b-00f62d3a6860.method_for_datation: An inscription found in the palace refers to the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tasim and scholars date the palace to around 220 / 835.
4ad5424f-dc5c-51b8-ae7b-00f62d3a6860.method_for_provenance: The tile fragment was found in Palace B and was probably produced *in situ*.
4ad5424f-dc5c-51b8-ae7b-00f62d3a6860.obtention: The tile fragment was found during archaeological excavations undertaken during the 1950s by the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities under the direction of Nasib Salibi.

4b603a95-53d0-5a95-be2d-d52aff93ad2c.name: Sprinkler
4b603a95-53d0-5a95-be2d-d52aff93ad2c.short_description: A sprinkler made of brownish glass with enamel decoration of sprigs with flowers. The sprinkler is made in a Bohemian workshop and imitates the glass production of the Istanbul workshops – the Beykoz glass. The shape with the screw stopper is identical to the Ottoman prototypes while the decoration is different and more naturalistic. Made in Bohemian workshops. A complex and well organized sales network was spread in the eastern Mediterranean and constituted a binding link between western knowledge and Islamic aesthetics preserving a lucrative market for European works of glass with shapes and decoration of oriental inspiration.
4b603a95-53d0-5a95-be2d-d52aff93ad2c.author: Mina Moraitou

4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.name: Mosque lamp.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.description:
Glass mosque lamps with enamel decoration were mainly made during the Mamluk period in Egypt or Syria. They were made on commission and were presented by Mamluk sultans as gifts to Cairo mosques.  
The most famous of the Museum of Islamic Art’s mosque lamps is made of honey-coloured glass, with a foot shaped like an inverse chalice and a belly-shaped body that turns, above an indentation, into a long conical neck. On the body there are six eyelets laid on and pressed into escutcheon-shaped spaces. Chains were attached to these in order to hang the lamp from the ceiling. An additional funnel-shaped small oil lamp, which emitted the light, was hung within this lamp.  
The decoration consists of two frieze inscriptions, and of flowers painted on a small scale that betray a Far Eastern influence through their lotus blossom motif. The frieze inscription over the body of the lamp has been done in gold over a blue background. It mentions the name of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, who ruled at various intervals (r. AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309 and AH 709–41 / AD 1310–41). The mosque lamp could have been commissioned for a mosque or school that contained or had an adjoining mausoleum. These kinds of building complexes were constructed in Cairo in AH 704 / AD 1304 and between AH 718 and 736 / AD 1318–35. The inscription in blue over a tendril ending in spirals and a background that was originally painted in gold is particularly apt for a mosque lamp as its subject matter is based on the ‘Light verse’ from the Qur’an (Sura 24, verse 35). Both inscriptions are written in the *thuluth* script typical of the Mamluk period.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.short_description: Glass lamps were produced for mosques, shrines and mausoleums. An inner container held the oil and wick. According to the inscription on its body, this lamp was made in the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. It is also adorned by the Light verse of the Qur’an (Sura 24 v.35).
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.initial_owner: Count F. von Pourtales, St. Petersburg.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.dates: Hegira first half of the 8th century / AD first half of the 14th century.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.method_for_datation: A large number of glass mosque lamps were made during the Mamluk era. This one states the name of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, who ruled in the 8th / 14th century.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.method_for_provenance: Mosque lamps were probably made in Syria as well as in Egypt. It is not yet possible to assign a precise origin to this piece.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.obtention: A gift from Count F. von Pourtales in 1913.

4bc307ac-f977-5e18-aec7-21b9827679aa.name: Cup with turned-out rim

4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.name: La Crucifixión
4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.description:
This piece was exhibited at the International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts exhibition in Paris, 1925, and won a Gran Prix Award.  
The Taller Mauméjean dates back to 1860, when Jules Pierre Mauméjean, aged 23, opened his first workshop in Pau (France). Jules Pierre Mauméjean was married to Marie Honorine Lalanne in Pau on 23rd July 1868 and they went on to have five children. All of their sons followed the same artistic career path as their father. However, although Joseph, Henri and Carl worked together, Léon remained independent in Paris, where he passed away on 1st March 1921.  
In 1890, Jules Pierre Mauméjean opened a workshop in Anglet, which he later moved to Biarritz in 1893. He passed away in San Sebastián in 1909, at age 72. Jules Mauméjean maintained permanent contact with the circles in Madrid that offered him various commissions and led to him becoming the official glass painter at the Casa Real de Alfonso XII.  
Joseph, known as José Mauméjean, the firstborn of the family, spent numerous periods in Madrid. Not only did he spend time in the city to keep an eye on his workshops, but also to capture new clients. It was here that he met Augustine Jeanne Pastora Vic, daughter of Joseph Julien Vic, from Hendaya, then general agent of Saint-Gobain Glass in the Spanish capital. Born of his marriage to Marie, Joseph opened a new Mauméjean workshop in Madrid in 1898, located on Calle Abascal, Nº39, before moving to Paseo de la Castellana, Nº24, where he created the pieces currently located in the Museum.  
Some years later, the Hermanos Mauméjean opened more branches in Barcelona, followed by San Sebastian. These workshops formed part of the S.A. Mauméjean Hermanos, with their headquarters in Madrid.  
The Hermanos Mauméjean opened a new workshop in Paris, registered in 1921. This was a Venetian Enamel-Mosaics workshop, changing its name to S.A. Mauméjean two years later, with headquarters in the same building. Shortly after, they opened a new, successful workshop in Hendaya.  
Henri led the workshop in Mauméjean and passed away in 1932, leaving the workshop to his brother José, who passed away in 1952, aged 83, followed by Carl five years later and his son Georges, in 1970.  
The Mauméjean dynasty were involved in many national and international exhibitions. The most notable international exhibitions included Madrid in 1894, Paris in 1925 and 1937, Philadelphia y Pamplona in 1926, Milan and Madrid in 1927 and Seville in 1930.  
In Spain, the Mauméjean workshops in Madrid, Barcelona and San Sebastian provided stained glass to all major Spanish cities. Depending on the buyer, the workshop created stained glass with different themes and styles. These themes were predominantly religious, heraldic, labour-related, commercial and fundamentally ornamental. All of the styles have a historicist feel, reminding us of the Gothic, Renaissance, Classicism, etc.
4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja
4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.bibliography:

4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.author: Paloma Pastor Rey de Viñas

4c65bc42-3da5-5499-a6f9-1f8b1d142feb.name: Saint Disco Ruby Sioux, Descendent of Clan Campbell
4c65bc42-3da5-5499-a6f9-1f8b1d142feb.short_description: The emerging American stained-glass artist Lauren Puckett is known for her colourful figurative stained-glass portraits that explore narratives of identity, our relationship to cultural heritage, and the importance of place within these personal constructs. ‘Saint Disco Ruby Sioux, Descendent of Clan Campbell’ was remarkably created during the periods in and out of the 2020 and 2021 UK Lockdowns by the artist, with limited resources and access to equipment.  And explores the impact and implications that this situation has had upon the younger generation. Cleverly using traditional symbols as indicators of this period, we see St Disco holding a snake in one hand and an arrow in the other - representing Covid-19 and medicine. Her head is encircled with a halo that contains within the cycle of the moon – the observation and endurance of the slowing of time that we have all experienced. The magpies at her feet represent on one hand the dream state in which we have just lived - not conscious but still aware of what is transpiring. And on another, healing and good luck to come -  signifiers that we will all get through this. Her dress is made up the textiles that reflect her cultural heritage both here in Scotland and within America, as do the foliage that surrounds her.
4c65bc42-3da5-5499-a6f9-1f8b1d142feb.author: Sarah Rothwell
keywords: Contemporary Glass; Studio Glass; Art Glass
materials: Stained glass, enamel, lead, steel frame

4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.name: Glass weight.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.description:
A glass weight produced in Egypt between the AH 2nd and 9th / AD 8th and 15th centuries, which would have been used to check the weights of prototype gold, silver, and copper coins. A gold *dinar* would typically weigh 4.25 g and a silver *dirham* would have weighed 2.97 g. Metal coins were hand-minted and it was, therefore, difficult to ensure the exact accuracy of the weight; tampering with the weight of hand-minted coins was also a problem. Glass weights such as this one were developed to monitor the accuracy of metal coinage, and were used by the sellers to make sure that the correct vale of metal was being paid in return for the goods being purchased. The Arabic texts stamped on these weights usually bore the name of the ruler or official who ordered their issue and were usually re-issued every time the ruler or official changed office. This particular example is orange in colour and has a stamped Arabic inscription on one side (still to be deciphered), while the back is flat and plain.  
  
These glass weights testify to Fustat's position as one of the richest cities of the Middle East during the Fatimid period (AH 296–566 / AD 909–1171). A busy port, the markets of Fustat traded a wide variety of goods that arrived from all over the world, from places as far away as China. Fustat was also an important manufacturing centre, producing fine ceramics, glassware, steel and copper products, soap, sugar, textiles and paper.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.short_description: This glass weight was made in AH 5th- / AD 11th-century Egypt. Merchants and shopkeepers used such weights to check the weight of gold or silver coins, making sure that they were of the right weight and nobody had tampered with their precious metal. They were marked with the same designs as on the coins.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: many comparable examples have been found in Fustat, Egypt, which have been dated to the Fatimid period after deciphering the scripts stamped on them.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.obtention: Donated to Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in 1929.

4e6e9d64-d9e6-52dc-bf77-c7cc94285b9d.name: Perfume Sprinkler
4e6e9d64-d9e6-52dc-bf77-c7cc94285b9d.description: This vessel from the Aga Khan Museum Collection has the typical features of a perfume sprinkler, a glass vessel created to hold and dispense perfume: a globular body that has been flattened on two sides and a long tapering neck with a bulge near its base. The bottom of the body has a shallow kick marked by the pontil, a hot metal rod with some glass attached to it. This was necessary to manipulate the details of the vessel and the neck, parts of which are missing.
materials: Glass, greenish, thin patchy silvery iridescence; free-blown, tooled, worked on the pontil

4ee99078-4b66-5d16-830e-595e4da0246e.name: Mosque Lamp
4ee99078-4b66-5d16-830e-595e4da0246e.short_description: This vase-shaped lamp belongs to a well-established lamp type made in the Mamluk workshops of Syria and Egypt, both great centres of glass making. The colourful palette of blue, red, green, yellow, and white with gilding remains subtle due to a considered distribution. Green and yellow, for example, are restrained, creating bright spots. The layout of calligraphy, from strong scrolls to arabesque and delicate lotus flowers, reflects precise planning in the layering clear in details such as the leaves that spread over the letters, themselves positioned over an arabesque background. The pseudo-*kufic* compositions, painted in blue and brick-red, placed prominently on the body of the lamp, are an original feature which creates a complementary visual contrast with the *thuluth* script (on the neck of the lamp), which reads: “mimma umila bi-rasm al-maqarr al-‘ali al-mawlawi al-‘amiri al-kabiri al-maliki" (What was made for his Excellency, the Elevated, the Servant of the Lord, the Great Amir, the Possessor). This lamp was commissioned by an unknown prince, likely intended to decorate the interior of his mosque or madrasa.

4f3557cc-0936-578a-a571-6681edacbf66.name: Lamp
4f3557cc-0936-578a-a571-6681edacbf66.description:
This kerosene lamp consists of a pear-shaped, mould-blown light blue glass body and cylindrical, colourless glass chimney. The burner is made of brass with decoratively finished ends. The lamp’s base is painted with enamel colours. The decoration was made according to templates in the familiar Mary Gregory style, depicting a child’s figure painted with white and grey-green tones. The base of the item is marked with a thin gilding strip characteristic of the Nacko Janković factory products.  
Decorated lamps such as these have their origins in Bohemian glass dating from the late 1870s in the glasshouse of Carl Hosch from Haida. This decorating technique was also familiar to other European glasshouses, and it appears in the factory of Nacko Janković & Son in Jagodina as supported by the decoration of this kerosene lamp at the end of the 19th century during the factory’s high level of production.
4f3557cc-0936-578a-a571-6681edacbf66.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.
4f3557cc-0936-578a-a571-6681edacbf66.method_for_provenance: By stylistic analysis and material dating

4f3557cc-0936-578a-a571-6681edacbf66.workshop: Manufactury of Nacko Janković & Son, Serbia
4f3557cc-0936-578a-a571-6681edacbf66.author: Biljana Crvenković

4fd53bcf-1bb0-5651-b370-d45f867c397c.name: Ewer
4fd53bcf-1bb0-5651-b370-d45f867c397c.short_description: Intaglio —the decoration of glass or gemstones via abrasion rather than cutting — is a laborious process only undertaken by the most masterful artisans. As with many aspects of glassmaking, the artists of mediaeval Iran expanded upon their pre-Islamic Sasanian traditions in the execution of finely crafted and elaborately decorated glass vessels. This example, with its gently rounded, pear-shaped body blown in pale blue glass, combines the techniques of both wheel-cutting and  wheel-abrasion in the elaborate decoration which covers nearly its entire surface: rosettes, floral buds, and almond-shaped patterns carpet the entire body, ceasing only at the neck and applied strap handle. A final flourish — a vertical, palmette-like sprig of vegetation — tops the handle. The closest parallel to this decorative programme is found on the contemporary carved rock crystal ewers so famed from Fatimid Egypt. It is possible that this vessel was intended as a beautiful, but lower cost, imitation of such wares from the distant Mediterranean.

509beb40-554b-58f8-a7ab-95550e4bee0f.name: Bowlegarnitur
509beb40-554b-58f8-a7ab-95550e4bee0f.description: An essential association for the foundation and development of Czech modern art was the one of Artěl – an initiative that was founded by two men: Alois Dyk, an art enthusiast, and banker. and Vilem Štech, an art theoretician and art historian also responsible for endorsing young Czech modernism. Several artists joined in the beginning, such as Pavel Janak, Jan Konupek and Helena Johnova. The name of the association was taken from Tolstoy’s novel *Anna Karenina* and meant a merely verbally agreed-upon community of people who work together and jointly vouch for each other, as well as have an equal share of the income. Since they lacked the finances, the Artěl could not afford their own workshop, and therefore performed manufacturing in different factories, such as the Rydl and Thon Company in Svijany-Podoli in Northern Bohemia for ceramics and porcelain, and the Pryl glass factory in Růženin in Central Bohemia for glass. Among the various artists that participated in Artěl, Josef Rosipal, even though he was an architect, was of particular importance for the implementation of the association’s ideas in the medium of glass. Rosipal’s most famous pieces are his cut services, created in simple shapes, commonly overlayed in red or blue with cut geometric decorative motifs Additionally, since the sentiment of the Artěl association was oriented more towards expressionism, and, even more, cubism, these tendencies can be seen most clearly in the decorative motifs of the glass. This long glass piece, part of a set consisting of a punch bowl, lid, spoon, and five other glasses, closely follows the cubistic tendencies in glass decoration of the Czech modernist applied arts, which Josef Rosipal applied gracefully.

514a81db-7510-53f7-ac77-3b802711bb9f.name: Bottle for perfumes or ointments
514a81db-7510-53f7-ac77-3b802711bb9f.short_description: This green glass bottle has iridescent turquoise and pink patterning due to a phenomenon of alteration of the original material. Typical of the Islamic medieval style, the bottle’s elongated pear-shape is used for objects intended to contain ointments or liquid perfumes. However, no direct comparisons have been made between this bottle and other examples intended for the same use. Islamic glass from the Middle Ages was highly appreciated in Asia, Europe and the Mediterranean for its high level of technical and artistic qualities. As one of the most productive sectors of trade, glass was both a luxury good exemplifying the technical, formal and decorative innovations of the Islamic masters, and a practical object created to contain oils, perfumes and liquids of all kinds. For its modest workmanship, the bottle examined here falls into the latter category for everyday use.

5154be5c-412b-5da8-b4a0-223cd042a640.name: Bucket
5154be5c-412b-5da8-b4a0-223cd042a640.short_description: With only four other Mamluk enamelled glass buckets known to exist, this object is a true rarity. This type of glasswork was commonly used as a finger bowl to rinse hands before and after meals, as suggested by the inscription around the middle: “ana ahtawi alma'a" (I contain water). Much of the technical and stylistic methods are common in glass of this period, thus helping to verify this piece. Designs analogous to those found here, in terms of monumental calligraphy, knotwork, palmette friezes, scrolls, lions in roundels and gold animals outlined in red can all be found on other Mamluk glass pieces. Every design element on the bucket can be found on other pieces of enamelled glass from this period, from the thick treatment of the enamels to the details of the motifs. While there was originally some debate as to the age, the distinctive base and comparison to metalwork seem to indicate a mid-eighth century AH / mid-fourteenth century AD manufacture.  The thick, red enamel ground, which was made using the impasto technique, is demonstrative of the enameller’s great skill and has been observed on only a small number of glass objects.

51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.name: ‘Keff’ or hand-palm amulet.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.description:
A small, moulded glass 'keff' hand, which would have been threaded with many others like it to make a chain or necklace; it may also have been sewn on to a garment or a headdress. The main function of the keff is to protect the wearer against the 'evil eye' by stopping the damage that evil thoughts and deeds can do to the wearer. This hand is made of coloured glass, which has been cast into a mould. The loop has been made by twisting the base of the hand (the wrist area) on itself; the loop is at the front of the hand in the palm area, and once threaded, the fingers of the hand would point down.  
  
The keff pre-dates Islam and has been fully incorporated into Islamic popular culture, used widely as a protective charm throughout the Middle East and North Africa. Although the keff is particularly prevalent on jewellery it also appears on paper charms and talismans, on textiles and embroidery, and on vernacular architecture.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.short_description: In popular Islamic cultures of the Middle East, small glass amulets such as this one would have been used both as decoration and for protection. The main function of the *keff* is to protect the wearer against the 'evil eye' by stopping the damage that evil thoughts and deeds can do to the wearer.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.dates: Hegira, late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th–early 20th century.

51a185b1-97b5-5ccf-b75f-501f4aa856ad.name: Le bouquet de Chagall
51a185b1-97b5-5ccf-b75f-501f4aa856ad.short_description:
This stained glass, owned by the Vitromusée Romont, is one of the few by the artist not to be integrated into a building. Only 13 stained glass panels of this type exist in private collections. These small, self-contained works served as a form of recreation for the artist, where he could let his imagination run free, unconstrained by a commission.  
  
This work is a leaded stained glass panel of irregular shape, composed of two pieces of double-glazed pink glass painted with grisaille and silver stain yellow. On the right, the work depicts a head in profile, looking to the left and wearing a hat. The left side is occupied by a bouquet of flowers held by a hand visible below. At the top, a bird flies to the right, topped by a small crescent moon. The artist's signature is visible at the bottom of the panel.

51a185b1-97b5-5ccf-b75f-501f4aa856ad.method_for_provenance: According to the signature, the documentary film (2012) and the research conducted.

5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.name: Kerosene lamp
5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.short_description: A cylindrical container filled with gas and injected with air heats a group of emerging pipes from the cylinder, which are surrounded by glass to shield them from air and assist in hashing its light into place. Kerosene lamps were used to light the streets of Amman until the first electricity generator began to operate. The beginning of the 20th century marked the re-urbanisation of Amman after 500 years of abandonment.
