539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.name: Bottle.
539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.description: A small cylindrical rock-crystal bottle, narrowing at the foot, with a silver mount. Carved with angular bevelled incisions on the sides is an abstract design, resembling a stylised leaf form. Rock-crystal is the purest kind of quartz and was particularly popular during the Fatimid period. The historian al-Maqrizi (AH 766–845 / AD 1364-1442) recounts that amongst the treasures of the Fatimid caliphs of Egypt were: '17,000 boxes, each one containing rock-crystal either decorated in relief, or plain'. It was also highly prized in Europe. Many of the surviving pieces of Islamic rock-crystal can be found in church treasuries in Europe where they were adapted for liturgical purposes, such as reliquaries. The silver mount on this object would have been added when the object reached Europe.
539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.short_description: Rock-crystal was highly valued during the Fatimid period but also sought after in Europe. Many rock-crystal objects made during the Fatimid period were later acquired by church treasuries, and often adapted for reliquaries.
539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.method_for_datation: Church inventories record pieces of rock-crystal arriving in Europe from Islamic countries by the second half of the 4th / 10th century. Although not identical in style, this bottle can be associated with a carved rock-crystal ewer in the treasury of San Marco, Venice, which bears the name of the Fatimid Caliph al-'Aziz (r. 365–86 / 975–86).
539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.method_for_provenance: That carved rock-crystal was fostered by Fatimid patrons in Egypt, probably in the capital Cairo, is proven by the existence of a few dated objects together with descriptions of the court treasuries.
539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.obtention: Acquired by the British Museum in 1894.
539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.bibliography: Contadini, A. *Fatimid Art at the Victoria and Albert Museum*, London, 1998, pp.26–36.
539cc0cc-894e-5945-b4c9-b62fae0a412d.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Incision; carving; rock-crystal; reliquary; religious object; sumptuary art

54061b49-5654-5a34-bb57-ed20127e9164.name: Gülabdan
54061b49-5654-5a34-bb57-ed20127e9164.short_description: It is known that there were workshops producing glass vessels around Beykoz in Istanbul in the 19th century. The first glass workshop was founded by Mevlevi Dervish Mehmed Dede during the reign of Selim III (1789-1807). There were European glass craftsmen working in those workshops as well. Cups, bottles, jugs, etc. made of colourful, colourless and opal glass were among Beykoz' productions. This *gülabdan* (a small flask for sprinkling rose water) is a Beykoz production. Its body is milk white on which floral patterns in dark pink, green and yellow were placed.
keywords: Beykoz ceramic; Turkish decorative arts

54217a87-4b7b-5e01-98db-28a4bcf5f9b0.name: Unguentarium
54217a87-4b7b-5e01-98db-28a4bcf5f9b0.description: This perfume bottle was blown from dark green transparent glass of good quality. It has a slender piriform body two-thirds of total height, a small rim folded out and flattened and a slightly flattened narrow base. Its short tubular neck was tooled at bottom. Part of the rim is broken and missing. The term "unguentarium" is mainly applied to a small vessel that held perfumed oils and cosmetic lotions. These vessels were found in relatively large quantities in the entire Mediterranean, where they were produced between the early Hellenistic and early Medieval periods. The glass unguentarium became popular by the 1st century AD, after the invention of a blowing technique which was originated in the Syro-Palestinian region before the middle of the 1st century BC. Formerly in the collection of Hüseyin Kocabaş.

5465e2c8-3a21-59c5-9071-fc1448c0a163.name: *Botijo* (*càntir*)
5465e2c8-3a21-59c5-9071-fc1448c0a163.description:
Inverted piriform, blown glass *botijo* (pitcher) with spiral moulding. Decorated with strands of crimped glass. Conical, near vertical neck and spout, with vertical, ring-shaped handle of circular cross-section, topped with a bird-shaped ornament.  
  
The *botijo* (càntir in Catalan) is a vessel for holding and drinking water. Along with the *porrón* (porró) and the *almorraja* (almorratxa), it is one of most typical Catalonian glass forms. High quality glass was made in Catalonia “a la façon de Venise” until the 17th century. Paste quality deteriorated beginning in the 18th century and glass became more folkish in nature. Throughout its evolution, the formal imagination exploded, allowing for a plethora of adornments applied to the surfaces of these pieces.
5465e2c8-3a21-59c5-9071-fc1448c0a163.obtention: Purchase, 1935. From the José Sánchez Garrigos collection.

keywords: Blown glass; folk style; Catalonia

552161b5-1f28-593b-b0d4-243b48261076.name: Perfume sprinkler '*qumqum*'
552161b5-1f28-593b-b0d4-243b48261076.short_description:
The body of this perfume flask or sprinkler was created by flattening a blown glass ball, from which a thin long neck was then drawn. On both sides of the body there are large relief inscriptions in Arabic, applied in blue enamel on a gold background: “The sovereign is fair, glory to his victory”. The inscriptions are bordered with an ornament of green trefoils.  
The shape of the vessel is believed to have originated in Syria in the 12th century. The 13th and 14th centuries witnessed flourishing of new décor, namely enamelling and gilding. As leading centres historians mention Aleppo and Damascus.  
At the same time, the tradition of using fragrances and aromatic substances as well as preserving them in glass vessels came to the Islamic world long before - from the Late Antiquity.  
In medieval Islamic culture, substances such as musk, amber, sandalwood or aloe were used not only as perfume but also as culinary ingredients, medicines and aphrodisiacs. In terms of concentration and value, these substances formed the basis of a mixture when dissolved in water in similar flasks or sprinklers.  
Although the sprinkler could contain a whole spectrum of different substances, most likely it was rose water. Obviously, the invention of Islamic civilization, rose water was made by heating fresh rose petals in a water bath, resulting in aromatic vapor condensing. In addition to being used in gastronomy, rose water was also used at certain stages in the process of serving and consuming food. For example, when guests were finishing their meal, they were offered to wash their hands and mouths with saline, flavoured with rose water. Or servants might walk around guests spraying their clothes with refreshing aromatic liquid.

556fb615-d7c2-5db3-b216-71ca0ef5be91.name: *Faun* statuette
556fb615-d7c2-5db3-b216-71ca0ef5be91.short_description: This statuette of a young faun (Pan) seated playing his pipes on a tree trunk among roots and foliage is in clear glass moulded in high relief and patined. Inspired by the classic repertoire, the figure also evokes the Rococo style.

55cedd5d-21f4-5e7f-b4c3-ab9f62c1548c.name: Modiolus
55cedd5d-21f4-5e7f-b4c3-ab9f62c1548c.description:
The Modiolus cup is a large glass cup, which was used for measuring and/or drinking liquids and/or pouring libations. This one is made of pale blue-green translucent glass by applying the free-blowing technique. It has a conical body, its rim is folded out and its base is supported by a thickly made foot. Below the flaring rim is decorated with a fairly even wheel art line. The later-applied handle has a subtle flagged decoration limited to the top part. It is in an intact situation, but some soil-encrusted weathering, blowing striations, partly flaked off dulling and a jagged pontil scar are also seen on the surface.  
After the free-blowing technique has been found, possibly around in the first quarter of the 1st century BC, the mould-blowing technique has developed and the desired glass forms and patterns were obtained by blowing into glass, terracotta, stone, metal or wood moulds. The melt at the end of the blowing rod is inflated in two or more pieces of the container until it covers the mould.  
The use of angular and patterned moulds has usually made it unnecessary to apply additional ornaments. With this technique, mass production of glasses with the same form, measurement, and decoration can be produced by using a single mould. In the form of quadrangular shaped moulds, the glass workshop's or the manufacturer's names were added by applying letters and symbols on the pedestal portion. Glassware that has been blown into a mould whose interior has a raised pattern so that the object shows the pattern with a concavity on the inside, underlying the convexity on the outside. Pattern moulds are not used to impart the final form to the object.

55dc9af5-2f7e-57e8-aec1-9a5889250732.name: Glass bowl in Millefiori technique
55dc9af5-2f7e-57e8-aec1-9a5889250732.short_description: The Millefiori technique was rediscovered in the eighth or ninth century in Mesopotamia and was probably used in the production of objects for the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad and Samarra. A number of surviving bowls and tiles suggest that the technique was used in both domestic furnishings and interior decoration. Examples such as this one demonstrate the sophistication and range of Abbasid glassmakers.

565dbb7d-9e5e-5655-9fed-f51efe12542a.name: Decanter
565dbb7d-9e5e-5655-9fed-f51efe12542a.description: This bottle made of crystal glass with round ornaments is a rare example of glass craftmanship from the Avram Petronijević Manufacture. The bottle's massive, ball-shaped body decorated with ground ellipses and high cylindrical neck capped by a ground mushroom-shaped stopper rests on a multisided, elevated base. The making of this bottle was entrusted to one of the more skilled craftsmen with experience in this kind of design and decoration. Since there were no glassmakers in Serbia at the time, craftsmen from the Czech and Bavarian workshops ran production. Although they were not the top craftsmen essential for the production in the European glasshouses, they were sufficiently experienced to transfer knowledge. For this reason, few items from the Petronijević Manufacture evidence a high level of craftsmanship. This bottle is one of those items, presented as a best man's wedding present by the manufacture owner, Avram Petronijević, to a prominent Belgrade family.

56fb3790-9116-5191-bac3-6c97bf4d4fb4.name: Flask Bottle
56fb3790-9116-5191-bac3-6c97bf4d4fb4.short_description: This gilded blue flask is said to have been made in or near what is today the small Syrian city of Raqqa, situated on the Euphrates in north-east Syria. In the mid-sixth century AH / mid-twelfth century AD, the city was a thriving centre for the production of pottery and glass, constantly refreshed by the appearance of craftsmen leaving the ailing Fatimid Empire in search of opportunities. The striking deep blue of the glass is extremely rare. Only about twenty such pieces are known from the Ayyubid and early Mamluk periods. The decoration of this flask — opposed birds flanking a pomegranate tree, evoking both earthly and heavenly gardens — corresponds to a gilded bottle in the British Museum inscribed to Atabeg 'Imad al-Din Zang, the founder of the Zangid dynasty and Turkish governor of Mosul (AH r. 520-540 / AD r. 1127-1146), making this bottle the only confirmed and datable example of sixth century AH / twelfth century AD Syrian gilded glassware.

572d0642-eeed-51ff-b840-e50c47614c23.name: Reverse painting on glass: The Arab hero Abdallah Ibn Jaafar and the Christian princess Yamina
572d0642-eeed-51ff-b840-e50c47614c23.short_description: As Tunisia fell under French rule in 1881, reverse paintings on glass were fashionable in Tunis and Sfax. The story of Abdallah and Princess Yamina was beloved. In 647, the first onslaught of Muslim Arabs reached the Byzantine province of Africa. Near today's city of Sbeïtla, they scored a decisive victory over the Eastern Roman commander-in-chief Gregorius. The event embedded itself deeply in the collective consciousness of the population, and at the time of the French Protectorate it was again unearthed. An image shows the Arab hero Abdallah ibn Jaafar and the Christian Princess Yamina fleeing on horseback. The pair miraculously saved themselves from the Eastern Roman pursuers. Abdallah kidnapped an infidel, conquered the enemy and wounded his dignity. Around 1900, this pictorial image was commonly displayed between Tunis and Algiers as a visual protest against the French colonial powers.

5759f401-121f-5cef-8f4b-62d3d8fa9962.name: Spoon

57cc5438-464a-5ea2-89ca-6cfeff071f02.name: Beaker; Cup
57cc5438-464a-5ea2-89ca-6cfeff071f02.description: During the 17th century AD, the art of glass thoroughly developed on the European peninsula, forming different movements and schools throughout the region. Among the most distinguished, Germany secured itself a strong position, producing glass with the spirit of Venetian glassmakers, yet simultaneously establishing its own singularities that have come to be recognised as symbols of German glassmaking of the late Baroque period. An outstanding practice developed in Bavaria, particularly Nurnberg, carries the name Scharzlotmalerei, meaning painting in black or sepia. This technique was borrowed from stained-glass artists and was used to decorate small cylindrical beakers often resting on three hollow ball feet, which became a preferred shape locally. The most famous artist of this glasswork school was Johann Schaper, whose opus can be recognised by paintings of delicate architectural and landscape compositions on glass with details etched using a fine point. Schaper has many followers who strived to accomplish his level of sophistication. Among the most distinguished of these artists are J. L. Faber, Hermann Bencherlt, Johan Keyll and Abraham Helmhack. Following the form of the favoured local style of glasswork, this beaker is decorated with a schwarzlot-frieze consisting of a miniature landscape of Purkersdorf on one side and bacchanal children on the other. The creator of this particular example is unknown. Based on sources, it is unlikely that Johann Schaper was the creator since he died in AD 1670 and the beaker is estimated to originate from AD 1678. This piece may be associated with one of his followers or later copiers who found inspiration in the craftsman’s work.
57cc5438-464a-5ea2-89ca-6cfeff071f02.author: Rainald Franz, Jana Zarkovic

57e870a3-328c-5454-8a46-128fb0cb4e2a.name: Pair of vases and pedestals
57e870a3-328c-5454-8a46-128fb0cb4e2a.description: The interlacing and the flower decoration of this pair of glass vases can be considered an example of the great influence exerted by the Turkish or Orientalist revival. The glass factories of the Austro-Hungarian Empire played an important role in the spreading of this style.

5a082aa0-76e8-53dd-96a8-55a9e05d3075.name: Bottle
5a082aa0-76e8-53dd-96a8-55a9e05d3075.short_description: The wheel-cut decorations of this aqua-coloured glass bottle remain nearly as crisp and distinct as when they were created a millennium ago. Requiring a steady hand and a steely nerve, the glassmaker would have held the free-blown, cooled glass vessel against a cutting wheel to achieve the pattern. Here, the decorative programme consists of vegetal and palmette motifs which are contemporaneous with similar designs found in a variety of media — from stucco to woodwork — clearly fashionable during the fourth and fifth centuries AH / tenth and eleventh centuries AD in Iran and Central Asia. The long neck as well as the border areas of the body are decorated with contrasting motifs which are sharper-edged and geometric. The bottle was likely used to offer liquids—such as a cooling sherbet — to guests and to family members.
5a082aa0-76e8-53dd-96a8-55a9e05d3075.bibliography: Walton, Michelle, *Imperfect Perfection - Early Islamic Glass*, Doha: Bloomsbury Qatar Foundation Publishing, 2012: 114.
keywords: Glass; Bottle; Free-blown; Wheel-cut; Samanid; Ghaznavid

5a46142a-412e-5798-9e05-25ab88ab4043.name: Bottle Flask
5a46142a-412e-5798-9e05-25ab88ab4043.short_description: This free-blown, wheel-cut glass bottle flask belongs to a group of glassworks that was very common during the early Islamic period. It has a globular body atop a low foot, with a long straight neck and a splayed opening. The decoration of wheel-cut or wheel-engraved glass was executed with a rotary and abrasive tool after the glass had cooled. The body of this flask is decorated with wheel-cut facets in a honeycomb pattern. Simple grooves encircle the bottle just below and above the honeycomb pattern. The base of the neck is decorated with a row of vertical rectangular facets topped by a circular indentation. This fine glass flask is made of clear and translucent glass in a pale blue colour. A remarkable number of these globular bottles with wheel-cut facets in a honeycomb pattern with long straight necks and splayed openings varying in colour, sophistication, and complexity of cutting are extant from the late 1st - 4th century AH / 8th- 10th century AD. The use of honeycomb-cut facets dating back to a Roman practice was common on Sasanian models in Iran and Mesopotamia and was later revived by glasscutters during the early Islamic period.
keywords: Glass; Bottle; Free-blown; Wheel-cut; Buyid

5b0d5e0c-6994-552e-a40b-2d6ddbac7a9f.name: Footed beaker with cover
5b0d5e0c-6994-552e-a40b-2d6ddbac7a9f.short_description:
It is a stroke of luck that this footed beaker has been preserved with the original cover; only in combination does the harmonious overall impression to which the glass artist aspired actually emerge.  
The glass itself was probably made in a glassworks in the Hirschberger Valley in Silesia. The decoration, on the other hand, is likely the product of one of the many workshops in this area, possibly at Warmbrunn, which was known for the production of engraved decoration. In the second quarter of the 18th century, dozens of glasscutters worked here producing items for public consumers such as visitors to the Silesian baths. At the same time, they created works for the local sovereigns, the Counts Schaffgotsch, in whose territory all the glassworks and glass refinement factories of the Hirschberger Valley were located. The glass vessel shown here was probably intended for a member of this family since the main face of the bowl exhibits the pine tree from the family’s coat of arms and, above it, the motto of the Schaffgotsch: *“Aucun temps ne le change”*.

5c488fcb-98f8-5023-9532-c8105b5dcb91.name: *Scenes from the History of the Swiss Confederation*
5c488fcb-98f8-5023-9532-c8105b5dcb91.short_description:
This work, created for the Zurich bookseller Hans Felix Haller and his wife, Elisabeth Vogler, is important both artistically and historically. Through their choice of images, the donors demonstrate an attachment to the history of their country. Like a patriotic picture book, the panel tells the story of the birth of the Old Confederation and keeps the viewer interested in its glorious past. It presents six episodes of Swiss history in three strips of two images. The individual scenes, framed by columns, are explained by detailed captions above the scroll cartridges.  
  
The scene in the upper left corner depicts the blinding of Heinrich of Anderhalden. In the upper right, the farmer Konrad Baumgarten from Altzellen, on his way home, kills the bailiff Wolfenschiessen in the bath. His wife, whom the bailiff wanted to force to share the bath with him, is standing at the door of the house.  
  
In the central strip of the panel, on the left, William Tell shoots the apple from his boy’s head in the presence of the bailiff. In the background, Tell escapes imprisonment by jumping from Gessler’s boat. In the scene on the right, the rebel Tell kills Gessler while riding with his sidekick in the Hohle Gasse near Küssnacht.  
  
In the lower left-hand corner of the panel, the peasants bring the tithe to the bailiff of Landenberg. He feels safe, while in the background the people are storming the castles of Sarnen and Rossberg. In the final scene at the bottom right, the three Confederates, Werner Stauffacher, Walter Fürst and Arnold von Melchtal, take the Rütli oath.  
  
The foot of the panel is occupied by a scroll cartouche flanked by the coat of arms of Hans Felix Haller and Elisabeth Vogler, with the donors’ inscription and the artist’s signature.

5d16fd5f-c364-50b9-a21f-0b26a5d30e2c.name: Perfume Bottle
5d16fd5f-c364-50b9-a21f-0b26a5d30e2c.description:
In the middle of the 1st century BC glass-makers along the Syro-Palestinian coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated with air through a hollow blow-pipe. This invention of ‘free-blowing’ revolutionized the glass industry. It allowed vessels to be mass-produced thus rendering them less expensive and available to a wider market so that by the end of the 1st century AD free blown glass vessels were used widely throughout the Roman Empire. The majority were undecorated utilitarian pieces, used for storage and transport, and tablewares, like beakers and plates, but others were embellished with applied decoration. In the free blowing technique, the glass melt, which is taken to the end of the continuous rotating blowing rod, is formed by rolling on the processing table and then blowing. After the internal volume is formed, it is taken to the noble bar from the opposite direction of the blowing rod (usually from the bottom of the container) for operations such as cutting a portion and forming the opening. The forming rod is attached to the container by a drop of the glass melt. Then, in the other direction, the tip of the form is cut or broken to remove the blowing rod. Attachments such as mouth edge profile, base, and handle are also made with auxiliary rods if necessary and then the glass is allowed to cool.  
The type of vessels as seen on this case were used to store liquid perfumes, herbal medicine, liquid seasoning, olive-oil, cider-like fluids and/or as toilet bottles. The technique used to form the thick-walled bottle is the free-blowing technique; blowing striations, bubbles and black impurities are also seen on the surface. The bottle is dark blue-green colour and has a few tool marks at its base. Its rim is folded out, over and in, with bevelled outer lip and flattened into side of mouth. The bottle is in an intact position and has a cylindrical neck and conical body which slightly goes concave to the bottom. On the surfaces, there are some deep weathering and pitting but it also has brilliant iridescence.

5d425d12-049a-5704-9607-305414bcdb67.name: Beaker
5d425d12-049a-5704-9607-305414bcdb67.short_description: Mamluk beakers are one of the most prolific types of enamelled glass vessels with a wide variety of forms and decorations. This tubular glass beaker has a flared top and a rounded foot. The overall composition of enamelled and polychrome decorations is divided into two main registers outlined by narrow red bands. The first register shows a scene with two figures depicted using thin red lines, each with an enamel, red and blue robe and turban. One of the figures is holding a small beaker while the other sits with his legs crossed. Above them an inscription outlined in red on a blue background reads: “al-malik al-sultan" (The King, the Sultan). These beakers were used as drinking vessels as often depicted in other media from that time.
5d425d12-049a-5704-9607-305414bcdb67.dates: AH late 7th century AH / AD late 13th century

5e5917b9-2cd4-5571-8cdc-0958086b9ee7.name: Bottle
5e5917b9-2cd4-5571-8cdc-0958086b9ee7.short_description: The decoration was made by cutting away the outer layer of glass. The pattern, characteristic of early Abbasid art, was first developed for stucco reliefs that decorated buildings in the capital of Samarra. The bottle’s stylized birds and entwined, abstract vegetal ornaments are motifs that frequently appear in the art of the period.
keywords: Bottle; animal decoration; vegetal decoration; vegetal motifs; Samarra; glass
materials: Colorless glass, with relief-cut decoration in a green overlay (modern neck)

5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.name: Pilgrim bottle.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.description:
A free-blown, globular-shaped glass vessel with enamel decoration. One of the wider sides and the lower half of both narrower sides are flattened. The colours of the enamel are wide-ranging: red, white, blue, pale-green, yellow, pink, mauve, and greyish black. Two applied handles sit on either side of the cylindrical neck. An eleven-pointed rosette within an eight-lobed flower containing vegetal scrolls decorates the flattened side. Decorating the curved side is a four-sided lobed motif, with a geometric shape filled-in with arabesques and surrounded by scrolls, terminating in human, animal, or bird heads. On the left of the curved side is a horseman in the act of killing an animal with a spear, he has a beard and a halo around his head and wears a conical hat with ribbons. Below this figure is a medallion with a female harp player, wearing a veil and a long tunic. On the other narrow side is a horseman under a tree killing a lion with a javelin; birds are flying overhead. He has a halo and wears a long coat and boots. In the circular medallion below him is a man sitting cross-legged, with a beaker in one hand, drinking. His tunic has decorative tiraz bands on the sleeves.  
The two horsemen recall those found in Christian iconography, whereas the figures in the medallions are typical of figures depicted in Islamic art. The mixture of motifs suggests the patron was either a Muslim who was familiar with Christian imagery or a Christian who appreciated the work of Muslim craftsmen. The shape of this vessel recalls leather flasks or unglazed ceramic pilgrim bottles, rather than other glass and metal objects. Although made of glass, this flask may have been carried on journeys or pilgrimages in a leather container. It was certainly a luxury object, perhaps made specifically as a gift.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.short_description: This enamelled glass pilgrim bottle is an interesting example of the crossover of Christian and Islamic cultures. Two of the figures decorating the vessel derive from Christian iconography of St George and the dragon, whereas the musician and drinker are found in Islamic art.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.dates: Hegira third quarter 7th century / AD third quarter 13th century.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.dimensions: Height 23 cm, length 23 cm, width 16.2 cm.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.method_for_datation: The decoration resembles late Ayyubid and early Mamluk compositions.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.method_for_provenance: The technique and decoration are close to other glass objects produced in the Mamluk domains of Egypt and Syria.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by Felix Slade in 1869.

5e68d23f-cf28-560b-a2ba-3eb4bc3170a3.name: The Northumberland House Glass Drawing Room
5e68d23f-cf28-560b-a2ba-3eb4bc3170a3.short_description: The use of coloured plate glass as one of the core components in the decorative scheme of the drawing room in Northumberland House is perhaps indicative of the status of glass in Britain in the mid-18th century. Designed by Robert Adam (1728-1792) for the fashionable 1st Duke and Duchess of Northumberland, and completed in 1775, the glass drawing room provided the backdrop for the well-attended entertainments hosted at Northumberland House. The huge panels of glass are backed with red and green metal foils, and they were then overlaid in gilt metal ornament in the neo-classical style that Adam was so renowned for.
5e68d23f-cf28-560b-a2ba-3eb4bc3170a3.author: Simon Spier

5f1722b5-a763-5dbc-ba03-66feeafcd183.name: Carafe
5f1722b5-a763-5dbc-ba03-66feeafcd183.short_description: This carafe, in a design known as the 'Well Spring', by the painter and writer Richard Redgrave (1804-1888), later Surveyor of the Queen's Pictures, was one of the designs made for Summerly's Art Manufactures. Summerly's Art Manufactures was a company founded by the educator Henry Cole in 1847, using the pseudonym Felix Summerly, hoping to promote public taste by recruiting well known artists to design functional objects. Redgrave made this design in 1847 and it was soon sold to A. J. F. Christy of the Stangate Glassworks in Lambeth, who produced it until 1850.
5f1722b5-a763-5dbc-ba03-66feeafcd183.obtention: Given by Edmund Christy to the Museum of Practical Geology, transferred to the V&A in 1901.
5f1722b5-a763-5dbc-ba03-66feeafcd183.bibliography: Bryant, Julius, *Art and Design for all: The Victoria and Albert Museum*, London: V&A Publications, 2011: 112.
5f1722b5-a763-5dbc-ba03-66feeafcd183.author: Simon Spier

5f98dc73-695f-5b59-8b01-c6619be572ab.name: Flask
5f98dc73-695f-5b59-8b01-c6619be572ab.short_description: This glass flask is commonly referred to as a pilgrim flask, based on its association with similarly shaped vessels made in both leather and metal that were brought back by pilgrims returning from the Holy Land during the Crusades. Made of free-blown glass, this example has two flat sides — referred to in Italian documents as *botacio fracado, inghistera fracada* (in Venice, meaning “flat-sided bottle”) – with two small loop handles attached. The overall shape of this flask bears a strong resemblance to glass vessels made by the Mamluks during the seventh and eighth centuries AH / thirteenth and fourteenth centuries AD. Venice had long been on the receiving end of the Islamic glass industry, whether importing raw materials for glasswork or finished objects from Egypt and Syria. This particular flask takes inspiration in both its shape and enamel decoration from its Mamluk precursors, such as the small, flat-sided perfume sprinkler known as a *qumqum*. The flask’s enamel decoration, a technique which Mamluk glassworkers excelled in, was only taken up by Italian craftsmen around 864 AH / 1460 AD, when the island of Murano developed as Europe’s leading glass industry.
5f98dc73-695f-5b59-8b01-c6619be572ab.dimensions: Height: 31cm, Width: 18cm, Diameter (at the widest point): 10cm
keywords: Glass; Flask; Free-blown; Enamelled; Renaissance
materials: Glass; free-blown with enamelled and gilded decoration

602f0cff-8dd6-5146-849e-6d56c9bbed60.name: Beaker
602f0cff-8dd6-5146-849e-6d56c9bbed60.short_description:
This beaker is made of blue calcedonio glass, a type of glass invented in Venice that imitates the gemstone chalcedony. The glass is also di-chroic, which means two-coloured, as it appears blue under reflected light, but a red-orange when light passes through it. The painted enamel decoration depicts a scene from the story of Pyramus and Thisbe in the Roman poet Ovid's 8th century work *Metamophoses*. They are lovers who belong to rival families in the ancient city of Babylon. Upon arranging to meet in secrecy Pyramus wrongly believes Thisbe to be killed by a lion and falls on his sword. When Thisbe arrives and sees the dead Pyramus, she also takes her own life. the story provided the inspiration for William Shakespeare's *Romeo and Juliet*.  
  
The cup arrived at the museum with an early leather bag and wooden carrying case, signifying its careful preservation since a least the 17th century. A note was also included which was inscribed 'In this bag is the Ancient Cup of our Familye, putt into this bagg, August 21 1694, by me C. ffairfax', making this one of very few Venetian Renaissance glass objects with a 17th century English provenance.
602f0cff-8dd6-5146-849e-6d56c9bbed60.obtention: According to a note kept with the beaker, this cup was in the possession of the Fairfax family in 1694. Purchased by the museum in 1959.
602f0cff-8dd6-5146-849e-6d56c9bbed60.bibliography: Liefkes, Reino (ed), *Glass*, London: V&A Publications, 1997: pl. 52.
602f0cff-8dd6-5146-849e-6d56c9bbed60.author: Simon Spier
materials: Turquoise dichroic glass beaker, enamelled and gilt

60bef031-ec19-5d57-8b30-278d1bbc2dd6.name: Glass bottle
60bef031-ec19-5d57-8b30-278d1bbc2dd6.short_description: Glass produced in Bohemia blending European and Middle Eastern styles. Acquired by Franks.
keywords: Orientalism; blue; decanter; revival

61a60b22-23e1-5985-b88f-77e487119af5.name: Cup and cover
61a60b22-23e1-5985-b88f-77e487119af5.short_description:
This cup and cover is a virtuosic example of Venetian glass-making in the 15th century. The applied 'prunts', or small blobs of glass fused to a glass body, in this case in bright colours, are intended to simulate a vessel encrusted with jewels. Paired with the moulded ribs on the foot that are giled, a feature that appears in similar forms on contemporary gold and silver work, the bowl and cover gives an impression of a highly prized object displaying vast technical skill.  
  
The bowl and cover was formerly in the collection of Alessandro Castellani (1823-1883), a member of the famous family of antique dealers and goldsmiths. The fact it was owned by Castellani emphasises the jewel-like appearance and its status as a luxury object in the 15th century.
61a60b22-23e1-5985-b88f-77e487119af5.obtention: Bought in 1884 by the museum at the sale of the collection of Alessandro Castellani, part of the well known family of Roman jewellers.
61a60b22-23e1-5985-b88f-77e487119af5.author: Simon Spier
materials: Footed, covered cup in colourless glass with applied red, blue and green glass prunts, enamelled and gilt

61ad82dc-3c9e-593e-99e4-c5bbfddbc008.name: Goblet
61ad82dc-3c9e-593e-99e4-c5bbfddbc008.short_description:
At the end of the 17th century a conscious effort was made by English glass-sellers to end their dependence on import products from Venice. In 1673 the Glass-Sellers’ Company engaged the glass-maker George Ravenscroft to carry out research into creating a recipe to rival Venetian crystal glass. Ravenscroft was official glass-maker to the Company from 1674, and strove to not merely imitate Venetian imports but create something to better them. He operated two furnaces in London, the Savoy furnace, which was run by Venetian glass-workers, and another at Henley-on-Thames run by glass-workers from Altare. Here, Ravenscroft perfected a recipe for 'flint glass', which used large amounts of lead-oxide in order to stabilise the recipe and produce a glass which resembled rock crystal.  
  
Large goblets such as this one are representative of the austere shapes of glass items that proliferated in England at the end of the 17th century, and the thick and heavy proportions that was well suited to this new type of glass.
61ad82dc-3c9e-593e-99e4-c5bbfddbc008.bibliography: Lanmon, Dwight P., *The Golden Age of English Glass 1650-1775*, New York: Woodbridge, 2011.
61ad82dc-3c9e-593e-99e4-c5bbfddbc008.author: Simon Spier

61d517e1-9410-5522-abb9-809bf66d22a5.name: Ewer
61d517e1-9410-5522-abb9-809bf66d22a5.short_description: It is known that there were workshops producing glass vessels around Beykoz in Istanbul in the 19th century. The first glass workshop was founded by Mevlevi Dervish Mehmed Dede during the reign of Selim III (1789-1807). There were European glass craftsmen working in those workshops as well. Cups, bottles, jugs etc. made of colourful, colourless and opal glass were among Beykoz' productions. This is an ewer made of dark blue opaline with a water-drop-shaped lid. On its body there are raised flower patterns and *kabaras*.
keywords: Beykoz ceramic; Turkish decorative arts

62f5fc11-72ae-520a-869a-7dd3301203f5.name: Cycle
62f5fc11-72ae-520a-869a-7dd3301203f5.short_description: In the form of a cube cast into the mould into which have been placed coloured glass bars. For this to be achieved, flat glass bars placed in the mould when hot are curved while waiting within it.
62f5fc11-72ae-520a-869a-7dd3301203f5.author: Şeyma Nur Hançerli, Elif Akgül

6425f1ec-7b3a-5e78-bbb5-1c3e1ec83fde.name: Beaker
6425f1ec-7b3a-5e78-bbb5-1c3e1ec83fde.description: The practice of migration of Italian glassmakers to Central Europe was already well-established in the 15th century AD, reaching its peak in the 16th and 17th centuries AD. The three main geographical centres for these newly arrived glassmakers were Tirol, Hall and Innsbruck. Yet, the presence of these magnificent craftsmen was not consistent – in Hall the greatest concentration of Murano glassmakers was from AD 1534 to 1540, while in Innsbruck it was between AD 1570 and 1588. One of the most famous glass furnaces was founded by Wolfgang Vitl in AD 1534 in Hall, close to Tyrol. Showing off their extraordinary skills from Murano, next to Venice, and from the North, these artisans created many wonderful works of different shapes, sizes and decoration. This even-surfaced, cylindrical glass presents an ideal example of the outstanding craftsmanship employed by Italian glassmakers in the Alps. Painted with gold and cold enamel, the glass is decorated with the coat of arms of Cardinal Prince Bishop of Trento Christoph Madruzz inside of a large golden cartouche, topped with a cardinal’s hat above and finished with golden bands above and below. Its form indicates the high craftsmanship and skillset of the artist, and its decoration follows the traditions of the Alpine area.
6425f1ec-7b3a-5e78-bbb5-1c3e1ec83fde.bibliography: Forster, Ellinor, *Geschichte und Region/Storia e regione*, 26: 1 (2017).
6425f1ec-7b3a-5e78-bbb5-1c3e1ec83fde.author: Rainald Franz, Jana Zarkovic
materials: Glass; blown, enamel painting, gold decoration

649c683b-d1f3-512e-8170-458ed534da19.name: Welcome panel with alliance coat of arms
649c683b-d1f3-512e-8170-458ed534da19.short_description: Hans Dietlin and his wife Anna Prücker are poised to shake hands. Behind them is a majestic blossoming tree around which a ribbon bears the inscription *Nach Leid komt Fröd* (After sorrow comes joy).

64e3e4fa-1a13-5862-88d5-b4956e026fd7.name: Perfume Sprinkler with Design of Marvered White-Trail Feather Pattern
64e3e4fa-1a13-5862-88d5-b4956e026fd7.short_description: A doughnut-shaped bottle made of bubbly translucent amethyst glass, blown with marvered opaque white trail decoration and dragged into a feather pattern. Opposing S-shaped handles applied in amethyst glass at shoulder and pulled up to neck. The globular form is flattened and tooled into an asymmetrical donut-shaped body. The thin elongated neck, tooled to constrict at its base and thus flattening the shoulder, is pulled up into a long tapering form with the rim rounded by heating. The base is flattened and kicked retaining a pontil mark; four small prunts of amethyst glass are applied on the sides as vestigial, but useless feet. There are losses in the neck and the body.
64e3e4fa-1a13-5862-88d5-b4956e026fd7.dates: Hegira Late 5th to late 7th century / AD 12th–13th century
64e3e4fa-1a13-5862-88d5-b4956e026fd7.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.

64ff73da-b0a3-513e-946c-31bbb8b1a9f4.name: Mardi Graj
64ff73da-b0a3-513e-946c-31bbb8b1a9f4.short_description: The artifact is a lacliver vase decorated by white, embossed imagery. The mouth of the vase is covered with geometric motifs, the body with human figures and, finally, the base by a pattern of herbal leaves.
64ff73da-b0a3-513e-946c-31bbb8b1a9f4.author: Şeyma Nur Hançerli, Elif Akgül

65097c39-9df2-5f70-8a5e-e60449cb5770.name: Plate
65097c39-9df2-5f70-8a5e-e60449cb5770.short_description: This is one of a set of twenty-four plates commissioned by the antiquarian Horace Walpole (1717-1797) from the Miotti family glasshouse in Venice during a visit in 1741. Each plate is made from glass whitened with an arsenic compound which makes it opaque, and is decorated with a different view of Venice. These were likely never intended for use by Walpole, and by 1774 were on display in his China Room at his villa Strawberry Hill, west London. Amongst Walpole's vast collection of ceramics - particularly English and European porcelain - these plates would have imitated this luxury material with their white colouring.
65097c39-9df2-5f70-8a5e-e60449cb5770.obtention:
Commissioned by Horace Walpole in 1741, and on display in Strawberry Hill by 1774;  
Transferred to the V&A from the Museum of Practical Geology in 1901.

656be3c6-61c1-54ad-b1d9-a2b1dcaa12a9.name: Nature morte à la corbeille de verres et aux roses blanches
656be3c6-61c1-54ad-b1d9-a2b1dcaa12a9.short_description:
This is a still life consisting of a basket of glasses, a present-day picture postcard of Romont Castle, an empty lemonade bottle with the label “Fribourg” and a vase of white roses. A rose branch with a shoot and a withered petal lies next to it. The basket covers the upper edge of a postcard lying underneath, on which a biblical scene (the healing of Tobias) appears.  
  
The work consists of glass with facet cut. It was created for the inauguration of the permanent exhibition of reverse glass at the Vitromusée Romont in October 2006, when the museum was renovated and its collection extended to include not only stained glass but glass art in general. Two compositional elements reference this context: the postcard of Romont Castle, which houses the museum, and the postcard depicting a reverse painting on glass by Swiss artist Franz Thaddäus Menteler the Younger (1751–94) from 1780. The glass basket is also a reference to the 17th-century Alsatian Mannerist Sébastien Stoskopff.  
  
The painting is notable for the delicate light effects on the glasses and the play between translucence and reflection of the vase and bottle. In Yves Siffer’s work, almost all the objects depicted recall human activities and evoke everyday life. His still life works are often allegories of transience.
656be3c6-61c1-54ad-b1d9-a2b1dcaa12a9.bibliography:
Jolidon, Yves, "Meister einer subtilen Kunst: die Hinterglasmalerei Yves Siffer", in Vitromusée Romont (ed), *Yves Siffer: peintre sous verre = Yves Siffer: Hinterglasmaler*, exhibition catalogue, Romont : Vitromusée Romont, 2009: 43-58.  
Vitromusée Romont (ed), *Yves Siffer: peintre sous verre = Yves Siffer: Hinterglasmaler*, exhibition catalogue, Romont : Vitromusée Romont, 2009.
656be3c6-61c1-54ad-b1d9-a2b1dcaa12a9.author: Elisa Ambrosio
keywords: still life; bottle; flowers; glass; basket; postcard
materials: Reverse painting on glass in acrylic paint

663070ca-fa8f-5048-83d1-4c619ee34607.name: Stained glass panel
663070ca-fa8f-5048-83d1-4c619ee34607.short_description: This stained glass window is one of four that take their designs from a number of panels that depicted imaginary scenes from the life of King René of Anjou. Originally these were intended to adorn an oak cabinet created for the artist Myles Birket Foster (1825-1899) who commissioned Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. to decorate the interior of his Surrey home, 'The Hill', in Whitley. Later the subjects were reused for other media. It is not known where the stained glass was originally planned to go, but it was possibly to exhibit at the 1862 International Exhibition in London. This particular panel was designed by the artist Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1828-1882) and is entitled 'Music'. It shows King René leaning over a small chamber-organ to kiss his bride Queen Isabella of Naples, and inscribed on the organ are the names of René's kingdoms: Naples, Sicily, Jerusalem and Cyprus.
663070ca-fa8f-5048-83d1-4c619ee34607.bibliography: Barringer, T., Rosenfeld, J. and Smith, A., *Pre-Raphaelites: Victorian Avant-Garde*, London: Tate Publishing, 2012: 84-85.
663070ca-fa8f-5048-83d1-4c619ee34607.author: Simon Spier

667720fa-07d8-57f8-870a-c8ad0e2f776f.name: Double glass kohl eyeliner vessel
667720fa-07d8-57f8-870a-c8ad0e2f776f.short_description: This Roman period glass work was intended as a container for kohl eyeliner. It is a translucent light green colour with two handles attached to the top rim.
667720fa-07d8-57f8-870a-c8ad0e2f776f.method_for_provenance: By stylistic analysis and material dating.
keywords: Glass; roman period; vessel; Jordan; kohl; translucent

6705b43d-ea3b-54fb-800b-da93e2af5313.name: Wedding bottle
6705b43d-ea3b-54fb-800b-da93e2af5313.short_description:
Enamel-painted bottles and drinking glasses with an image, a year and an 18th century motto constitute a main focus of the collection. The turtle doves and the year 1723 with the words *lieb du mich allein oder lass gar sein* are proof that the bottle was a token of love or a wedding present.  
Flühli, in Entlebuch in the canton of Lucerne, was an important production centre for enamel-painted glass. The products known as *Flühliglas* (glass from Flühli) were characterised by their unpretentious rural imagery.
6705b43d-ea3b-54fb-800b-da93e2af5313.obtention: Donation of Heinrich Angst (1847–1922), first director of the Swiss National Museum, on the occasion of his retirement in 1903

67588ccf-7bc8-58e5-9aa6-c4888f344477.name: Flask
67588ccf-7bc8-58e5-9aa6-c4888f344477.description: This large free-blown bottle of green glass is unique for having survived completely intact except for a silvery iridescence on the surface. Its three loop handles are too small to have supported the weight of the bottle with its unknown contents. Instead, they may have been used in conjunction with a stopper on the bottle’s thick, short neck. Slightly above the vessel’s centre, three stamped discs with three short lines of angular *kufic* script surrounded by a circle have been applied. The Arabic text reads "Abu Ja‘far al-Mu‘ammar" (the work of Abu Ja'far), perhaps referring to the maker of the glass vessel or the owner of the glass workshop where it was produced.
materials: Glass, green, applied discs with impressed inscription; free-blown, tooled, worked on the pontil

67e4f746-f9b3-5718-ba2d-1a3899a55af1.name: Water Glass
67e4f746-f9b3-5718-ba2d-1a3899a55af1.description:
The tall glass is cylindrical in shape and rests on a low circular stem and base. It is decorated with an oval medallion on the front featuring a photographic portrait of King Alexander and Queen Draga Obrenović against a white background. The oval medallion is highlighted with a partially gilded ornament of stylized leaves and vine strips. Two thin gilded lines encircle the rim.  
This type of glass featuring a royal portrait had been appearing in Serbia since the mid-19th century. Portraits of the Obrenović dynasty were often applied to glass tableware. It is presumed that they were most likely produced as memorabilia. The glass with King Alexander and Queen Draga's portrait can certainly be interpreted in terms of promoting the last royal couple of the House of Obrenović.

67f4df91-a582-5ce9-8042-be924c60d2f3.name: Bowl, 'Woman into Hare'
67f4df91-a582-5ce9-8042-be924c60d2f3.short_description: This glass bowl was engraved by artist Alison Kinnaird MBE in 1981. The copper-wheel engraving is done on a bowl of colourless glass flashed purple, by Lindean Mill Glass. The engraving, titled *Woman into Hare* depicts a female human form transforming into a hare. An owl hunts the hare. The image is accompanied by two inscriptions done in diamond point: ''I sall goe intil ane haire/ with sorrow and sych and/ meikle care', 'And I sall goe in the divellis name aye whill I com hom againe". These words were meant to be a spell for turning into a hare. They are associated with Isobel Gowdie, who in 1662 confessed to being a witch. Her confession at trial provided a vivid description of 'witchcraft' and its practices for early-modern Scottish society. In this piece, Kinnaird combines her artistic use of the human form with Scottish history and folklore. The themes of myth and transformation or shape-shifting are seen across her works, inspired by the qualities of glass. The work is signed and dated by the artist.
67f4df91-a582-5ce9-8042-be924c60d2f3.method_for_datation: Purchased from artist, signed and dated by artist

688042f1-194a-5e79-832f-582d091dc74d.name: Game Piece
688042f1-194a-5e79-832f-582d091dc74d.short_description: Chess and game pieces of the Islamic periods vary in shape and material. They appear in the form of a complex figure or as a simple abstract in different materials such a glass, ivory or stone. As a strategic war game introduced into Iran potentially from India sometime during the beginning of the sixth century, chess remained a popular game in royal and aristocratic circles. Simple glass gaming pieces such as this green coloured piece – likely a pawn – were certainly not of a royal or courtly quality, given the simplicity of its shape. It has a circular, widened base for better balance, and a spherical knob on its top.

keywords: Glass; Game piece; Moulded; Abbasid

69cc7401-e44f-50d5-a6a0-750d3c2094e7.name: Beaker
69cc7401-e44f-50d5-a6a0-750d3c2094e7.description: The pattern on this cylindrical beaker of slightly irregular form with bulging sides consists of rows of lozenges arranged in a honeycomb pattern, one of the most popular decorative patterns used since late antiquity. The rather unusual blue colour of this beaker points towards an Iranian origin, possibly as late as the 11th to 13th centuries. It may be contemporary with long-necked, mould-blown bottles sharing the same or similar patterns.

6a69950f-daf4-5791-bc21-86b2151f1204.name: Teapot, teacups with saucer
6a69950f-daf4-5791-bc21-86b2151f1204.short_description:
The industrial designer Wilhelm Wagenfeld (1900-90) received his training at the Bauhaus in Weimar, among other places. From 1931 to 1934 he worked as a freelance designer for the Jena glass factory Schott & Gen., and during this time he designed the company’s tea service with its famous teapot.  
  
The cooperation between Schott & Gen. and the Bauhaus began in the first half of the 1920s, in particular with the production of lamps, and, from the mid-1920s onward, household objects. Many of them were advertised with the slogan “Directly from the fire to the table”.  
  
The Schott & Gen. tea service, like the one shown here, was handmade. For the pot, the glassblower first made the body of the vessel with the help of a model. He then placed a batch of hot glass, still attached to the blow pipe, on the outside wall of the vessel. By blowing through the pipe, the hot gob was slightly curved outwards, extended with pliers to create a tube, and then shaped into a spout. The solid handle was attached to the wall in a further step.

Manske, Beate (ed), *Wilhelm Wagenfeld (1900-1990)*, Ostfildern-Ruit: Hatje Cantz, 2000.
6a69950f-daf4-5791-bc21-86b2151f1204.author: Erwin Baumgartner, Sibylle Walther

6a8ae693-2d75-5f78-8237-d88af864c11f.name: Token or weight.
6a8ae693-2d75-5f78-8237-d88af864c11f.description:
Colourless glass token with a relief border, in a reasonable state of conservation, weighing slightly more than one quarter of a *dirham*, which is 0.66 g. The token is marked only with a two-line inscription in *kufic* characters in the middle of the front face. The first line reads ‘*al-imâm*’ and the second ‘*Ma‘add*’, which refers to the Caliph al-Mustansir.  
Traditional Byzantine glass tokens were generally used as monetary weights, and this use was particularly common among Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs as well as among the Egyptian Tulunids and the Aglabid of North Africa. Shi’ite caliphs also used tokens for other means, particularly from the time of al-Mu‘izz (AH 341–65 / AD 953–75). The fact that many of the tokens found are of identical weight suggests that they were used as ‘fiduciary coins’ in place of bronze coins, particularly as bronze was extremely rare in Egypt at that time. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that no glass tokens have ever been found in Syria, where bronze was abundantly available. These tokens are inscribed on at least one of their faces, bearing the name of the caliph and sometimes even the mint. Most Fatimid tokens come from the time of two caliphs in particular, Abu ‘Ali al-Hakim (AH 386–411 / AD 996–1021) and al-Mustansir (AH 427–87 / AD 1036–94), although a large number also come from the time of al-Zahir, al-Amir and other caliphs.
6a8ae693-2d75-5f78-8237-d88af864c11f.short_description: Glass token probably used as a fiduciary coin in place of bronze coin.
6a8ae693-2d75-5f78-8237-d88af864c11f.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
6a8ae693-2d75-5f78-8237-d88af864c11f.dimensions: Diameter 13 mm, depth 3 mm; weight 0.7 g.
6a8ae693-2d75-5f78-8237-d88af864c11f.method_for_datation: Historical chronology (years of reign of Fatimid caliph).
6a8ae693-2d75-5f78-8237-d88af864c11f.method_for_provenance: Inscription with the name of the caliph.

6ac7d68d-dd1a-5e3a-afaa-4d2652475c9f.name: Concavity. Deppari; Projection Series
6ac7d68d-dd1a-5e3a-afaa-4d2652475c9f.description:
Toshio Iezumi (1954) began to work with glass in 1983, at the Tokyo Glass Art Institute. It was at this time that he began to work with glass sheets. His sources of inspiration are very broad, from the bronze originating in Ancient China to the most recent works of Constantin Brâncuşi and Donald Judd.  
Upon graduating in 1985, Iezumi developed and perfected the technique for which he is known today. He began sticking the sheets of glass using a special adhesive cured by UV light, creating an initial block with a similar shape to a cube. It should be noted that the sheets are not placed at random. The sheet which will be furthest away from the spectator tends to be a mirrored sheet. This is a way in which to play with the reflective properties of the glass itself. Thermal glass can be interspersed or finished among the normal sheet glass in order to play with the refraction of light from the different types of glass. He then grinds and sculpts this block until the desired shape is achieved. After this initial grind using a diamond blade, a pneumatic machine is used to sand and polish the piece. This step involves seven sub-steps in order to achieve a pure, delicate finish (with a pneumatic water fed grinder with a grain of between 60 and 1000, finished with a felt disk in cerium oxide). After hours of work he achieves the depth, optic effects and the degree of transparency desired for his work.

6c5c8e73-e448-5d73-a3ad-4f85d6d02cff.name: Cup
6c5c8e73-e448-5d73-a3ad-4f85d6d02cff.description:
The production of raw glass in Cordoban workshops is documented at least since the 10th century. By using vegetable fluxes to replace natron, it was possible to implement local production and multiply its presence in luxury crockery.  
As glass crockery was understood as a sign of refinement, Abbasid caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid might have sponsored their industry in Baghdad. Similarly, it is thought that some of the great workshops found in the Iberian Peninsula may have been sponsored by rulers of al-Andalus, both in the Caliphate period and later.

6c64959a-ef24-5b36-b22d-27aafad34901.name: *Adam with Seth and his Family*
6c64959a-ef24-5b36-b22d-27aafad34901.short_description:
Painted on highest-quality mirror glass, this gold glass painting reproduces, in reverse, a print by Johann Sadelers I of a lost drawing by Maerten de Vos. It represents the rarely depicted scene in which the 130-year-old Adam brings home the harvest and is greeted by his third son, Seth, while Eve is preparing a meal with her children.  
  
The provenance of this reverse glass painting is verified by the signature of the artist, copper engraver and court glass painter Gerhard Janssen, who worked in Vienna.  
  
On several occasions, Janssen produced reverse glass paintings for Prince Karl Eusebius of Lichtenstein. The latter’s inventories show that Janssen not only made images on gold, but also in “blue with silver” on glass. He did not introduce the *eglomisé* technique to Vienna as a novelty as it was already known in the region of Bohemia and Austria around 1600 and prized by the nobility.

6f2eacf0-0a07-5e6f-9be7-65ddf43a782b.name: Glass Model
6f2eacf0-0a07-5e6f-9be7-65ddf43a782b.short_description: In 1863, the Bohemian-based glassmaker Leopold Blaschka started making models of sea invertebrates at the instigation of an admirer of his glass botanicals. These initial models were based on the illustrations of Philip Henry Gosse published in his treaty ‘A History of the British Sea-Anemones and Corals’, later observations were taken from live specimens shipped directly to the studio and kept in aquariums on site. Around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and over the years they produced models of anemones, cephalopods, mollusca, nudibranchs, and protozoans as well as the vast collection of botanicals held by Harvard University. In 1866, the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art was one of the first UK institutions to order invertebrate models from Leopold Blaschka after its Director Thomas Archer had viewed the then Natural History section of the British Museum’s collection. A set of actinia arrived in 1866, followed by a batch of 58 medusae and mollusks in 1868. In 1910, Ewen Kennedy, a private collector, donated his collection of 123 Blaschka models. The Blaschka models are now highly regarded for their beauty and realism and are still considered ‘an artistic marvel in the field of science and a scientific marvel in the field of art’.
6f2eacf0-0a07-5e6f-9be7-65ddf43a782b.method_for_datation: In the mid-1860s Leopold started selling models, around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and then in 1890 the Blaschkas signed an exclusive contract to produce glass flowers for Harvard University, and stopped producing any other zoological models.
6f2eacf0-0a07-5e6f-9be7-65ddf43a782b.obtention: Donated to the Museum on the death of Mr Kennedy in 1910
6f2eacf0-0a07-5e6f-9be7-65ddf43a782b.bibliography: Swinney, G.N., "Enchanted invertebrates: Blaschka models and other simulacra in National Museums Scotland", *Historical Biology*, 20 : 1 (2008): 39-50.
6f2eacf0-0a07-5e6f-9be7-65ddf43a782b.artist: Leopold Blaschka (1822, Český Dub, Bohemia - 1895, Dresden); Rudolph Blaschka (1857, Dresden, Saxony - 1939, Dresden)
6f2eacf0-0a07-5e6f-9be7-65ddf43a782b.author: Sarah Rothwell
keywords: Blaschka; lampworked glass; glass models

6f8d6482-6333-5e44-8f9e-903c41299c06.name: Der Eulenruf
6f8d6482-6333-5e44-8f9e-903c41299c06.short_description:
Abstract composition with two stylized owls in a forest landscape. According to the artist, owls, like ghosts and bats, populate the night, and their call is considered a harbinger of doom. Wirtl-Walser finds iconographic inspiration in the world of nature, fossils and archetypes. She prefers to use old, mouth-blown glass as a support for her work, because it has more texture and greater irregularities than industrially produced glass. Over many years, in several workshops and through long series of experiments in her own studio, she has learned various ways of working the surface of the glass – from binding agents to painting techniques to the uses of various glues, and from layering and cutting to engraving and mounting.  
  
The artist created the mirror surface of the reverse glass painting presented here after studying old recipes for silver mirroring. An almost extinct mirror-making skill, silver mirroring has become one of her consistently recurring means of expression over many years.

6fb1ca3c-651f-5085-a0a9-f84a82621d78.name: Bottle
6fb1ca3c-651f-5085-a0a9-f84a82621d78.description: As well as the history of Austrian glassmaking was established in the 19th century, there was one movement that gradually paved the way for a different perception of glassmaking, and its customers, and that was Biedermeier. Known for being a decorative art favoured by the middle class, this style was witness to a great revival of glassmaking in Bohemia where new kinds of glass were being produced for a new kind of clientele. This period is characterised by a particular glass cutting technique, and it was used to create these new, marvelous pieces. This unique example of a bottle (along with a stopper) made of clear glass with white, polished, cut and opaque overlay, is the ideal visual for understanding the great achievements of Biedermeier glasswork and how its vibrant shapes and colours filled the tables and rooms of Germanic Europe in the beginning of the 19th century.

702677f9-4405-5434-9c9b-77538dd0a391.name: Wine glass
702677f9-4405-5434-9c9b-77538dd0a391.short_description:
This lead glass wine glass is wheel-engraved with a scene showing the biblical figures David and Jonathan but also shows a coded message of love between two men. Jonathan was the son of Saul, the first king of the Israelites, and David was the handsome shepherd boy who was anointed to become the future king of the Israelites. David becomes important to Saul's court, playing music for the king and slaying the philistine giant Goliath, winning the admiration of the Israelites. He also forms a strong bond with Jonathan, which eventually drives Saul to banish David in a fit of jealous rage. The scene on this goblet shows David and Jonathan sealing their friendship through an embrace.  
  
Somewhat uncommonly, the depiction of David and Jonathan also shows that the figure on the right has his foot placed on top of the figure on the left. It has been suggested this alludes to sexual desire between men, as in the late 17th century, when homosexuality was illegal and men accused of it could face the death penalty, court records describe that treading on each others feet was one way men discreetly expressed their wish for sexual contact with each other whilst in public.
702677f9-4405-5434-9c9b-77538dd0a391.bibliography: Laméris, A., *Amicitae, a Toast to Friendship*, Amsterdam: Fridés Laméris, 2018: 7.
702677f9-4405-5434-9c9b-77538dd0a391.author: Simon Spier

7030a53b-c9dd-5d53-9b01-c53042f5dec9.name: Stand for Sweets
7030a53b-c9dd-5d53-9b01-c53042f5dec9.description:
The sweets stand was made in the factory of Nacko Janković & Son in Jagodina in the last decade of the 19th century. It is made of pressed, partially transparent, partially opal blue glass. The stand consists of a plate with a raised, wave-pattern rim set atop a high stem attached to a smaller base, decorated with radial rings and stars.  
Serbia’s movement toward the European way of life during the 19th century included the acceptance of new cultural models. Everyday life, especially in urban areas, changed with the introduction of novelties such as the use of porcelain and crystal sets to the culture of dining. High quality glass could be seen at first only in formal cultural settings. Later, imported glass products were augmented by the more accessible domestic glass products, whose design relied on the imported products. Thus, the Nacko Janković & Son factory had a wide range of items for sweets consumption. In addition to various types of fruit, cakes and sweets stands, candy bowls and saucepans, the Nacko Janković & Son factory produced various dishes for the traditional *slatko*, a special delight prepared from fruit, bowls for sugar or "*ratluk*", sweet Turkish delight, etc.

70400fa1-9e1b-5253-b587-686c8eff3455.name: Head
70400fa1-9e1b-5253-b587-686c8eff3455.description:
Martin Janecký is one of the best-known Czech artists for his use of a technique based on modelling from inside a bubble of melted glass, known as “inside sculpting”. This technique requires great precision in order to control the thickness of the glass, its temperature and ductility, in addition to great skill in managing the tools. Martin works with the help of incredibly skilled assistants who work with him in perfect synchronisation. Janecký can be identified primarily for his head and hand sculptures,  
created with diverse attitudes, textures and tones.  
Martin began to work with glass at age 13 in his father’s factory. He graduated from the Glass School in Nový Bor in 1998, and it wasn’t until 2003 that he began to gain international acknowledgement following his trip to a glass symposium at the Corning Museum of Glass.  
He has been a guest artist at numerous glass schools, workshops and museums across the globe, demonstrating how he creates his sculptures. Some of these include the Corning Studio, Museum of Glass (USA), Pilchuck Glass School, Tacoma Museum of Glass, Stand Wood, Chrysler, Norfolk, Bronholm, Rietvel and at the Real Fábrica de Cristales de La Granja, where he created this piece during his stay in 2017.

70f529e6-c9fa-52a5-bd8f-5c428e73af4d.name: Jug
70f529e6-c9fa-52a5-bd8f-5c428e73af4d.short_description: This jug is a rare example of early Islamic glass that carries an inscription by or signature of the maker. In the early medieval period it was highly unusual for artisans to sign their work, especially objects carrying blessings for the owner. Made of mould-blown turquoise glass, the jar has a drop form with a flat base and a narrow neck. The upper part of the spout is missing, but the remains of an applied handle can still be identified on the object's shoulder. On its body a two-line *kufic* inscription appears between plain lines revealing the name of its maker. The inscription reads, “baraka li-sahibihi, ʿamal Muhammad ibn al-Ahzan" (Blessing to the owner. The work of Muhammad ibn al-Ahzan). The rich turquoise colour and the clarity of the inscription on this jug make it stand out from other early Islamic glasswork of this group.
70f529e6-c9fa-52a5-bd8f-5c428e73af4d.bibliography: Walton, Michelle, *Imperfect Perfection - Early Islamic Glass*, Doha: Bloomsbury Qatar Foundation Publishing, 2012: 82.
keywords: Glass; Jug; Free-blown; Abbasid

73591acc-1e71-5f44-af5c-7f30c06e4c55.name: *Ceres*
73591acc-1e71-5f44-af5c-7f30c06e4c55.short_description:
The rondel represents Ceres, the goddess of wheat and harvest and symbol of the fertility of the earth and of agriculture, in a landscape that evokes the harvest of cereals. A mythological figure, sometimes confused with the Greek figure Demeter, Ceres can be identified by her two attributes: the sickle and the sheaf of wheat. She was widely depicted in Europe during the Renaissance thanks to isolated engravings as well as mythographies that fixed her appearance and attributes.  
  
Curiously, this rondel does not seem to correspond to any pre-existing iconographic model, whether ancient or Renaissance, and the costume and headdress of Ceres, devoid of any indication, make attribution and dating uncertain. However, a date prior to the engraving by Hieronymus Cock after Lambert Lombard (1568) appears unlikely, since the rondel features the same motif of a cart drawn by two horses.

74d2d092-c2c8-5979-ab6f-215b4280585d.name: Glass fragment.
74d2d092-c2c8-5979-ab6f-215b4280585d.description:
The fragment of thick, bubbled glass shows an enamelled and gilded decoration consisting of an inscription written in a tall cursive style outlined in red against a blue background. Two gilded bands, also outlined in red, frame the inscription that can be read as *'izz li-mawlana* (glory to our lord). The colours are partly painted one upon the other so that they give information about the working process. First, the gilded script, from which only slight remains are preserved, and the gilded upper and lower border were executed. Then the letters and the framed borders were outlined in red. Finally, the background was painted in blue. The colours were applied cold and fixed by firing at a low temperature. The routinely executed enamelling of this fragment suggests that these kinds of glass bottle were produced in large quantities for everyday use. The fragment of round cross-section might have been part of a glass bottle with a tall neck, like surviving Mamluk glass bottles, with a decoration scheme corresponding to the gold-framed inscription of the fragment. The slightly flaring sides and the rimless opening indicate that it was the upper part of the neck.  
In the Mamluk period, enamelled glass, whose technique was developed between the AH 6th and 9th centuries / AD 12th and 15th centuries, was manufactured in Egypt and Syria. Red and blue, in combination with gold, were the most prominent colours.
74d2d092-c2c8-5979-ab6f-215b4280585d.short_description: Fragment of thick glass. Its enamelled and gilded inscription reads ‘glory to our lord’. The fragment probably belonged to a bottle with tall neck. In Mamluk times, glass objects were manufactured in Egypt and Syria, predominantly with red and blue colours combined with gold.

74d2d092-c2c8-5979-ab6f-215b4280585d.method_for_datation: The use of red for outlines, blue for inscriptions or large areas, and gold for smaller sections became the rule by the middle of the 8th / 14th century.

75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.name: Two glasses
75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.description:
The Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade houses highly significant utilitarian glass objects that reflect the courtly culture of the Obrenović dynasty. These objects are not only testaments to a bygone era, but they also reflect the aesthetic sensibilities of the ruling dynasty, as well as their cultural refinement and enlightenment. The royal family paid special attention to the culture of dining, salons, and dining rooms. In this context, a need arose for acquiring certain exclusive glassware sets, including those intended for private ceremonies, which were imported from abroad and ordered according to specific typologies.  
The Obrenović dynasty ruled Serbia from 1815 to 1842, and again from 1858 to 1903. Its progenitor was Miloš Obrenović (1783–1860), also known as Miloš the Great, leader of the Second Serbian Uprising against the Ottoman Empire and Prince of Serbia twice, from 1815 to 1839, and from 1858 to 1860. During the rule of Prince Miloš Obrenović, in 1830, Sultan Mahmud II issued a hatt-i-sharif granting Serbia the status of an autonomous principality, while Serbia’s full independence was confirmed at the Congress of Berlin, in 1878, during the rule of Prince (later King) Milan Obrenović (1854–1901).  
Among the Obrenović dynasty-related objects from the collection of the Museum of Applied Art is a pair of water glasses, skilfully decorated with an engraved royal cypher of King Alexander Obrenović (1876–1903). Made using the glass casting technique, the glasses have exceptionally thin walls and a characteristically flat base. In their central section, the initial letter "A", topped with a royal crown, is lavishly engraved. The glasses were acquired by the Museum of Applied Art in 2008. They were originally owned by the Kozinc family from Slovenia, and later became part of the Višnjić family collection in Belgrade.  
King Alexander Obrenović was the last ruler of the Obrenović dynasty. Together with his consort, Queen Draga, he was assassinated in Belgrade, in the May Coup, on the night of 10–11 June \[O.S. 28–29 May\] 1903, which resulted in the dynasty’s extinction.
75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analisys with related material.

75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.author: Jelena Vukadinović, Draginja Maskareli
keywords: tableware, glass, Serbia, the Obrenović dynasty.

761cee32-45ca-549f-9579-2d2f21862b17.name: Goblet
761cee32-45ca-549f-9579-2d2f21862b17.description: In the complete course of art history, rarely has there been a movement in which the decorative arts played such an integral role as Art Nouveau. Among these arts, glass held the most important role by far. As a very flexible and mostly transparent material, glass provided an ideal medium in which artists of the movement could express their ideas that were inspired by nature and organic forms. The style, originating in England, spread throughout Europe; yet the most notable places it set its roots were Belgium, France, the Czech Republic, Germany and Austria. Known as Jugendstil in the German-speaking lands, the movement beared witness to divine glass creations from many, now world-famous, craftspeople who have truly earned honourable mentions in the history of the decorative and applied arts. An essential place for the birth and development of the Jugendstil in Vienna was the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshops), founded by Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser. The main aim of the workshops was to bring the artist or designer closer to the craftspeople and technicians entrusted with the execution of their designs, while also encouraging the designers to be their own crafters. This glass is a product of the collaboration between Josef Hoffman and Matilde Flögl, Hoffmann’s student at the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts, where she learned design, applied graphics and creative enamelling. After graduating, she became a member of Wiener Werkstätte. Her style is characterised by radiant colours, various organic and natural shapes, motives sourced out of the flora and fauna. On the bowl of the glass, Flögl depicted several representations of humans, animals, potted plants and garlands, or ribbons. On the foot of the glass there are depictions of doves, which in between them have ribbons. The stem of the glass is flanked with blue and white stripes, making a clear distinction between the foot and the bowl of the glass.

788f0e63-c4f7-5c41-990a-179fc68adeac.name: Cup
788f0e63-c4f7-5c41-990a-179fc68adeac.short_description: This unusually large, domed, cylindrical cup with slightly flared rim and flat foot is engraved with staggered rows of circular, wheel-cut depressions. The large wheel-cut facets form a honeycomb lattice pattern, a decorative feature found on numerous Sasanian and post-Sasanian glass vessels. Made during the Abbasid period some centuries later, this technique of glass decoration demonstrates continuation of a style previously made in Iraq and Iran. Similar excavated examples have been attributed to the site of Nishapur.
788f0e63-c4f7-5c41-990a-179fc68adeac.bibliography: Walton, Michelle, *Imperfect Perfection. Early Islamic Glass*, Doha: Bloomsbury Qatar Foundation Publishing, 2012: 48.
keywords: Glass; Free-blown; Wheel-cut; Abbasid

78cf374a-fef2-5a8f-8290-e091efaa9c9c.name: Glass carafe.
78cf374a-fef2-5a8f-8290-e091efaa9c9c.description:
A glass carafe that is distinguished by its delicacy and beautiful proportions. It is composed of a conical-shaped base, the bottom of which is a prominent circle. The body is characterised by sloping shoulders, the lower portion of which slopes into a round bowl. Its long, elegant neck terminates with a slightly undulating mouth. The body is decorated with arabesque vegetal motifs executed in enamel and gilding inside three simple roundels; one of which holds a stylised lotus blossom depicted in white against a background of blue enamel. The neck of the vessel bears a gilded inscription in small letters on which the name Sultan al-Nasir Salah al-Din Yusuf appears. The mouth of the vessel is embellished with simple decorative bands.  
It is clear from the inscription that the vessel was designated to the Ayyubid Sultan, al-Nasir Yusuf II, the ruler of Aleppo and Damascus in the period AH 634–58 / AD 1237–60. Enamel-painting on glass is considered to be a popular decorative style of the Ayyubid period, which became widespread in the Mamluk period. A considerable number of these vessels with enamel decoration are found in various museums worldwide. A similar vessel in the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin is decorated with a painting of two horsemen playing polo. It dates to the Ayyubid period in the AH 7th / AD 13th century and originated in Syria.
78cf374a-fef2-5a8f-8290-e091efaa9c9c.short_description: The production of glass reached its peak of excellence in Egypt and Syria in the AH 6th–9th / AD 12th–15th centuries under the patronage of the Ayyubid and Mamluk Sultans. Many glass pieces were decorated with gilding and enamel, of which this is fine example.
78cf374a-fef2-5a8f-8290-e091efaa9c9c.dimensions: Height 32 cm, diameter (of the body) 15 cm.
78cf374a-fef2-5a8f-8290-e091efaa9c9c.method_for_datation: The vessel is dated based on the fact that it bears the name of the last Ayyubid Sultan al-Nasir Yusuf II, ruler of Aleppo and Damascus in the period 634–58 / 1237–60.
78cf374a-fef2-5a8f-8290-e091efaa9c9c.method_for_provenance: The production and use of enamelled glass vessels was widespread in Egypt and Syria during the Ayyubid period (7th / 13th century).
78cf374a-fef2-5a8f-8290-e091efaa9c9c.obtention: The vessel was donated to the museum in 1915 by Amir Yusuf Kamal, who was one of the princes of the family of Muhammad Ali who ruled Egypt from 1805–1952.

78d84236-d562-548a-87c9-6243be0e9d2c.name: Glass
78d84236-d562-548a-87c9-6243be0e9d2c.description:
Transparent, cylindrical, blown glass of slightly truncated conical form, with yellow and black decorative enamel. The rim is encircled by a sequence of 12 squares, each representing one of the signs of the zodiac. The names of the corresponding months are depicted below each of these squares, followed by a series of columns of three sections per row (with 11 rows in total), in which the days of the month are recorded. Some days are highlighted against a yellow background.  
  
The base of the glass features an image of Venus, to be discovered once the contents have been drained. The inscription "1920" forms an arc around the image, announcing the arrival of the new year.  
  
The object, created in 1919, reflects the modern Viennese graphic style that originated in the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshop), of which the artist was a member. According to Alberto Bartolomé Arraiza, the piece was most likely a special order.
78d84236-d562-548a-87c9-6243be0e9d2c.obtention: Dation in payment of taxes, 1999. From the Torsten Bröhan collection.

7b48bcae-f423-50f0-a39f-b04c846f5673.name: Square Bottle
7b48bcae-f423-50f0-a39f-b04c846f5673.description:
This pale green square bottle with a patterned bottom is a fine example of mould-blown glassware. After the free-blowing technique has been found, possibly around in the first quarter of the 1st century BC, the mould-blowing technique has developed and the desired glass forms and patterns were obtained by blowing into glass, terracotta, stone, metal or wood moulds. The melt at the end of the blowing rod is inflated in two or more pieces of the container until it covers the mould. The use of angular and patterned moulds has usually made it unnecessary to apply additional ornaments.  
With this mould-blowing technique, mass production of glasses with the same form, measurement, and decoration could be produced by using a single mould. In the form of quadrangular shaped moulds, the glass workshop's or the manufacturer's names were added by applying letters and symbols on the pedestal portion. Accordingly, the bottle has a moulded design in relief, which comprises a rosette of five or six irregular petals within a raised circle. (For square bottles in the West decorated with rosettes on the bottom, see Alarco 1975: 49 nos. 29-32.)  
The bottle has a thick rim which is folded out, over and in, and flattened on the top to form an uneven and irregular mouth; cylindrical neck; horizontal shoulder with steeply sloping corners, and a square body with vertical sides. On the side below the handle a diagonal line is raised, and another side has bulged out over the top of the mould. It has a concave bottom; a strap handle applied to edge of the shoulder which drawn up and trailed onto the neck and underside of the rim. The bottle is in an intact situation, except for one corner at the bottom that is broken and mended. Black, enamel-like weathering is covering most of the surfaces; dulling, blowing striations; many pin-prick bubbles and iridescence also exist.
