7ec7333d-9cff-5b8d-b9c4-f322d00e2d87.name: Megaplanet
7ec7333d-9cff-5b8d-b9c4-f322d00e2d87.description:
Artist Josh Simpson has been influenced by the Studio Glass movement since his career began in 1972. However, a creativity crisis in 1989 led to a U-turn in his career. He decided to take a break and delve into the world of Venetian glass in order to learn the Murrine and Filigree techniques. Inspired by his wife’s experiences and images of the Earth and Space, as captured by NASA, he embarked on the creation of his series of work, *Megaplanets*.  
These pieces are very challenging to create. They were born of the creation of the murrines and filigrees for each individual planet. These murrines were then stored for months until they were used. Upon creation of the Megaplanet, silver was melted with a small gob inflated piece of glass. He then continued to work with the marble, adding sheets of glass, one by one, as required. Sheets of gold or platinum, glass enamel, bubbles and many more are then added to these layers. The process takes around eight hours. It is then placed into the annealing furnace. Depending on the size of the Planet, this process can take months. This technique creates pieces similar to paperweights which recreate impressive landscapes.  
In 2003, the Museo Tecnológico del Vidrio organised an exclusive exhibition of his work. Following its closure, the artist donated this piece to the Museum.
7ec7333d-9cff-5b8d-b9c4-f322d00e2d87.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja

7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.name: Mosque lamp.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.description:
An enameled glass and gilt mosque lamp with a wide flaring mouth and a squat globular body, a steeply sloping shoulder and flattened base. The body rests on a tall pedestal foot. Six applied loop handles are placed around the shoulder at regular intervals. The lamp holds extensive enamelled decoration on the mouth, body and foot, enhanced by gilding; the mouth having a large Qur’anic inscription in *thuluth* script executed in blue enamel and outlined in red. The inscription is interrupted by three roundels containing a *fleur-de-lys* blazon in red against a white background. The base of the mouth shows a delicately drawn scroll-band interrupted by cusped floral cartouches.  
The top of the shoulder displays a narrow band with cusped floral medallions, while the main part of the body has a wide inscription band in *thuluth* script that reads, translated: ‘This is one of the objects made for his most noble and high Excellency, the learned, the just, the administrator, the councilor, the regent, the vizier Najm al-Din Mahmud ibn Ali ibn Shirwin, the officer of al-Malik al-Muzaffar (Hajji), regent of the noble Islamic provinces, may Allah the Exalted make his victories glorious’. The inscription, set against a blue background, is interrupted by six lozenge-shaped areas that hold the trailed suspension loops.  
The underside of the body has further *fleur-de-lys* roundels and floral detailing. The foot (half of which is a replacement) holds a succession of five horizontal bands filled with abstract scrolling that alternates, linearly, with thickly drawn detailing. The horizontal bands are interrupted by three lozenge-shaped medallions that hold abstract vegetal motifs.  
The lamp dates exactly to AH 746–7 / AD 1346–7, during the short reign of al-Malik al-Muzaffar Hajji. Interestingly, the donor Najm al-Din Mahmud ibn Ali ibn Shirwin, did not begin his career as a slave contrary to usual practice. It is known that he arrived in Cairo in AH 737 / AD 1337, having been a vizier (a minister) in Baghdad. The red *fleur-de-lys* on his lamp is his heraldic device. Najm al-Din’s lamp is especially important because it appears to be the earliest example of a *fleur-de-lys* used as the badge of an official, a motif previously reserved only for sultans.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.short_description: Glass mosque lamps with enamelled decoration were commissioned in large numbers by the Mamluk elite in Egypt and Syria. Decorated with Qur’anic inscriptions and the titles of the patron, they were destined for the numerous mosques and *madrasas* endowed by the Mamluks throughout Cairo and the empire.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.initial_owner: Najm al-Din Mahmud ibn Ali ibn Shirwin.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.method_for_datation: The lamp was commissioned by an officer of al-Malik al-Muzaffar Hajji, who reigned for less than two years between 746–47 / 1346–7.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.method_for_provenance: Mamluk mosque lamps of this type are generally ascribed to Syria, where they were made for export to Mamluk Egypt.

7fd4088e-fd30-5315-911f-4cef0bf18853.name: Bottle
7fd4088e-fd30-5315-911f-4cef0bf18853.short_description: This bottle reflects a syncretism between traditions of late antiquity and technical innovations of early Islam. Cutting into the surface was a technique widely used from Egypt to Iran between the late first and the fourth century AH / eighth and the tenth century AD. Unlike the Roman cameo glass style, which is characterized by encasing other pieces of glass into the main body, this bottle bears two applied layers of green glass featuring two horses. Other animals such as hares, lions or birds were commonly used to decorate applied glass. This piece demonstrates the mastery of the craftsman, also covered with incised ornaments combining geometric and fish scale patterns to reveal the contrast between colours of the different glass layers.

7fee46c7-2496-508c-978f-4c40ead375bd.name: *Fama*
7fee46c7-2496-508c-978f-4c40ead375bd.short_description:
This stained glass represents a winged female figure, blowing a trumpet held in her right hand. In her other hand, she holds a ribbon with the inscription “FAMA”. She is dressed in a golden robe and a blue-white cloak. Her wings are multicoloured. The figure is set in a landscape consisting of various plants, flower, trees and hills.  
  
The inscription identifies the figure as Fama, the personification of renown and rumor. As a figure from Roman mythology, she is described by Virgil in the “Aeneid” as a winged creature, covered in feathers all over her body and with multiple tongues, mouths and ears. She spreads evil tidings, not resting even at night. The 14th-century English poet Geoffrey Chaucer wrote that Fama announces renown, fame or notability (positive attributes) from a trumpet of gold and scandalous rumor and gossip (negative attributes) from a trumpet of black tin. The glass painting therefore shows Fama’s positive side, which does not appear fearsome or evil.  
  
Stylistic elements substantiate an attribution to the Swedish-born Carl Almquist, who spent almost his entire artistic life in England. Some of the details in the stained glass windows of the small church of Betws Bledrws in the county of Ceredigion, Wales (1886–87) exhibit an affinity with Fama, suggesting a proximate dating. Almquist’s stained glass paintings of this time demonstrate the influence of the pre-Raphaelite circle around Edward Burne-Jones; the impact of the English Arts and Crafts movement is also apparent.

8036a330-a9a9-5365-82f2-1e9fa471a32c.name: Glass
8036a330-a9a9-5365-82f2-1e9fa471a32c.description:
Transparent blown glass, enamelled in various colours, including red, black, white, blue and yellow. Red, annular foot, cylindrical body and flared rim. A decorative scene covers the entire glass: the interior of a hat shop featuring several stylized male and female figures amid drapery and hats displayed on stands.  
  
Dagobert Peche was responsible for the glass’s decorative design. He joined the Wiener Werkstätte in 1915 and became artistic director of the organisation in 1919; the piece was thus designed during his tenure. From an ornamental standpoint, Peche contributed a new repertoire of forms, breaking with the austere, geometric style of Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser in favour of European Expressionist and Surrealist influences. The hat shop motif can be seen as well in the work of German Expressionist August Macke. Macke’s influence coincided with the arrival of the avant-garde to Czechoslovakia, an event that occurred somewhat late, due to the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.  
  
Moreover, the hat shop motif reveals the importance of fashion in the Wiener Werkstätte, which, in addition to textiles and clothing, produced designs for hats, jewellery, handbags and other accessories. Peche was one of the most prolific designers of these fashion items and the interiors of the galleries in which they were displayed.
8036a330-a9a9-5365-82f2-1e9fa471a32c.method_for_datation: Analysis of style and technique; Wiener Werkstätte inscription on base.
8036a330-a9a9-5365-82f2-1e9fa471a32c.obtention: Dation in payment of taxes, 1999. From the Torsten Bröhan collection.

827fcea0-a7e5-521a-ba2b-5bc656744345.name: Beaker
827fcea0-a7e5-521a-ba2b-5bc656744345.description: Beaker of pale, yellowish-green, glass with a slightly flared rim, rounded by reheating, and long cylindrical body. The rim has a dark blue trail applied which winds down and around the body four times and is left in relief. From this last horizontal trail, the body is decorated with two irregular, blue, vertical, zigzag trails on opposite sides and four applied blue trails, attached at top and bottom to create open loops. From each is suspended a ring: one is now missing, two are yellow-brown glass and one is a weathered bronze. The beaker has an applied base ring; the underside is kicked and retains a pontil mark. Irregular weathering crust unevenly distributed over the surface.

836e7782-e057-5a94-8952-509fcfc07fe6.name: Flask.
836e7782-e057-5a94-8952-509fcfc07fe6.description:
The flask of translucent bluish glass consists of the neck and the body. The lower part of the long conical neck has three rings in relief that divide the surface into sections of different widths. The round opening has a flanged rim. A wide horizontal strip around the body divides the four sides of the flask into two equal sections. The shoulders are faceted and ornamented in high relief with double triangles. In the lower section towards the base the tapering sides are faceted, sloping to form four elongated feet, which are now missing.  
This flask belongs to the type of 'molar' flasks, so called after the shape of their elongated, wedge-shaped feet that resemble the root of a molar tooth. The purpose of this shape was probably functional. Flasks of this type were articles for everyday use and intended to contain perfume or essence.
836e7782-e057-5a94-8952-509fcfc07fe6.short_description: Small flask of translucent bluish glass with a long conical neck and a four-sided body. A characteristic of this kind of flask is their elongated, wedge-shaped feet, which are missing here. These flasks were probably used for perfumes or essences.
836e7782-e057-5a94-8952-509fcfc07fe6.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).

836e7782-e057-5a94-8952-509fcfc07fe6.method_for_datation: In the relevant literature the generally accepted dating of molar flasks is the 3rd–4th / 9th–10th centuries.

844d8f4e-5970-519a-b2e8-49263b459e0c.name: Cup
844d8f4e-5970-519a-b2e8-49263b459e0c.description:
In the middle of the 1st century BC glass-makers along the Syro-Palestinian coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated with air through a hollow blow-pipe. This invention of ‘free-blowing’ revolutionized the glass industry. It allowed vessels to be mass-produced thus rendering them less expensive and available to a wider market so that by the end of the 1st century AD free blown glass vessels were used widely throughout the Roman Empire. The majority were undecorated utilitarian pieces, used for storage and transport, and tablewares, like beakers and plates, but others were embellished with applied decoration. While still hot their bodies were rolled over loose glass chips of contrasting colours and then marvered flush with the wall of the vessel. Next, the pieces where reheated and further inflated and manipulated, so that when their necks were pulled out of their bodies the splashes also became elongated.  
This plain cup is under the category of undecorated free-blown vessels and it is in an intact condition. These type of Roman glasses were widely used as drinking cups. This one has everted, rounded and slightly thickened rim; vertical side, with a bulging ridge at the junction with the bottom. The cup has a convex bottom which flattened and thickened at the centre. The greenish colourless surface has a creamy weathering, iridescence and traces of a pontil (noble) mark.

858c3d8c-738b-5228-9f30-7612bfcde5ee.name: Seal of Shah Tahmasp
858c3d8c-738b-5228-9f30-7612bfcde5ee.short_description:
This wheel-cut rock crystal seal was made for Shah Tahmasp. Seals were widely employed in the Safavid chancelleries and used for the most varied purposes. They were often re-carved and for security reasons eventually disposed of.  
A cursive inscription expressing Shi’ite devotion is in the lobed corner cartouches, while the names of Allah, Muhammad and ‘Ali together with the date 963 are on the sides. The name of the Shah and his title of ‘Servant of the King of Holyness’ occupy the central area. The inscriptions emphasize the bond between Shi’ism and the Safavid dynasty.  
  
Seal inscription:  
Centre: I am the servant, Shah Tahmasb, the guardian of the faith  
Lower right corner: When they entangled our name with a crime  
Lower left corner: They weighed our deeds on the scale  
Upper left corner: More than anyone else, our sin was great/ heavy, but...  
Upper right corner: They forgave us out of love for Ali.  
Allah, Muhammad, Ali. 963  
  
Centre: Bandeh Shah-e Velayat Tahmasb  
Lower right corner: Chon nameh-ye jorme ma beham paychidand

86ba73c0-7a63-5e24-ac7d-4ed99ca1aa85.name: Glass weights.
86ba73c0-7a63-5e24-ac7d-4ed99ca1aa85.description:
Dark-gray coloured glass weights used to verify the weights of coins, most of which were produced in Egypt. The weights are small, round glass discs with an impressed inscription of the name and title of the caliph or the name of the governor on them.  
  
The glass weights depicted here are from the Fatimid period a dynasty which broke away from the Abbasid caliphate and established a new caliphate in North Africa and Egypt during the period AH 297–567 / AD 909–1181, such weights are principally from the reigns of the two Fatimid Caliphs al-Zahir (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36), and al-Mustansir (r. AH 427–87 / AD 1036–94).  
  
The weights bear the following titular inscriptions written in foliated kufic script:  
  
J.16546: bears the name of the commander of the faithful: **الامام معد ابو تميم المستنصر (امير المؤمنين)** ('Al-Imam Mu\`id Abu Tamim al-Mustansir Billah (Amir al-Mu\`minin)' within an embossed frame and circle.  
  
J.16547: bears the name of the commander of the faithful **الظاهر لاعزاز دين الله (امير المؤمنين)** 'al-Zahir li-izaz Dein Allah (Amir al-Mu\`minin)' within an embossed frame and circle.  
  
J.16550: bears only the name of God: **الله** 'Allah'
86ba73c0-7a63-5e24-ac7d-4ed99ca1aa85.short_description: Glass weights from Ayla in Aqaba, used to verify the weights of coins. These small, round glass discs have impressed inscriptions; two bear the names of the Fatimid Caliphs al-Zahir (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36), and al-Mustansir (r. AH 427–87 / AD 1036–94), while the third bears the name of God.
86ba73c0-7a63-5e24-ac7d-4ed99ca1aa85.dimensions: Diameter (in the range) 26–27 mm, weights 4.68 g; 5.02 g; 5.15 g.
86ba73c0-7a63-5e24-ac7d-4ed99ca1aa85.method_for_datation: The weights have inscriptions impressed on one side of them that give the names and titles of two Fatimid caliphs: al-Zahir (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36), and al-Mustansir (r. AH 427–87 / AD 1036–94).
86ba73c0-7a63-5e24-ac7d-4ed99ca1aa85.method_for_provenance: These weights were probably manufactured in Egypt during the Fatimid period a dynasty which broke away from the Abbasid caliphate and established a new caliphate in North Africa and Egypt during the period AH 297–567 / AD 909–1181.
86ba73c0-7a63-5e24-ac7d-4ed99ca1aa85.obtention: The weights were recovered during the course of an archaeological excavation carried out in 1990 at the site of Islamic Ayla, modern-day Aqaba.

873771d8-3234-54f2-933c-1a7e96765d53.name: Pair of flasks
873771d8-3234-54f2-933c-1a7e96765d53.short_description:
These spirit flasks were decorated by the independent glass and porcelain painter Ignaz Preissler. Preissler came from a family of independent decorators who have been recorded working in eastern Bohemia and are known for their painting in black and iron-red - known as 'Schwarzlot' - in a fine detailed way that contrasted with earlier Venetian decoration.  
  
Independent decorators such as the Preisslers were known as 'Hausmaler', literally meaning 'house-painter', and such work was most often carried out on smaller vessels with a very fine brush.
873771d8-3234-54f2-933c-1a7e96765d53.author: Simon Spier

8808a080-0640-50c7-9586-5a95e86ace0a.name: Stengelglas
8808a080-0640-50c7-9586-5a95e86ace0a.description: In the complete course of art history, rarely has there been a movement in which the decorative arts played such an integral role as Art Nouveau. Among these arts, glass held the most important role by far. As a very flexible and mostly transparent material, glass provided an ideal medium in which artists of the movement could express their ideas that were inspired by nature and organic forms. The style, originating in England, spread throughout Europe; yet the most notable places it set its roots were Belgium, France, the Czech Republic, Germany and Austria. Known as Jugendstil in the German-speaking lands, the movement beared witness to divine glass creations from many, now world-famous, craftspeople who have truly earned honourable mentions in the history of the decorative and applied arts. An essential place for the birth and development of the Jugendstil in Vienna was the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshops), founded by Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser. The main aim of the workshops was to bring the artist or designer closer to the craftspeople and technicians entrusted with the execution of their designs, while also encouraging the designers to be their own crafters. The Wiener Werkstättewas host to a large number of Austrian craftspeople, such as Dagobert Peche, Otto Prutscher and Ludwig Heinrich Jungnickel. This drinking glass is the creation of Otto Prutscher, who produced his best works in the period between his graduation from the Kunstgewerbeschule in AD 1901 and the outbreak of World War I. Standing on a long stem, the bowl of the glass is decorated with silver-stained oval facets. This object is an excellent example of Prutscher’s early designs, which borrowed heavily from the rectilinear and modular language that Josef Hoffman and Koloman Moser worked out in the beginning of the century.

888b131a-0e0c-56fd-85b2-18c10cf7045d.name: Vase
888b131a-0e0c-56fd-85b2-18c10cf7045d.description: In the complete course of art history, rarely has there been a movement in which the decorative arts played such an integral role as Art Nouveau. Among these arts, glass held the most important role by far. As a very flexible and mostly transparent material, glass provided an ideal medium in which artists of the movement could express their ideas that were inspired by nature and organic forms. The style, originating in England, spread throughout Europe; yet the most notable places it set its roots were Belgium, France, the Czech Republic, Germany and Austria. Known as Jugendstil in the German-speaking lands, the movement beared witness to divine glass creations from many, now world-famous, craftspeople who have truly earned honourable mentions in the history of the decorative and applied arts. An essential place for the birth and development of the Jugendstil in Vienna was the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshops), founded by Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser. The main aim of the workshops was to bring the artist or designer closer to the craftspeople and technicians entrusted with the execution of their designs, while also encouraging the designers to be their own crafters. The Wiener Werkstätte was host to a large number of Austrian craftspeople, such as Dagobert Peche, Otto Prutscher and Ludwig Heinrich Jungnickel. The Wiener Werkstätte was one of Hoffmann’s central projects throughout his long life. Therefore, his contribution to the art of the Austrian Jugendstil is a multi-faceted one, ranging from architecture to the decorative arts. Standing on a wide and small foot, this milky-blue glass bowl is covered with a green overlay in the form of triangles and continuing into stripes along the foot of the glass. In between there are isolated green leaves. This presents an ideal combination of Hoffmann’s inspirations from nature and rectilinear forms.

88a2f54a-f12b-5e20-b62c-51efeefc845a.name: Goblet
88a2f54a-f12b-5e20-b62c-51efeefc845a.short_description:
This particularly extravagant exhibition goblet in Renaissance style is a masterpiece by the Bohemia glass engraver Franz Paul Zach (1819–1881). It is made in two pieces, both of colourless, clear glass, with a thin, blue glass overlay. The bowl is attached to the stem with a cut glass screw thread.  
  
Zach has engraved through the blue overlay on the bowl, to reveal a lively, flowing mythological scene in the manner of the glass engraver Georg Schwanhardt the Elder (1601-67). We see Bacchus, the Roman god of wine, riding a goat, and wife Ariadne, a Cretan princess, riding a panther. Bacchus’s followers, including a goat-hooved satyr, are carrying a type of staff topped with a pine cone which is called a thyrsus, a symbol of fertility.

8940b15a-5b7f-57aa-8f6f-9a3ab5729e1d.name: Molar Flask
8940b15a-5b7f-57aa-8f6f-9a3ab5729e1d.short_description: One of the first techniques that were used to shape glass was casting. Molten glass was poured into a mould, producing a solid block or a thick-walled vessel. When cooled, it was then drilled and deeply carved. This small moulded transparent blueish green colour molar flask made using that glass technique. Its body has a narrow shoulder, a cylindrical neck and a flat top. At the midpoint of each side of its body, triangle motifs with diamond-shaped knobs can be identified. It has four pointed feet, one at each corner resembling the roots of a molar tooth, a shape which gave these objects their name, molar flasks. They were most commonly produced as small flasks for valuable cosmetic liquids such as oils or perfume.

8ba6e315-d0e4-5566-8dc1-7c316457da69.name: Trance
8ba6e315-d0e4-5566-8dc1-7c316457da69.short_description: Glass sculpture, entitled Trance by Preston Singletary, 2006, Tlingit, Seattle, Washington, USA, North America. Blown and sculpted in the shape of a black Tlingit oystercatcher rattle. The sculpture has a buff coloured handle, red beak, a crouching figure on the back of the bird's body. The breast of the bird features a form line hawk design. For Tlingit shaman the oystercatcher represents the border world between water and land, existing in parallel with shaman who represent both the human and spirit worlds. In this artwork Singletary has made a contemporary interpretation of traditional wooden oystercatcher rattles.

8bd2685c-4d66-5da7-a343-412c67377856.name: *Birds in a Park*
8bd2685c-4d66-5da7-a343-412c67377856.short_description:
The source for this reverse glass painting has been identified as an oil painting of the same title by Flemish painter David de Coninck (or de Koninck), also known as Rammelaer. The glass painting was bought on the art market in 2016 as a work attributed to Anna Maria Franziska Pfyffer von Altishofen von Sonnenberg (1688–1757). However, the recently concluded restoration of this reverse glass painting uncovered a monogram and a date inscription previously obscured by the frame. Thanks to these elements, the work was re-attributed to her daughter, Maria Anna Pfyffer von Altishofen (1731).  
  
Mother and daughter came from a patrician family in Lucerne and were influenced by the painting style of Anna Maria Barbara Abesch (1706–73). Their reverse glass paintings have so far been little researched and were unknown to the public for a long time, as they remained in the private possession of the family.

8d462af1-76f7-503e-9ff1-34b14cf92d10.name: Glass cup.
8d462af1-76f7-503e-9ff1-34b14cf92d10.description: A fine enamelled glass cup decorated with three bands, the upper and lower of which are enamelled geometric patterns, with the addition of gold crescents on the top band. The middle band consists of an Arabic inscription written in naskhi (cursive) script that reads: 'In the name of God, where with God willing, Sultan, year.' The decoration also includes a tulip or lily. This beautiful cup is enhanced by the magnificent luminescent colouring of dark-blue, light-brown, brown, violet and gold on a transparent background.
8d462af1-76f7-503e-9ff1-34b14cf92d10.short_description: Glass cup decorated with three bands, the upper and lower of which are enamelled geometric patterns, with gold crescents on the top band. The middle band has an Arabic inscription that reads: ‘In the name of God, where with God willing, Sultan, year.’
8d462af1-76f7-503e-9ff1-34b14cf92d10.method_for_datation: This glass cup was dated by stylistic analysis and by comparing it with other glass objects from the Ottoman period. The shape of the cup, the cursive script, the crescent on top of the upper band, and the form of the loop itself, all indicate that this cup was made in the Ottoman period.
8d462af1-76f7-503e-9ff1-34b14cf92d10.method_for_provenance: The provenance is unknown but this vessel may well have been produced in Syria which during the Ottoman period was famous for its glass, especially enamelled vessels such as this one.

8e7d84ba-9059-5c63-9b62-20ca88488664.name: *The Arrival of the Sclavonians in Venice*
8e7d84ba-9059-5c63-9b62-20ca88488664.short_description:
The veduta painted in reverse shows a sea harbour under a bright, open sky with galleys on the right being loaded by seamen. In the foreground, a pipe-smoking man sits on a pile of crates facing his fellow merchants. Next to gun barrels, rudders and anchors, two men in fashionable dress stand in conversation. A palace backdrop with strongly diminishing perspective rounds off the scene to the left.  
  
The source print for this work is drawn from Melchior Küssel’s (1622–83) *Iconographia* of 1671. The original picture, which carries no inscription indicating the location, is meant to show “the arrival of the Sclavonians in Venice with the prospect of the ships and galleys” after sketches by Johann Wilhelm Baurs (1607–42).  
  
In this interpretation, J.W. Baumgartner largely follows the template of the print, while simplifying the ornamentation of the galleys and palace friezes to improve the legibility of the reverse glass painting. Surprisingly, he also leaves out the dog sitting prominently in the foreground.

8f7d2a93-9bbc-5639-a80e-3049fce77e6c.name: Las palabras las lleva el viento
8f7d2a93-9bbc-5639-a80e-3049fce77e6c.description:
Alberto Gambale was born in Ferrara. He trained at the Academia de Bellas Artes de Bolonia, before embarking on an immense search and experience within the pictorial and sculptural field, discovering glass as the core material for his work. He perfected his work by way of many other courses with significant artists within the contemporary glass field, such as: Detleft Tonz, specialist in Tiffany glass; Gil Reinolds, German-American Bullseye Artist; Elimer Preder; the great, internationally renowned Italian-American artist, Narcissus Quagliata and S&K Higuchi, Japanese experts in molten glass.  
In 1992, he participated in the Polariscope programme, that took place at the Fundación Centro Nacional del Vidrio, in which glassworkers of various nationalities were involved. They all created a piece inspired by a common topic: water. Since, Alberto Gambale has maintained contact with the Escuela del Vidrio at the Foundation, providing several monographic courses, both in stained glass and alternative techniques.  
He currently works in his workshop in Ferrara, experimenting in the field of molten glass, as we can observe in this piece, in addition to teaching classes in different Glass Schools, such as the Escuela de Vidrio de Bolzano and the Escuela de Vidrio de la Real Fábrica de Cristales.

90125812-6d25-5c71-907f-5f0277cdf7b9.name: Mosque Lamp
90125812-6d25-5c71-907f-5f0277cdf7b9.short_description: Enamelled and gilded mosque lamps are a well-established type of glass vessel made in workshops of Syria and Egypt, both important centres of glass making during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods. This Mamluk mosque lamp has a globular body, a long-flared neck and a splayed foot. Six small loop handles are applied around its body. On the neck, two narrow horizontal bands with sketchy vegetal motifs outlined in red frame a broad register with red and white enamelled floral decoration on a blue background accented by three circular medallions with a badge that usually would refer to the donor. The body of the lamp shows another wide register containing a red outlined inscription on a blue background. The *thuluth* inscription reads: “izzli-mawlana al-sultan, al-malik, al- alim, al’adil" (Glory to our Lord, the Sultan, the King, the Wise, the Wise, the Just). The underside of the body shows the same floral pattern as the broad band on the neck. This mosque lamp probably belonged to a Cairene mosque as a donation from an unknown ruler, sultan or high officer. The floral decoration of the mosque lamp, however, is very similar to other mosque lamps belonging to the Complex of Sultan Hassan (r. 748-752 and 756-762 AH / 1347-1351 and 1355-1361 AD).

materials: Glass; free-blown with tooled, enamelled and gilded decoration

90b53651-7f88-581f-b948-a57f23d38d9f.name: Scarlet glass tiered box
90b53651-7f88-581f-b948-a57f23d38d9f.description: The Lord of Satsuma was not only a collector of European glassware, but also founded a small glass industry, copying Western – all Bohemian – crystal glass. For a short period of 17 years (AD 1846–1863) so called "satsuma kiriko" was produced for the Japanese luxury market, and few pieces found their way to Europe. The story of satsuma kiriko glassware begins in the first half of the 19th century AD, when the feudal lord of the Satsuma Domain (now Kagoshima Prefecture), Narioki Shimazu, oversaw the beginning of glass manufacturing in his province. Narioki had set particular emphasis on the production of medicine and therefore needed the adequate containers to store it, so he invited glass artisans from Edo to come to Satsuma. The name “satsuma kiriko” refers to cut-glass products made in the Kagoshima prefecture. They are quite thick and heavy, which is what primarily distinguishes them from Edo kiriko glass, another variety of Japanese glass-cutting artisanship, based in Tokyo. The thicker glass used in satsuma kiriko allows for carvings of varying depths and the creation of colour gradients. These distinctive graduations are hand-made individually by artisans. A characteristic technique used while creating this type of glassware is a technique called “iro-kise” (colour layering), where one transparent layer is overlaid with a coloured layer so that carving a pattern creates a contrast between the clear and coloured sections.

90b53651-7f88-581f-b948-a57f23d38d9f.author: Mio Wakita-Elis, Jana Zarkovic
keywords: Satsuma kiriko; glass; japan; Edo-period

91600251-afb0-5953-bd71-925aa7b4154a.name: Molar glass flacon
91600251-afb0-5953-bd71-925aa7b4154a.short_description: This tiny cut-glass container owes its name to its shape, which resembles a molar tooth with its four wedge-shaped, pointed feet. Originally provided with a stopper, these bottles were used most probably to store and convey expensive perfumes, oils and cosmetic essences. Rich consumers had the shape copied in ivory, metal or even rock crystal.
keywords: Flacon; Abbasid; Glass; cosmetic; cut-glass decoration

9170e068-3b4c-52f1-9c02-806ab9a113f0.name: Jar
9170e068-3b4c-52f1-9c02-806ab9a113f0.description:
This jar is a large glass cup, which was most possibly used for store liquids. This one is made of pale blue-green translucent glass by applying the free-blowing technique. It has a globular body, sloping shoulder; its rim is rounded and turned outwards; and its neck goes concave to the body. It is in an intact situation, but some soil-encrusted weathering, blowing striations, partly flaked off dulling are also seen on the surface. The jar is light green in colour, with a bluish tingle on some parts.  
After the free-blowing technique has been found, possibly around in the first quarter of the 1st century BC, the mould-blowing technique has developed and the desired glass forms and patterns were obtained by blowing into glass, terracotta, stone, metal or wood moulds. The melt at the end of the blowing rod is inflated in two or more pieces of the container until it covers the mould. The use of angular and patterned moulds has usually made it unnecessary to apply additional ornaments. With this technique, mass production of glasses with the same form, measurement, and decoration can be produced by using a single mould. In the form of quadrangular shaped moulds, the glass workshop's or the manufacturer's names were added by applying letters and symbols on the pedestal portion. Glassware that has been blown into a mould whose interior has a raised pattern so that the object shows the pattern with a concavity on the inside, underlying the convexity on the outside. Pattern moulds are not used to impart the final form to the object.

92b4c27b-fe74-52f2-a879-77344c6edb4d.name: Virginal
92b4c27b-fe74-52f2-a879-77344c6edb4d.short_description:
The maker of this glass-covered virginal is still unknown, and it has no known parallel among keyboard instruments, making it highly unique.  
  
The majority of the faces of the instrument are either enamelled or adorned with lamp-worked rods (tooled and fused in the open flame of a lamp or torch), whorls and florets. However, the inner lid is set with 18 panels which depict scenes from the Roman poet Ovid's work *Metamorphoses*. These intricately and exquisitely detailed scenes are framed within scrolling borders and each is labelled with the name of the characters who appear in the 25 books that constitute the poem. Included are Acteon, the hunter who, after catching sight of the goddess Diana bathing was transformed into a stag and killed by his own hounds.  
  
The uniqueness of the virginal has meant it has been associated with a glass virginal that was described as in the possession of Elizabeth I at Hampton Court. A German traveller named Paul Hentzner wrote in 1598 of 'a musical instrument made all of glass except the strings'. However, other contemporary descriptions of instruments at Hampton Court describe them being encrusted with jewels and inscribed with the Queen's cypher, which this instrument is unfortunately lacking.

92d88fbe-43be-5ab5-9828-cbb90f835f7e.name: Ewer
92d88fbe-43be-5ab5-9828-cbb90f835f7e.description: The ewer has a tall slender neck and a piriform body with a long, slender, flattened serpentine spout and a pedestal base. The transparent glass is covered with cobalt blue decoration. The gilded countered lines divide the body into panels each filled with enamelled flower motifs. Half of the spout is covered with brass. The foot, spout and handle were attached later. It is a form that was usually used by the palace and its surroundings.

93402ef7-daa4-558f-a519-d36b24a126b5.name: Pendant
93402ef7-daa4-558f-a519-d36b24a126b5.description: This tiny core-formed glass pendant represents a male head with opaque black face,  pointed chin, yellow fleshy lips, black bulbous nose, black pupils on white ground and black ears decorated above and below with white earrings. A yellow spot is applied to the centre of the forehead. The broken suspension loop on top of the head has been restored. During the 6th century BC, similar pendants were produced in Syria, Cyprus and in the port city of Carthage. Formerly in the collection of Hüseyin Kocabaş.

95395e54-4c90-599d-9ae0-19998e172279.name: Stopper
95395e54-4c90-599d-9ae0-19998e172279.description: As well as the history of Austrian glassmaking was established in the 19th century, there was one movement that gradually paved the way for a different perception of glassmaking, and its customers, and that was Biedermeier. Known for being a decorative art favoured by the middle class, this style was witness to a great revival of glassmaking in Bohemia where new kinds of glass were being produced for a new kind of clientele. This period is characterised by a particular glass cutting technique, and it was used to create these new, marvelous pieces. This unique stopper, as an essential element of a bottle, is made of clear glass with white, polished, cut and opaque overlay. This piece, along with its bottle, is the ideal visual for understanding the great achievements of Biedermeier glasswork and how its vibrant shapes and colours filled the tables and rooms of Germanic Europe in the beginning of the 19th century.
95395e54-4c90-599d-9ae0-19998e172279.bibliography: Thun-Hohenstein, Christoph, et al. (ed), *MAK Guide Wien 1900: Design/Kunstgewerbe 1890–1938*, Curated by Christian Witt-Dörring, exhibition catalogue, Munich: Prestel, 2013: 155, 223.

96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.name: Mosque lamp.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.description: Lamp in the form of a jar with six rings for suspending it and a tall truncated cone-shaped foot. It has an inscription in duplicate on the neck and on the rounded part with the following text: 'This is one of the objects made for the mausoleum of Amir Alan al-Din Ali, son of his Excellency Sayf al-Din Baktamur, *al-hajib* (chancellor), may God grant him mercy.' Three blazons divide the inscription on the neck into equal parts, while another three blazons alternate with stylised arabesques around the lower section of the rounded part. The tall foot has three medallions with simple trefoil motifs. The circular blazon is divided into three fields: the upper and lower areas are white, while the central field contains the image of a horse with a structure in the form of a cupola on its back.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.short_description: The lamp’s inscription dates it to c. AH 721 / AD 1321: ‘This is one of the items made for the mausoleum of Amir Alan al-Din Ali, son of his Excellency Sayf al-Din Baktamur, *al-hajib* (the chancellor), may God grant him mercy’. The shape and decoration of the lamp are typical of the Mamluks.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.dates: Later than Hegira 23 Muharram 721 / AD 21 February 1321.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.dimensions: Height 31 cm, diameter (of rim) 21 cm, diameter (max.) 20.5 cm, diameter (of base) 13.5 cm.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.method_for_datation: Dated, according to the inscription, a short time after the death of the Amir Ali ibn Baktamur, on 21 February 1329.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.method_for_provenance: By expert examination, stylistic and comparative analysis and published catalogues.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.obtention: It came from the collection of Baron Gustave de Rothschild, purchased from Philip Sassoon through Joseph Duveen, in London, on 8 November 1919.

96a0554c-7a9b-535e-bf39-66e5c5a9ead1.name: Bowl
96a0554c-7a9b-535e-bf39-66e5c5a9ead1.description: Glassmakers from Europe started travelling to the capital of China in the beginning of the 18th century AD. This progress was made possible through means of commercial and diplomatic interactions between China and the West, the latter being significantly represented by Venetian glassmakers from Murano. This alliance provided the Chinese with, on a practical level, novel mirrors, lenses, windowpanes and production skills. But also, in artistic terms, the alliance provided them with Aventurine glass and enamel materials, which would soon enough become their own productions. The Western glassmakers were invited to produce glassware mainly in the Chinese style, often copying ceramic forms. Normally glass was used for small snuff bottles and bowls were rare. Therefore, these types of bowls are esteemed for their beautiful form and colour, presenting signature techniques and shapes of Murano glassmaking.

96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.name: Mosque lamp.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.description: An enamelled glass mosque lamp with a flaring mouth and squat body standing on a low foot. The glass is brownish, with decoration in blue and white enamelling, and highlights in red, green, yellow and gold. The decoration consists almost exclusively of an inscription in majestic *thuluth* script, with additional bands of exuberant floral decoration around the neck and just above the foot. The inscription includes verses from the Qur'an (83:22, 24–5) and the phrase 'Glory to our lord, the Sultan, al-Malik al-Muzaffar, the learned, the just, Rukn al-Dunya wa'l-Din, may God grant him victory'. This refers to the Mamluk Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II, who ruled only for a short period, from AH 708–9 / AD 1309–10, before being overthrown and killed. He did, however, govern with a fellow officer as co-regents for the captive al-Nasir Muhammad Ibn Qala'un, beginning in AH 698 / AD 1299. He also built a fine complex in Cairo, containing his tomb as well as a lodge for Sufis, between AH 704–8 / AD 1306–9. Inscriptions in the building – immediately erased by his successor – referred to him even then as Sultan. Since the Qur'anic inscriptions on this lamp refer to the afterlife, it may have been intended to hang in the tomb chamber. The lamp's decoration is also similar to that found in a large Qur'an that Baybars had commissioned for the same complex, suggesting that there may have been a team of designers consciously working to give a unified look to the decorative programme there.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.short_description: An enamelled glass lamp of typical Mamluk form, whose decoration is almost exclusively calligraphic. It includes Qur’anic verses and praise of the short-lived Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II. The verses refer to the afterlife, implying that the lamp may have been intended for the sultan’s tomb.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.method_for_datation: The lamp dates from the brief reign (708–9 / 1309–10) of the Mamluk Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II, to whom the phrase in the inscription, 'Glory to our lord, the Sultan, al-Malik al-Muzaffar, the learned, the just, Rukn al-Dunya wa'l-Din, may God grant him victory', refers.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that glass lamps like this were made in Cairo, as it would have been easier and safer than making them elsewhere and then transporting them.

98166e18-bb09-5f58-b629-24f5548e3e32.name: Goblet
98166e18-bb09-5f58-b629-24f5548e3e32.short_description:
This goblet is one of at least 12 surviving engraved drinking vessels attributed to the Venetian-born glass maker Giacomo Verzelini. Verzelini arrived in England in 1571 and worked at a glasshouse at Crutched Friars in London, producing luxury glass alongside utilitarian products such as window glass. by 1574 Verzelini had obtained a monopoly to make 'drynkinge glasses' of a Venetian type. Before this, from the end of the 14th century until the mid-16th century, all luxury 'cristallo' glass - the Italian word for a fine colourless glass that resembled rock crystal - had been imported from Venice.  
  
This particular goblet has engraving attributed to a French immigrant glass engraver named Anthony de Lysle, who was recorded as working in London in the early 1580s. The inscription reads 'God Save Qyne Elisabeth' and the initials 'RP' and 'MP' over the date '1586', and could possibly signify this goblet as a wedding or wedding anniversary gift.
98166e18-bb09-5f58-b629-24f5548e3e32.bibliography: Liefkes, Reino (ed), *Glass*, London: V&A Publications, 1997: 83 & fig. 101.

98166e18-bb09-5f58-b629-24f5548e3e32.author: Simon Spier
materials: Glass, with mould-blown stem, trailed decoration, diamond-point engraving and gilt

98c2d5f1-e64c-5f9b-8fff-be3cc70af02b.name: Bottle for sprinkling rosewater
98c2d5f1-e64c-5f9b-8fff-be3cc70af02b.description: Green glass rosewater sprinkler decorated with floral and geometric motifs from India. It was used to spray scented water in reception areas such as the majlis. It was widely used during special events such as weddings. In the Qatari dialect, this sprinkler is called a *marash*.

98f86770-ae1c-5bcc-937a-b89afe2716be.name: Hookah Bottle
98f86770-ae1c-5bcc-937a-b89afe2716be.description:
The bottle has a ball-shaped body and an elongated, cylindrical neck with uneven decoration consisting of eight divided vertical fields covering the entire surface of the bottle. Every other vertical field is painted red. There is a red painted band joining all eight vertical fields just below the rim of the bottle. Each of the four red fields are enlivened by floral ornaments. Ochre-yellow volutes with gilding remain visible on each red field near the top of the ball-shaped body. The other four fields of colourless glass are decorated vertically with alternately set flower motifs and black rhomboids.  
The culture of tobacco consumption was widespread in 19th century Serbia. Newspaper articles in the mid-nineteenth century, while openly expressing opinion against tobacco, verify that tobacco was consumed by the majority of the population. A large number of items from that period have been preserved to date, further evidencing the popularity of tobacco consumption and use of various accessories. The widespread use of pipe and cigarette holder from the middle of the 19th century further evidence the decline of the use of the hookah bottle, a smoking accessory which had become increasingly rare. Smoking accessories can best be appreciated in the Museum's collection which, besides different types of pipes, chibouks, (Tur. *Kamış*) and cigarette holders, also contains hookah bottles. A few of these bottles were made by Avram Petronijević Glass Manufacture. Their shape and decoration confirm these designs originate from the Czech glasshouses of the time.

9aeb3d63-30bb-5c86-8ae4-6351d96de1ed.name: Kriegsglas (Glas Nr G/6)
9aeb3d63-30bb-5c86-8ae4-6351d96de1ed.description: In the complete course of art history, rarely has there been a movement in which the decorative arts played such an integral role as Art Nouveau. Among these arts, glass held the most important role by far. As a very flexible and mostly transparent material, glass provided an ideal medium in which artists of the movement could express their ideas that were inspired by nature and organic forms. The style, originating in England, spread throughout Europe; yet the most notable places it set its roots were Belgium, France, the Czech Republic, Germany and Austria. Known as Jugendstil in the German-speaking lands, the movement beared witness to divine glass creations from many, now world-famous, craftspeople who have truly earned honourable mentions in the history of the decorative and applied arts. An essential place for the birth and development of the Jugendstil in Vienna was the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshops), founded by Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser. The main aim of the workshops was to bring the artist or designer closer to the craftspeople and technicians entrusted with the execution of their designs, while also encouraging the designers to be their own crafters. The Wiener Werkstätte was host to a large number of Austrian craftspeople, such as Dagobert Peche, Otto Prutscher and Ludwig Heinrich Jungnickel. This wartime cup presents an ideal example of collaboration between craftspeople and designers in the Wiener Werkstätte. While the form was designed by Prutscher, the design of the decoration, consisting of zig-zag lines in black and yellow, was implemented by Peche. The years painted on the rim of the cup (1914-1915) present the prime time of Peche’s creative expression within the Wiener Werkstätte.

9be9d769-5c24-5c6d-9cf1-7cfea3f480c3.name: Bottle
9be9d769-5c24-5c6d-9cf1-7cfea3f480c3.description:
Lavishly enamelled, purple blown glass piece, with figurative, geometric, botanical and pseudepigraphic motifs. It features a round, flattened, piriform body; oval foot and two vertical handles extending from a bulbous neck.  
  
At the centre of the piece is a tondo-style portrait of a man on one side and a woman on the other. Both figures are dressed in courtier fashion. From the bottle's neck to its shoulder appears an inscription in white, pseudo-*kufic* script, between gilded lines.  
  
This is a highly valuable piece, given its age and rarity. To this day, its origin remains unclear. Experts have suggested Venetian provenance; however, it may also have been blown in the Crown of Aragon (Mallorca, Barcelona or Valencia), where high-quality glass was produced “a la façon de Venise”. Since the piece was found at a Majorcan antique market and had come from a palace in the city, Mallorca appears to be the most plausible place of production.  
  
The use of the vessel also remains uncertain. Commonly known as the Catalan term pixter, these bottles have traditionally been displayed as ornamental or flower vases. Authors such as Justina Fernández García take the view that these are luxurious containers–either for holding scented water or simply for decoration. They are quite similar in form to the so-called ampullas or pilgrim flasks, made from a great variety of materials by cultures widely separated by both space and time.  
  
Pilgrim flasks were traditionally made in pairs as wedding gifts, which may have been the case with this example, given its figurative decoration.

9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.name: Spherical bottle.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.description:
A spherical bottle made of thick, grey-yellow glass with a short opening. Its body is completely covered with decoration that has been cut and deeply engraved into its surface. The decoration consists of a main frieze in which medallions with peacocks and with plant-motifs alternate. Minor side friezes adorn the body. The bottle’s stopper, with which its short opening would have been closed, appears to be missing.  
The bottle’s carefully incised patterns, along with the stylisation of the peacocks and of the ornamentation, find a parallel in the exceptional rock-crystal receptacles that were made in Egypt during the Fatimid era, and which were brought over to Europe after the dissolution of Fatimid treasures. It is therefore possible that this spherical bottle was made by a workshop in Egypt that possessed the knowledge of how to work with, and decorate, rock-crystal. The bottle’s quality suggests that the person who commissioned its making was a member of the court. Its form is similar to that of spherical ceramic vessels known as a ‘sphero-conical vessels’. There is no available information regarding its past use, but, given its workmanship, it must have contained something equally precious.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.short_description: This unique bottle of thick glass is adorned with a deeply cut frieze in which triangles with ornamental patterns alternate with birds in medallions. Fatimid Egypt was famous for its glass and especially rock-crystal vessels, which were highly esteemed in Europe where many survived in treasuries.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.method_for_datation: Dating the object with accuracy is very difficult as few close parallels exist. Only a general date can be offered to place it within the Fatimid period.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.method_for_provenance: Stylistic comparison to polished glasswork from the excavations in Fustat, Cairo’s old town, as well as the particular colouring of the glass, suggest that the object probably came from Egypt. Only new research or new findings will add further information.

9c229d9e-79a7-54ac-9713-e02f195eb59a.name: Bottle
9c229d9e-79a7-54ac-9713-e02f195eb59a.description: With its clean lines and simple designs, this bottle has an almost minimalist aesthetic. Due to the complete weathering in numerous shining colours on a silvery ground, the wheel-cut details are difficult to see. The decoration on its perfectly shaped globular body consists of a simple band around the shoulder. Its circular footring was made by folding. On the pushed-in base is a pontil mark. Its long, cylindrical neck has four main horizontal bands of faceting between four plain minor bands. The uppermost minor band is next to the bottle’s rim. Some of the main bands have a type of diagonal faceting also noticeable on the geometrical relief-cut bottle in the Aga Khan Museum Collection. Like its relief-cut counterpart, this bottle was likely produced in Iran between the 9th and 10th centuries. However, bottles of a related shape are found well into the 11th century in this region.

9ea082f6-5ffe-51c2-accb-120488f26240.name: Hanging Lamp
9ea082f6-5ffe-51c2-accb-120488f26240.description: In many Islamic societies, lamps from pre-Islamic periods continued to be used in both secular and religious contexts. Over time, however, changing needs and tastes inspired craftsmen to reshape these older forms or invent new ones. Though clay or metal remained popular materials for these vessels, glass was highly valued for its translucency and ability to transmit light. This lamp, probably made in the Syrian region due to the use of aquamarine glass, is a beautiful example of Islamic glasswork. Its globular body, with a wide neck of the about the same diameter as the body, rests on a footring that was achieved by folding and pushing in the underside of the base. Six suspension rings or handles of dark blue glass were applied on its shoulders. Its shape is a recognizable type; a nearly identical lamp—though larger and with a dark blue thread around the rim—can be found in the Khalili Collection.

9ec702fb-8729-598a-ab20-ae8d02904fce.name: Glass dish.
9ec702fb-8729-598a-ab20-ae8d02904fce.description: A dish of green-tinted moulded glass, with the pattern impressed on the outside surface of the dish's base. The inside surface is plain and smooth. The design of the impression consists of a central star with seven corners, surrounded by seven roundels, each of which contains an arrangement of circles. The star is also filled with an arrangement of small circles. Mould-blown glassware was made primarily for everyday use. The green colour of the transparent dish is achieved by mixing iron oxides with the original frit mixture, from which glass is made.
9ec702fb-8729-598a-ab20-ae8d02904fce.short_description: Mould-blown glassware was made primarily for everyday use. This shallow dish is plain on the inside but impressed with a pattern on the outside. Many glassmakers from different parts of the Islamic Middle East flocked to work in Fustat’s glass-making industry, which had flourished since pre-Islamic times.
9ec702fb-8729-598a-ab20-ae8d02904fce.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the style and manufacturing techniques used to make this dish resemble similar examples of Fatimid glass wares, especially some of those found in the Aegean Sea shipwreck at Serçe Limanı, off the south-west coast of Turkey, which has been dated to AH 415 / AD 1025.

9ece1ead-7c0b-528b-bdd1-e15c148b868c.name: Medallion
9ece1ead-7c0b-528b-bdd1-e15c148b868c.short_description:
In Rome in the 4th century, glass-makers fully exploited the technique of sandwiched gold glass. Religious subjects - predominantly Christian but also Jewish - as well as portraits of families and individuals such as this piece were depicted in gold leaf with stippled and painted decoration. This was then placed between two layers of colourless glass that were fused together.  
  
The identity of the man in this portrait is not known, but the costly process of this technique means it was somebody of high status. Medallions formed by this method were sometimes made as decorative pendants for wearing, but most were set into the base of bowls and dishes to commemorate a special occasion or present as a wedding gift. The portrait disks were later broken out of the dishes to be re-used as grave markers.

a00cd867-2b09-5d0b-990c-81502a78b6fc.name: Diodata Vase
a00cd867-2b09-5d0b-990c-81502a78b6fc.description:
This vase, entitled *Diodata*, was designed by Ettore Sottsass in 1974 for the Murano-based Vetreria Vistosi, a facility that remains active to this day. The piece is included in a collection of ten designs, reproduced in a limited edition of 250 examples. An inscription on the bottom of the foot indicates that this is example 142 of 250.  
  
This may be considered the artist’s first great glass collection. The Austrian-born, ethnically Italian designer devoted himself to glass design from 1947 through the rest of his career. He collaborated with numerous traditional firms in Murano and, beginning in the 1980s, with industrial companies such as Baccarat and Swarovski.  
  
Sottsass saw in glass an extraordinary mystery and excitement, and, as with ceramics, he was drawn to the elements of magic and uncertainty inherent in the introduction of fire to his work. The scope of his playful and vibrantly colourful designs ranged widely, from ceramics, to furniture, to lighting.

a0cf2656-1033-510e-b3c1-b2bc561df823.name: Flask.
a0cf2656-1033-510e-b3c1-b2bc561df823.description:
Glass flask made with two types of paste: fine, whitish and transparent in the body and deeper blue at the top of the neck and the decoration. It has a slightly flattened globular body and a long, thin, cylindrical neck finished with an out-curving brim. The base is made up of a truncated-cone foot-ring. It is decorated with fine threads of blue glass paste that wind in a spiral around the neck, and a thread that marks the base, of which little has survived.  
Andalusian glassware and the techniques associated with it originated in the East in the area of Syria, Palestine and Egypt. The body of the piece was blown, a technique that originated in the Middle East and dates back to the 2nd century BC. This technique enabled the manufacture of large glass objects and their export around the Mediterranean area.  
It has been decorated using overlaying, a technique of equally remote origin that was widespread in Roman times. This technique takes advantage of the flexibility of the glass, which at high temperatures can be stretched into threads and easily attached to the hot surface of the object. During the Almohad period, this technique seems to have been widely used in eastern Andalusia in the AH 6th / AD 12th century and in particular during the first half of the AH 7th / AD 13th century. Although in principle it is a decorative element, it was also used for practical ends to provide the object with greater stability and to strengthen the more fragile areas, as is the case with this piece, whose long neck and base have been reinforced.  
The study of glass from al-Andalus is hampered both by the problem inherent in the fragility of the material and its scarcity, distribution and the inability in many cases to determine its exact origin.
a0cf2656-1033-510e-b3c1-b2bc561df823.short_description: The disappearance of most Hispano-Muslim glass objects makes this Almohad-period flask extremely valuable. It was blown and decorated with a blue glass filament that also served to strengthen the neck and base.
a0cf2656-1033-510e-b3c1-b2bc561df823.method_for_datation: Recent studies on materials from digs in the Almohad period enable us to date this piece to that era. It has parallels with objects from digs in eastern Spain (Cieza, Murcia and Aspe, Alicante) dated from between the 6th and 7th / 12th and 13th centuries.
a0cf2656-1033-510e-b3c1-b2bc561df823.method_for_provenance: This piece comes from Villaricos, Almería. In the 7th / 13th century, Ibn Said mentioned the towns of Murcia and Almería as centres of glass production, which is supported by recent archaeological discoveries. Although there are not standard types of Andalusian glassware to reference, the closed forms and long thin neck must have been relatively common. The piece may have been made locally after contemporary Syrian models.
a0cf2656-1033-510e-b3c1-b2bc561df823.obtention: This piece and two other flasks are part of the extensive Siret Collection, which was donated to the National Archaeological Museum in 1935.

a11eb8bc-636b-52de-9a47-47405abc140d.name: Chandelier
a11eb8bc-636b-52de-9a47-47405abc140d.short_description: During the nineteenth century, a vogue developed in western and southern Asia for European glass. Manufacturers such as Baccarat in France responded to these markets by producing glassware with motifs and aesthetics that they believed would appeal to these new consumers. This chandelier is thought to have been made for export to India. Indeed, Doris Duke purchased the chandelier in 1966 from the estate of Salar Jung, a noted collector in Hyderabad, India.

a237773b-cce0-5972-a24d-1e563fd1cb62.name: Little jar with crested handle
a237773b-cce0-5972-a24d-1e563fd1cb62.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century and as a training school for specialising artisans. The concept was part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The tendency of Murano's industries in using bizarre shapes, often of zoomorphic inspiration, gave life to manufacts not so much functional as extremely representative of the decorative needs, and it was very successful. The motif of glass filaments worked with pincers to look like crests, typical of the 17th century objects, is used also in the little ruby-red jar with gold leaf from the second half of the 19th century and resembling objects from Cinquecento and Seicento.
a237773b-cce0-5972-a24d-1e563fd1cb62.holder: Museo Artistico Industriale, National Gallery of Ancient Art in Palazzo Barberini
a237773b-cce0-5972-a24d-1e563fd1cb62.author: Marina Minozzi

a27191fc-6c79-50d0-a839-de3c555b4495.name: Anonymous
a27191fc-6c79-50d0-a839-de3c555b4495.short_description: This work, designed as a double-headed fish, is executed using the fusion technique. Whilst the main body of the fish has been finished in transparent glass, upon which red fish have been fused, the head and tail part of the fish is red and white.

a2abf9d6-891e-59a0-9c6b-0f36d803394d.name: Beaded Water Glass
a2abf9d6-891e-59a0-9c6b-0f36d803394d.description: A massive glass made of transparent, grey-toned glass with bubbles, cylindrical shape, set on a low, round pedestal base, from Avram Petronijević's Manufacture. The walls of the glass are wrapped with a bead embroidery with floral motifs. The central decoration is a wreath pattern, displaying the Cyrillic initials "M.C.", with the year 1855 shown on the opposite side of the glass. The initials are those of the embroiderer, Marija Stojković (Cyrillic: Марија Стојковић) from Belgrade, with the year reflective of the time of the ornamentation. The appearance of glassware items decorated with beads was very popular in the bourgeois houses of the 19th century where women's hand-made works were highly appreciated. Several similar items with beads originating from Belgrade families, including this beaded water glass, have been preserved in the collection of the Museum of Applied Arts.
a2abf9d6-891e-59a0-9c6b-0f36d803394d.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.

a2e5bb5b-7819-5d32-b10a-45c9c949d4e7.name: Stangenglas (Tumbler)
a2e5bb5b-7819-5d32-b10a-45c9c949d4e7.short_description:
The Stangenglas tumbler, with its raised foot (or base), is a characteristic glass from the second half of the 16th century. It generally came with a lid.  
The shape and decoration attribute the 30cm tall tumbler to the Hall glass workshops near Innsbruck, Austria. The courtly glass workshops in Hall employed Venetian glass-blowers who were able to decolourise glass. With their diamond-engraved decor, glasses from Hall numbered among top-quality products traded at high prices and were popular goods at the time – in Switzerland as well. In the early 16th century, the glass came into the ownership of Christoph Oeri, goldsmith and guild master of the Zimmerleuten guild in Zurich, Switzerland. As a goldsmith with experience in the technique of diamond engraving, he added further inscriptions to the already decorated glass. The following can be read around the top edge of the glass: *Christoffel Öri det diß Glaß ver Ehren der Zumfft zu Ehren*. The year 1632 and the names and coats of arms of further members of the guild and of Zurich families were also engraved.  
In the 16th century, it was almost tradition for the proud owners of this type of glass to have virtually the whole surface retrospectively engraved with signatures.
a2e5bb5b-7819-5d32-b10a-45c9c949d4e7.initial_owner: Christoph Oeri (1599–1637), goldsmith and guild master of the Zimmerleuten guild in Zurich
a2e5bb5b-7819-5d32-b10a-45c9c949d4e7.workshop: Hall glass workshop near Innsbruck, Austria

a4481384-fc41-5853-929a-c2b5ad719277.name: Vase
a4481384-fc41-5853-929a-c2b5ad719277.description: In the complete course of art history, rarely has there been a movement in which the decorative arts played such an integral role as Art Nouveau. Among these arts, glass held the most important role by far. As a very flexible and mostly transparent material, glass provided an ideal medium in which artists of the movement could express their ideas that were inspired by nature and organic forms. The style, originating in England, spread throughout Europe; yet the most notable places it set its roots were Belgium, France, the Czech Republic, Germany and Austria. Known as Jugendstil in the German-speaking lands, the movement beared witness to divine glass creations from many, now world-famous, craftspeople who have truly earned honourable mentions in the history of the decorative and applied arts. An essential place for the birth and development of the Jugendstil in Vienna was the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshops), founded by Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser. The main aim of the workshops was to bring the artist or designer closer to the craftspeople and technicians entrusted with the execution of their designs, while also encouraging the designers to be their own crafters. The Wiener Werkstätte was one of Hoffmann’s central projects throughout his long life. Therefore, his contribution to the art of the Austrian Jugendstil is a multi-faceted one, ranging from architecture to the decorative arts. This example follows the more nature-oriented aspect of Art Nouveau glassmaking, presenting a blow moulded, tulip-formed vase with bulges. The radiant yellow colour further symbolises the beauty of primary, natural colours. These kinds of objects were supposed to harmonise themselves among other objects in their area and were deliberately made for specific interiors and purposes.

a470fa1a-6e06-50f5-bd4e-767c5c5ced63.name: Perfume Bottle
a470fa1a-6e06-50f5-bd4e-767c5c5ced63.description:
This is a fine and early example of a series of janiform head-flasks in glass. It was made in a two part mould and each of the two heads (related to the Roman god, Janus) is the same. Such mould-blown janiform bottles seem to originate in the first century AD and widely seen around the Eastern Mediterranean region. Janus masks continued being made into the third and fourth centuries. The janiform bottle has been used as a scent bottle which most probably belonged to the wealthy Roman households. It was used to store aromatic and herbal oils, as well as perfumes.  
The double-faced glass bottle is made from clear glass which is light-blue in colour and it has a long cylindrical neck which protrudes from the centre of the head. The head has wavy hair and clear facial features which provide a naturalistic appearance. The bottom of the neck has been flattened so as to make a base for the bottle.
a470fa1a-6e06-50f5-bd4e-767c5c5ced63.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and material dating

a4e3deec-cae3-5c1a-a173-eb24aba52ed1.name: Vase with *chinoiseries*
a4e3deec-cae3-5c1a-a173-eb24aba52ed1.short_description: Glass has always been used to imitate more valuable materials. This baluster vase with *chinoiseries* imitates much more costly porcelain in form, material and decor. The production of opaque white glass started in the early 15th century and enjoyed a heyday in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. At the same time, porcelain was becoming more widespread. Painted cups, small jugs, plates, sugar pots and decorative vases were a more affordable alternative to expensive porcelain crockery.

a56a9bf0-2b17-5702-8aa1-d72790e9ec02.name: Tumbler
a56a9bf0-2b17-5702-8aa1-d72790e9ec02.description:
The glass is bell-shaped and rests on a wider, cylindrical base. It is embossed with engraved motifs. The front displays the initials "A.K." encircled by a garland. The opposite side and rim display a floral motif. An 1844 Austrian coin was placed inside the glass' stand.  
It was determined by comparison and stylistic analysis that the glass was most likely created in the first glass manufactory of the Principality of Serbia, which was owned by Avram Petronijević, the then Minister of Foreign Affairs and the envoy at the Sublime Porte. At the invitation of Avram Petronijević, glassmakers came from Bohemian and Bavarian glasshouses. Considering that the manufactory operated during a very short period, from 1846 to 1852, only a small number of items can be reliably linked to its production and few have been preserved. Most items were caste or mould blown. They are distinguished by their common characteristics: a greyish tone of glass that testifies to the presence of lead, the presence of bubbles in the glass mass, and the thick walls of the object. They were heavy, but harmonious shapes, such as this very rare example that was most likely made for a particular person.
a56a9bf0-2b17-5702-8aa1-d72790e9ec02.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.

a6804749-4db3-5928-ab59-97dac2ce7b41.name: Bottle
a6804749-4db3-5928-ab59-97dac2ce7b41.description: This striking bottle of bluish-green glass has a globular body and long, thin cylindrical neck leading to a flanged opening. Its high pronounced footring was made by folding. On the underside of the circular pushed-in base is a pontil mark. Its unusual patterns demonstrate two techniques popular until the early 13th century. One involves blowing a glass gather into a mould; the other involves manipulating glass threads to decorate certain parts of the vessel. It would be well-suited to holding perfumed water such as rosewater.
materials: Glass, bluish with green tinge, white weathering; mould-blown, tooled, applied, worked on the pontil

a6b1ce7e-6a95-56a8-99c6-e54ab8761d25.name: Pocket tumbler
a6b1ce7e-6a95-56a8-99c6-e54ab8761d25.description:
Pocket tumbler of translucent, somewhat milky glass, decorated with twists of thread embedded in the paste to form irregular bow shapes of red, white and blue colour.  
  
This type of piece is characterized by a flattened form, similar to that of the hip flask, lending to its portability in either a waist pouch, small pocket or cloth bag worn by women under a skirt or apron. Many of these tumblers were made by special order, as evidenced by frequent inscriptions of ownership and dedication.  
  
The *filigrana* decoration of threads inserted in the vitreous paste—associated with the products of Murano—was a style that spread widely and was much imitated in Spain.
a6b1ce7e-6a95-56a8-99c6-e54ab8761d25.type: Glass and crystal; objects for personal use
a6b1ce7e-6a95-56a8-99c6-e54ab8761d25.provenance: La Granja de San Ildefonso, Segovia, Spain

a7db21f3-7be7-5d4b-8f81-38cd6e153579.name: Glass tumbler.
a7db21f3-7be7-5d4b-8f81-38cd6e153579.description:
Found in Palace B, a translucent, honey-coloured glass tumbler that is entirely decorated with floral and vegetal motifs organised in multiple horizontal bands along the edges and alternating vertical fields along the body. The decoration is incised into the glass, incorporating styles that are occasionally found on carved wood or metal from the period, but not usually on glass.  
Technically speaking the tumbler is of great importance since the thin, engraved glass was worked with a sharp tool, and although the technique was known in the Roman period, it was usually used in tandem with other techniques. In the Islamic period, however, it was used as a stand-alone technique, and the incisions were cut deeper into the glass.  
Raqqa, a region that lies between the Euphrates and Balikh rivers, flourished during the Abbasid period. A group of Abbasid palaces, parts of which were excavated during the 1950s and labelled with the letters A, B, C and D, are found there.
a7db21f3-7be7-5d4b-8f81-38cd6e153579.short_description: Although the production and ornamentation of glass in Syria has an ancient heritage, this glass tumbler reveals an example of delicate and precise decoration by incision, a technique which flourished under early Islamic rule.
a7db21f3-7be7-5d4b-8f81-38cd6e153579.method_for_datation: The tumbler is believed to be contemporary to Palace B, which has been dated to the period of Caliph al-Mu'tasim Billah (r. 218–27 / 833–41).
a7db21f3-7be7-5d4b-8f81-38cd6e153579.method_for_provenance: The tumbler was found during an archaeological excavation at Raqqa. There is no way of establishing whether it was made locally or imported, as similar glass production flourished in both Baghdad and Damascus.
a7db21f3-7be7-5d4b-8f81-38cd6e153579.obtention: The tumbler was found during archaeological excavations undertaken by a delegation from the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities during the 1950s under the direction of Nasib Salibi.
