a835149f-ed2d-538e-8ad7-25be906b507d.name: Crystal Pathways
a835149f-ed2d-538e-8ad7-25be906b507d.short_description: The optical properties of glass coupled with developments in technology that allowed digital imagery to be laser etched into blocks of glass have been used by artists and scientists alike to capture the imperceptible elements of our bodies, bringing degenerative conditions or the result of injury or illness into focus and discussion. The Museum chose to explore this artistic glass output to illustrate the brain of a volunteer on the Lothian Birth Cohort Project who was being scanned to gauge the cognitive aging of the brain for a new gallery display. The work shows a brain split into two showing their neural pathways, and how this individual has a slightly lop-sided white matter.
a835149f-ed2d-538e-8ad7-25be906b507d.obtention: The model was commissioned from the company by the Museum in 2015 for display in the Enquire gallery.
a835149f-ed2d-538e-8ad7-25be906b507d.author: Sophie Goggins, Sarah Rothwell
keywords: Contemporary Glass; Model

a98831d9-536c-5277-9779-66a5c608c1a8.name: Serpent glass *à la façon de Venise*
a98831d9-536c-5277-9779-66a5c608c1a8.description: The delicate nature and dainty shape of Venetian glasses are still fascinating today. The fragile glass is supported by an ornate “serpent stem” with white spiral threads. The shape is characteristic of Venetian glass, which, in the form of valuable wine glasses, adorned opulent tables in the 17th century. North of the Alps, Venetian glass was a term for highest quality colourless fine glass mass. For a long time, these glasses, produced in Venice using a perfect technique to achieve an elegant shape, were seen as the yardstick for glass-making. Glass works north of the Alps tried to imitate these glasses. In the 16th century, glass-blowers who had fled from Venice started to establish their own works in other parts of Europe. Their products gave rise to the term *à la façon de Venise*. This term was used for glassware from the 16th and 17th century, mainly for glasses made from decolourised glass mass and for shapes that were less common north of the Alps. With the rise of Bohemian and English glassware in the 18th century, Venetian glass lost its exclusivity.
a98831d9-536c-5277-9779-66a5c608c1a8.obtention: Unknown. The glass was probably obtained at the end of the 19th century.
keywords: Serpent glass à la façon de Venise; Glass; Blown

a999f862-64ab-5ce2-8f77-55cdb9ec19dd.name: Cycle
a999f862-64ab-5ce2-8f77-55cdb9ec19dd.short_description: The work is made out of white opal glass, formed into an empty bird's nest, an effect obtained by a styling technique in the flame. With this skin, the glass has been dilated to the desired extent allowing it to then be entangled into an empty bird's nest.
a999f862-64ab-5ce2-8f77-55cdb9ec19dd.author: Şeyma Nur Hançerli, Elif Akgül
keywords: Glass; Sculpture; Contemporary
materials: Glass; flasher styling technique, hot glass editing

aa9ee7a9-70e0-5d32-a3df-58b534ae7733.name: Stag glass
aa9ee7a9-70e0-5d32-a3df-58b534ae7733.short_description:
The conspicuously shaped drinking glass has an inserted attachment in the shape of a stag with a peacock on its back. The hollow shaft and hollow body of the animal are used as a suction pipe via the stag’s muzzle. It required a great deal of skill to be able to drink from this glass successfully.  
There were no limits to the range of forms of trick-puzzle glasses. Producing them must have been a great pleasure for glass-blowers. Popular motifs included pigs, dogs, boots and pistols, as well as phallic glasses, which are evidence of hilarious drinking games in the 16th and 17th centuries.
aa9ee7a9-70e0-5d32-a3df-58b534ae7733.obtention: Donation of Heinrich Angst (1847–1922), first director of the Swiss National Museum, on the occasion of his retirement in 1903
materials: Colourless glass *à la façon de Venise*

aab7756a-7fbc-5383-97de-198c2614e471.name: Token or weight.
aab7756a-7fbc-5383-97de-198c2614e471.description:
Green glass token with a relief border, in a reasonable state of conservation, weighing slightly less than one whole *dirham*, which is 2.97 g. The token is marked only with a three-line inscription in *kufic* characters within a circle in the middle of the front face. The first line reads ‘*al-imâm al-Zâhir*’, the second ‘*al azaz din Allâh*’ and the third ‘*amîr al-mu minin*’.  
Traditional Byzantine glass tokens were generally used as monetary weights, and this use was particularly common among Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs as well as among the Egyptian Tulunids and the Aglabids of North Africa. Shi’ite caliphs also used tokens for other means, particularly from the time of al-Mu’izz (AH 341–65 / AD 953–75). The fact that many of the tokens found are of identical weight suggests that they were used as ‘fiduciary coins’ in place of bronze coins, particularly as bronze was extremely rare in Egypt at that time. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that no glass tokens have ever been found in Syria, where bronze was abundantly available. These tokens are inscribed on at least one of their faces, bearing the name of the caliph and sometimes even the mint. Most Fatimid tokens come from the time of two caliphs in particular, Abu ‘Ali al-Hakim (AH 386–411 / AD 996–1021) and al-Mustansir (AH 427–87 / AD 1036–94), although a large number also come from the time of al-Zahir, al-Amir and other caliphs.
aab7756a-7fbc-5383-97de-198c2614e471.short_description: Glass token probably used as a fiduciary coin in place of bronze coin.

aadfbd26-bbc6-5010-9278-b328b5482f27.name: Sprinkler Bottle
aadfbd26-bbc6-5010-9278-b328b5482f27.description:
This little sprinkler bottle is a fine sample of the use of the mould-blown glass forming technique. After the free-blowing technique has been found, possibly around in the first quarter of the 1st century BC, the mould-blowing technique has developed and the desired glass forms and patterns were obtained by blowing into glass, terracotta, stone, metal or wood moulds. The use of angular and patterned moulds has usually made it unnecessary to apply additional ornaments. With this technique, mass production of glasses with the same form, measurement, and decoration can be produced by using a single mould.  
The sprinkler bottle has a pale yellow-green body, light green rim, and a very short cylindrical neck. Its rim is broad and flaring; folded over, in and flattened with cut-out underneath and there is a constriction inside at the junction with the body. The body was most possibly blown in a two-part mould; the rim and the neck were blown separately and added to the body. There is a small jagged pontil scar towards the edge of the flattish bottom. Its globular body is almost in an intact situation, except for one small, later filled hole. Zig-zag pattern of elongated, hollow lozenges and two raised concentric circles are clearly seen on the body and on the bottom. The body is partly covered with enamel-like weathering which mostly flaked off and left iridescence and faint pitting on the surface. There are also many large and pinprick bubbles on the surface.

aae0ca9a-c9fe-584a-8b53-3218823e3dee.name: Glass vessel
aae0ca9a-c9fe-584a-8b53-3218823e3dee.short_description: Professor Joseph Black, 1728-1799, was a distinguished researcher and teacher of chemistry at the University of Edinburgh. He was the first to identify carbon dioxide within the air and is understood to have used this large glassware in his classroom.  It is believed that this glassware was a special commission from Archibald Geddes’ glass factory in Leith, which more usually made bottles, and that Joseph Black’s chemical expertise made him a valuable consultant for his friend Geddes on glass composition and manufacture. These piece of apparatus were used for distillation, and the functional elegance of their forms reflects the skill of the blower to free blow a form beyond a bottle mould that was aesthetically pleasing and practical.

ad175864-1054-546a-bf3e-d53d2c69fccb.name: Kubus
ad175864-1054-546a-bf3e-d53d2c69fccb.description:
Modular set of ten stacking food storage containers, arranged on a tray. Formed of pressed, transparent, heat-resistant glass. Some of the pieces bear the signature of a double X, inscribed within a rectangular hexagon.  
  
*Kubus* (*Kubus-Geschirr*) is one of Wilhelm Wagenfeld’s most renowned and innovative creations. Originally trained as a metalsmith, Wagenfeld joined the Bauhaus metal workshop, where he later taught for several years. Between 1935 and 1947, he was artistic director of Vereinitge Lausitzer Glaswerke, where he focused on producing blown and pressed glass sets, citrus squeezers, dishes, jugs, vases and glasses, among other objects. He became an industrial designer and took charge of his own publicity.  
  
Typical of the Bauhaus approach, *Kubus* is a product whose form is perfectly suited to its function. Likewise, it reflects the organisation's commitment to the standardised forms and affordable prices of socially responsible industrial design.

ad371140-da9f-5bda-9c54-d24e826bb7ef.name: Ribbed Bowl
ad371140-da9f-5bda-9c54-d24e826bb7ef.description:
The production technique of the ribbed bowls which are dated before the invention of the blowing technique could not be finalized. The forms and conditions of these bowls need to be carefully defined. A ribbed bowl which has sharp introversion in the rim and a narrowing rim from the trunk should be made by using the mould-blowing technique, not by simply moulding. Some researchers have suggested that ribbed bowls are made in a hollow mould, while others have used the lost wax technique. It is conceivable that a ribbed disc can be poured onto the mould, and after it has cooled down, it can be collapsed again with the help of heat on a semi-spherical inner mould. During some experimental production stages of a ribbed bowl, it is understood that the ribs can form the glass melt by means of a pair of tweezers that can be compressed by means of a spacer (without the mould).  
Monochrome coloured and naturally coloured ribbed bowls of the late first century BC and first century AD, presumably developed from the Syro-Palestinian monochrome ribbed bowls of the early first century BC. This type of monochrome and/or naturally coloured ribbed bowls were the pre-eminent among cast tableware that can be ascribed to the early imperial period. The earliest classes of Roman ribbed bowls have many stylistic and technical features in common with those ascribed to the late Hellenistic period. Ribbed bowls such as this one were produced from Tiberian times to the end of the Flavian period, making monochrome ribbed bowls one of the last types of Roman glassware to be made by casting techniques.  
The ribbed bowl in our collection is light blue-green coloured; sagged; rotary-polished on the interior, the outside of the rim and across the tops of the ribs; fire-polished on the rest of the exterior and has an almost flat bottom. On the exterior, thirty-one ribs of varying length are slanting downwards vertically; the ribs end beyond the junction of the side and the bottom and the side of the bowl is convex between some of the ribs. The bowl has small amount of lime encrustation, milky weathering, dulling and fine pitting on the surface.

ad7466a2-5fe7-545f-9873-cd226f645d31.name: Mosque lamp
ad7466a2-5fe7-545f-9873-cd226f645d31.description: Among the many forms of art present and flourishing on the territory of Syria, glassmaking was of particular importance. Syrian artisans seem to have been masters of the art, practicing various techniques from the earliest of times, for much of the best Roman glass was made in this area. The early development of glassmaking in Syria is primarily attributed to the Phoenicians, who previously inhabited the coastal belt. The mastery of techniques has continued into the Muslim period, since blown, moulded, and cut glass were made for the Muslim patrons. An essential aspect of the complete practice was the one of enamelled glass – a technique familiar to us from Roman times, but one that truly flourished and completely evolved under the Islamic rulers. A particular characteristic of this fruitful period is the decoration of a very distinctive form of lamp, with a large bulging base and upper section and narrow waist in between. Earlier examples are usually assigned to the 13th century AD, but the majority belongs to the 14th century AD or maybe even later. *Kufic* or *naksh* script were frequently the central element of decoration, whereas in Egypt, there was presence of motifs with heraldic significance. This magnificent example is decorated with gold, blue, red and green enamel, which create floral and organic forms, as well as arabesques.

aeb579b2-8023-5a4b-adbc-9cc17cab243b.name: Stengelglas
aeb579b2-8023-5a4b-adbc-9cc17cab243b.description: The animal designs covering the cylindrical bowl of this glass are typical for the painter L. H. Jungnickel, as he is well known for his animal print cycles. This particular example features monkeys. Originally, the confined chessboard pattern was supposed to be used for the glass’s stem and foot as well. This stemware was shown at the Exhibition of Works from the Austrian Arts Industry in the Museum of Art and Industry in AD 1911/12 along with Josef Hoffmann´s first Bronzite decorated glasses. It also was one of the objects presented at the Kölner Werkbundausstellung (exhibition of Deutscher Werkbund in Cologne) in AD 1914. For a similarly designed glass with a round bowl also exhibited AD 1911/12, Jungnickel chose different animals set in medallions. Subsequently these designs were used to decorate a jardinière.

aee4b09c-deb2-5cae-9bb8-35b97edcff1a.name: Beaker
aee4b09c-deb2-5cae-9bb8-35b97edcff1a.short_description: This beaker is of conical form with a narrow base extending to a wide opening. Its size and shape suggest that it was a nesting beaker, one of a collection of three other similar examples. The base includes the addition of a thin ring added to provide more stability. This technical feature confirms the beaker’s slightly later production during the second half of the seventh century AH / thirteenth century AD. The beaker is decorated with a central frieze comprised of seated figures interspersed with medallions and flanked by two fine horizontal bands; one with an Arabic calligraphic inscription and the other with a stylized scroll motif. The inscription reads, “al'-izz li-mawlana al-sultan al-malik al-'amil .... al-murabit, al-muthagir, al-mu'ayyad al-muzaffar" (Glory to our Lord, the Sultan, the King, the Diligent, the Defender, the Protector of Frontiers, the One helped [by God], the Triumphant). Benedictory inscriptions such as these naming an unspecified ruler appear frequently on Mamluk glassware. The seated figures – most probably musicians –represent a common decorative feature found on Mamluk glass. Forming part of a visual language known as the "princely cycle", such figures were intended to illustrate a courtly pastime likely enjoyed by a ruler or emir.
aee4b09c-deb2-5cae-9bb8-35b97edcff1a.dates: AH late 7th century / AD late 13th century
aee4b09c-deb2-5cae-9bb8-35b97edcff1a.bibliography: Greenwood, William J., et al., *The Hunt: Princely Pursuits in Islamic Lands*, Milan: Silvana Editoriale, 2015: 152-153.

materials: Glass; free-blown with tooled and enamelled decoration

b00aafcf-8e21-51f7-9183-e6c70742dd92.name: Glass bottle
b00aafcf-8e21-51f7-9183-e6c70742dd92.description:
This small green blown-glass bottle was discovered during the 2003 excavation of the city of al Zubarah. It dates from the AH 12th–13th century / AD 18th to 19th centuries.  
  
Due to its small size, this container was used to store perfume or precious oils and was probably manufactured in the Levant

b0353cc2-2f07-5775-95f5-857ed2ba17a2.name: Glass weight.
b0353cc2-2f07-5775-95f5-857ed2ba17a2.description:
A glass weight produced in Egypt between the AH 2nd and 9th / AD 8th and 15th centuries, which would have been used to check the weights of prototype gold, silver and copper coins. A gold *dinar* would typically weigh 4.25 g and a silver *dirham* would have weighed 2.97 g. Metal coins were hand-minted and it was, therefore, difficult to ensure the exact accuracy of the weight; tampering with the weight of hand-minted coins was also a problem. Glass weights such as this one were developed to monitor the accuracy of metal coinage, and were used by the sellers to make sure that the correct vale of metal was being paid in return for the goods being purchased. The Arabic texts stamped on these weights usually bore the name of the ruler or official who ordered their issue and were usually re-issued every time the ruler or official changed office. This particular example is pale-green in colour and has a stamped Arabic inscription on one side (still to be deciphered), while the back is flat and plain.  
  
These glass weights testify to Fustat's position as one of the richest cities of the Middle East during the Fatimid period (AH 296–566 / AD 909–1171). A busy port, the markets of Fustat traded a wide variety of goods that arrived from all over the world, from places as far away as China. Fustat was also an important manufacturing centre, producing fine ceramics, glassware, steel and copper products, soap, sugar, textiles and paper.
b0353cc2-2f07-5775-95f5-857ed2ba17a2.short_description: This glass weight was made in AH 5th- / AD 11th-century Egypt. Merchants and shopkeepers used such weights to check the weight of gold or silver coins, making sure that they were of the right weight and nobody had tampered with their precious metal. They were marked with the same designs as on the coins.

b0353cc2-2f07-5775-95f5-857ed2ba17a2.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: many comparable examples have been found in Fustat, Egypt, which have been dated to the Fatimid period after deciphering the scripts stamped on them.

b07925c9-6a74-5708-ae78-2988cae0e279.name: Flask
b07925c9-6a74-5708-ae78-2988cae0e279.short_description:
Core-formed cobalt blue unguent jar, of krateriskos form, with a lip and foot rimmed with yellow. The neck and body is decorated with applied thread decoration in white bordered by yellow, and there are separately formed handles in blue.  
  
This vessel was made at the time of Amenhotep III and perhaps for the pharaoh himself. Excavation of numerous fragments at Amenhotep's palace at Malkata suggests that it was the site of an important glasshouse.
b07925c9-6a74-5708-ae78-2988cae0e279.obtention: Purchased by the museum in 1868 from the dealer John Webb

b0e82547-2897-5f74-a18e-287a0eac8692.name: Geissler tube
b0e82547-2897-5f74-a18e-287a0eac8692.short_description: In the mid-19th century, the visual effects achievable by running an electrical discharge through a partially evacuated tube were the subject of both scientific and visual exploration.  Among the most prominent researchers working with discharge tubes from 1857 was Heinrich Geissler (1814–1879) who gave his name to a type of these tubes. A multitude of fluorescent colours and effects were achieved by modifying the gaseous and solid contents of the tube.  These scientific and ornamental tubes led to the discovery of gases including neon, argon and xenon, and developed into neon lights, fluorescent lights, Xray tubes and cathode ray televisions as well as complex sculptural compositions created by lampworkers.
b0e82547-2897-5f74-a18e-287a0eac8692.obtention: Donated to the Museum by Albert E. Pullar alongside 39 other vacuum tubes in 1928

keywords: Glass artistry; scientific glass

b0f2ada4-d89f-5ebd-98c2-104083b59dcb.name: Janiform Bottle
b0f2ada4-d89f-5ebd-98c2-104083b59dcb.description: This cosmetic bottle was made of opaque cobalt blue glass. It has a free-blown flat inward-folded rim, cylindrical neck and flat base. The mould-blown body has a male face in relief on each side. One of the faces is thin and long with a serious expression while the other is round and smiling. Iridescent weathering and scratches on the surface. Some chips at the rim. Bottles of this type are named janiform after the double-headed guardian Roman god Janus, who protected the city gate by watching those who entered with one face and those leaving with the other.

b1a4f699-afff-51c0-903e-f100253de647.name: Ranftbecher Place de la Bibliotheque Imp:le et Roy:le et la Statue Joseph II à Vienne
b1a4f699-afff-51c0-903e-f100253de647.description: Anton Kothgasser spent most of his life working for the Vienna Porcelain Factory, yet he is mostly remembered for a series of beakers, usually signed and dated, that he painted with genre and topographic scenes. The specific technique used not only in this example, but almost all Kothgasser’s work, is translucent enamelling. Usually implemented on colourless, clear glass, it produces more delicate effects and is quicker that the previously practiced, original method of cutting out shapes in glass of different colours and leading them together. This particular example is gilded with golden decoration, with a star cut base and silver stain presenting a colourful vedute, inscribed with: “Place de la Bibliotheque Impériale et Royale et la Statue Joseph II à Vienne” (Square in front of the Imperial and Royal Library and the statue of Joseph II in Vienna).

b299ad41-8424-57f0-b306-b124b166a435.short_description: This exquisite perfume bottle is designed as a gem-set fish, entirely decorated with uncut rubies, emeralds, turquoise and pearls. The tip of the small bottle opens with a screw cap. It was most probably meant to contain perfume or a powder for cosmetic use. Jewelled objects from the Mughal period, such as this bottle, were commissioned for the courtly elite and would probably have been worn attached to a belt or around the neck.

b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.name: Stucco stained-glass window.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.description:
A large arched rectangular stained-glass window with a wooden frame of 7.5 cm wide. It also has two interior frames of stucco that are each 5 cm wide. Together the frames contain the entire window. Flanking the two plaster frames is a decorative band that is 10 cm wide. The window has 10 decorative elements, consisting of one-, two-, three- or four-leafed blossoms. Circles with a fan-like circumference divide these units from each other.  
The principal decorative scheme of the window consists of an upper section and a lower one connected by a circle. In each section there are 14 circles; each of which has a circumference of 20 cm. The circles encompass vegetal decoration in the form of bifurcating branches, which surround the interior circumference of each section and meet above it. The decoration in the upper section includes the text of the *Basmala* (“In the name of God …”) and in the lower section, a verse from “Surat al-nisa'” “Chapter of the Women” (4: 125), which reads “Allah did Take Abraham for a Friend”. The epigraphic inscriptions are coloured in white glaze to accentuate them.  
The manufacture of stucco windows inset with stained glass requires a number of stages. The first stage is the preparation of a solid wooden frame to contain the finished window. Liquid plaster is then poured into the frame and left to dry completely. The window is then placed on an iron mount where an imprint of the decoration is made on the surface of the plaster. This can be done by transferring the design from a sheet of tracing paper with the use of a needle and lead filings, and then using a cutting tool. The carving is done directly on to the plaster by hand with the use of precision tools. The work is extremely exacting as the plaster is fragile, making the window vulnerable to damage. The carving is done at a level of deflection of 45 per cent, allowing light to fall at the centre of the mosque hall. The glass is slotted into the empty spaces from the back. Finally, the window is transferred from the workshop to the site where it is mounted. To produce a window such as this would take between nine and 12 months.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.short_description: The windows at al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock as well as other religious buildings are made from plaster and coloured glass. This window from al-Aqsa Mosque is adorned with vegetal, geometric and epigraphic decoration. The fragility of these windows has led to their being replaced almost every century.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.dimensions: Height 288 cm, width 166 cm, depth 9.5 cm.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.method_for_datation: The date of the object was established by analysis of its decoration, and by comparison with other similar windows that had already been reliably dated, some of which are preserved at the Islamic Museum, while others remain *in situ* at the Dome of Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production as a stained-glass stucco-window workshop is still operational at the Haram al-Sharif to this day. Furthermore, a window such as this would have been difficult to transport due to their extreme fragility, so it is likely to have been crafted *in situ*.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.obtention: The window was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum during restoration of the mosque after a fire in 1969.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.bibliography: Flood, F. B., “The Ottoman Windows in the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque”, in S. Auld and R. Hillenbrand (eds), *Ottoman Jerusalem*, London, 2000.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: stucco; stained-glass; vegetal decoration
materials: Wood, plaster (stucco) and stained-glass crafted using casting, carving and mounting.

b3cbd45b-e370-5849-965d-3c998be8f738.name: Bottle
b3cbd45b-e370-5849-965d-3c998be8f738.short_description: Influenced by Seljuk ceramic bottles of the fifth century AH / eleventh century AD, finely blown globular bottles with long necks became a common product of Iranian glassmakers during the fifth and sixth centuries AH / twelfth and thirteenth centuries AD. This pale green, mould-blown glass bottle is of globular shape with a long narrowing neck and a flared, round opening. A honeycomb pattern covers the entire body and ends abruptly near the base of the neck. The honeycomb motif was widespread on Sasanian models in Iran and Mesopotamia and continued to be popular as a decorative element in Iranian glass production.
b3cbd45b-e370-5849-965d-3c998be8f738.bibliography: Carboni, Stefano, *Glass from Islamic Lands*, London: Thames & Hudson, 2001: 236-237.
keywords: Glass; Bottle; Mould-blown; Seljuk; Khwarezmid; Mongol
materials: Glass; mould-blown with applied and tooled decoration

b93fd12a-4d27-5f35-9bfe-b260f6a56e42.name: Bowl
b93fd12a-4d27-5f35-9bfe-b260f6a56e42.short_description:
This ribbed bowl is made of coloured strip mosaic, employing short strips of coloured cane, a technique employed in Italian factories and notably in Rome itself. This masterpiece is possibly the only surviving complete example of the ouput of this city.  
  
The bowl came to the museum in 1868, as part of a large collection of 'Ancient glass' owned by the antique dealer John Webb. The bowl, and the rest of the collection, was first shown in the South Kensington Museum's 1862 'Special Exhibition of Works of Art of the Medieval, Renaissance, & More Recent Periods', which coincided with the large International Exhibition of the same year. The bowl stayed on loan to the museum until acquired six years later.

materials: Mosaic glass, fused and slumped, with applied foot. Clear marks of lathe turning around the outside of the rim and foot and on the interior of the bowl.

ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.name: Sprinkler.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.description:
A small but heavy glass vessel made of dark purple glass, decorated with gilding and with white, red, and pale- blue enamels. The vessel's shape links it to a group of similar vessels referred to as 'spheroconical': the upper section is almost hemispherical, while the lower section tapers to a point at the base. The neck of the vessel is also tapered at its opening. The main decorative motif is a band of white calligraphy which reads, 'Glory to our lord, the sultan, the ruler, al-Ashraf Abu al-Fath ‘Umar, son of the sultan al-Malik al-Muzaffar'. Above the inscription, floral motifs alternate with circular medallions filled with coloured triangles. Below the inscription, similar floral motifs alternate with pointed circles.  
  
Spheroconical vessels, which are more often made of ceramic than of glass, are a bit of a puzzle. Their function is unclear, and suggestions have included hand grenades, loom weights, containers for holy water, and perfume sprinklers; a recent theory has it that they were drinking vessels for a beer-like beverage called fuqqa'. This vessel belongs to a group of about 50 objects made under the Mamluks as gifts for the Rasulid sultans of Yemen, with whom the Mamluks had close diplomatic ties and trade relations. The sultan named in the inscription is al-Malik al-Ashraf ‘Umar II Ibn al-Muzaffar (r. AH 694 / AD 1295–6). The circular medallions enclosing patterns of triangles are thought by some to be a personal emblem of his, and here it is indeed used in place of the usual emblem of the Rasulids, a rosette with five petals.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.short_description: A small glass vessel of ‘spheroconical’ shape and uncertain function, with enamelled decoration including an inscription band naming a certain sultan of Yemen. This is one of a group of wares known to have been made under the Mamluks for export to Yemen, possibly as diplomatic gifts.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.initial_owner: al-Malik al-Ashraf ‘Umar II Ibn al-Muzaffar, Rasulid Sultan of Yemen.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.method_for_datation: The inscription names a Rasulid Sultan of Yemen who only reigned for one year (694 / 1295–6).
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.

ba9dfd19-1ccf-584b-a17a-2317598063c4.name: Beaker
ba9dfd19-1ccf-584b-a17a-2317598063c4.short_description: Mamluk beakers are one of the most prolific types of enamelled glass vessels with a wide variety of forms and decorations. This tubular glass beaker has a flared top and a concave, circular foot. The upper part of the beaker is decorated with a thick deep blue horizontal band and outer gilded bands. The inner band presents a gilded inscription against a blue background: “Izz li-mawlana al-sultan al-malik al-alim al-adi[l]" (Glory to our lord the Sultan, the king, the learned, the just). The lower part of the beaker is decorated with two fish outlined in red. These beakers were used as drinking vessels as often depicted in other media from that time.

bacbe4e8-e3da-5f3c-b2cc-631888efe5ed.name: Horse (bookend)
bacbe4e8-e3da-5f3c-b2cc-631888efe5ed.short_description:
The Saint-Prex Glassworks, established in 1911, is still the largest producer of glassware in Switzerland. From the end of the 1920s until 1964, the firm also had a department that produced *verrerie artistique* or art glass, in particular a wide variety of vases. For the 1939 Swiss National Exhibition, Saint-Prex created a brand-new item, unique in both form and production technique: a three-dimensional, rearing horse made of black glass, like the ones shown here.  
  
Both the preliminary sketch of the horse and the metal form made by the firm Étienne Franckhauser in Paris to press the horse have been preserved. A horse of this kind had not been represented in any publicly accessible collection until recently when three copies were acquired for Vitromusée Romont’s collection.
bacbe4e8-e3da-5f3c-b2cc-631888efe5ed.method_for_datation: By historical documents: According to the sources, this horse was created for the Swiss National Exhibition that took place from May to October 1939. In December 1938 a preparatory wax model was sent from Saint-Prex to Paris, where a metal mould was made.
bacbe4e8-e3da-5f3c-b2cc-631888efe5ed.method_for_provenance: By historical documents: According to the sources, this horse was created for the Swiss National Exhibition that took place from May to October 1939. In December 1938 a preparatory wax model was sent from Saint-Prex to Paris, where a metal mould was made.
bacbe4e8-e3da-5f3c-b2cc-631888efe5ed.obtention: Purchased from a private collection in 2018
bacbe4e8-e3da-5f3c-b2cc-631888efe5ed.bibliography: Baumgartner, Ernst, "Glaspferde aus Saint-Prex - eine Spurensuche", *Zeitschrift für Schweizerische Archäologie und Kunstgeschichte*, 75 : 1 (2018): 69-82.
bacbe4e8-e3da-5f3c-b2cc-631888efe5ed.author: Erwin Baumgartner, Sibylle Walther
keywords: Saint-Prex; horse; bookend; black glass

bb0cbae2-4cdc-5b6e-a8ea-7cc05358a8e7.name: Ewer
bb0cbae2-4cdc-5b6e-a8ea-7cc05358a8e7.short_description: This rock-crystal ewer belongs to a small group that has survived from the Fatimid period. These luxury items were found in large quantities in the Fatimid caliphs’ treasuries in Cairo. The treasuries were plundered in the 1060s, after which the ewers that have been preserved found their way to European churches, used as containers for precious relics.
keywords: Ewer; Fatimid; Crystal

bb565fb2-2c2f-53f8-b2c2-7f4f0f79df7b.name: Flask
bb565fb2-2c2f-53f8-b2c2-7f4f0f79df7b.description:
After the free-blowing technique has been found, possibly around in the first quarter of the 1st century BC, the mould-blowing technique has developed and the desired glass forms and patterns were obtained by blowing into glass, terracotta, stone, metal or wood moulds. The melt at the end of the blowing rod is inflated in two or more pieces of the container until it covers the mould.  
The use of angular and patterned moulds has usually made it unnecessary to apply additional ornaments. With this technique, mass production of glasses with the same form, measurement, and decoration can be produced by using a single mould. In the form of quadrangular shaped moulds, the glass workshop's or the manufacturer's names were added by applying letters and symbols on the pedestal portion. Glassware that has been blown into a mould whose interior has a raised pattern so that the object shows the pattern with a concavity on the inside, underlying the convexity on the outside. Pattern moulds are not used to impart the final form to the object.  
It is understood that this light green flask which dates to the Late Roman times was pre-moulded and then free-blown, in connection with its unstable bottom and twisted ribs. The fine spiral ribs were most probably formed in a mould and then twisted during re-inflation, on the shoulder and the body, slanting down from left to right. Its rim is folded out, over and in, then pressed into the inside of its mouth. The flask has a bulbous body shape; small, horizontal shoulder and a little kick at the centre of the unstable bottom. It is in an intact situation, but some soil-encrusted weathering, blowing striations, large pinprick bubbles, partly flaked off dulling and a jagged pontil scar are also seen on the surface.
bb565fb2-2c2f-53f8-b2c2-7f4f0f79df7b.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and material dating

bbbfa200-67bd-57f5-a156-a4123aa2b382.name: Tray; Plate
bbbfa200-67bd-57f5-a156-a4123aa2b382.description: In the entirety of the formation and establishment of Viennese glass culture, no name stands out like that of the company J. & L. Lobmeyr. Setting the standards of technique and execution in 19th century AD Austrian glasswork, the company also collaborated with many famous artists of the time, such as Oscar Strnad, Josef von Storck, Josef Hoffmann and Otto Pruscher. It is thanks to these collaborations that J. & L. Lobmeyr covered a wide range of styles, techniques, ornaments and decorations. A particular design that was popular until the turn of the century is oval colourless glass platters with Renaissance style rim decoration and figurative representations. Several artists were known to have done such designs, and in the example presented here we see the designs of August Eisenmenger and Josef von Storck. Depicting Triton and Nereid in a close embrace, the intaglio-cut figures fill the colourless glass surface, creating a clear composition and contrast.

bc369253-62f1-5c62-88c5-9c6d8162b6ca.name: Small glass kohl bottle
bc369253-62f1-5c62-88c5-9c6d8162b6ca.short_description:
A small glass bottle with a typically cylindrical body, flat base, sloping shoulders, and everted neck. The exterior is decorated with overlapping bands of black and light turquoise chevrons, giving to the flask an overall ‘marbled’ look or marvered finish.  
Marvered glass is created by rolling warm glass over a polished surface to shape and cool. Bands of coloured glass can be added at this stage to create ‘feathered’ patterns. This bottle is made of a dark glass with bands of lighter glass added during the marvering process.
bc369253-62f1-5c62-88c5-9c6d8162b6ca.author: Hazelle Page

bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.name: Mosque lamp for the mausoleum of Amir Aydakin al-‘Ala'i al-Bunduqdar
bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.short_description: Mamluk amirs adopted emblems, often connected to their ceremonial roles at court, which decorated the objects and buildings they commissioned. Here the two gold crossbows against a red shield indicate that the patron of this lamp held the high-ranking office of *bunduqdar* (keeper of the bow) at the Mamluk court. The inscription states that the lamp was ordered for the mausoleum of Aydakin al-‘Ala’i, who died in Cairo in 1285.
bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.dates: Shortly after Hegira 686 / shortly after AD 1285

bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.name: Bottle with polo-playing riders.
bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.description:
This bottle depicting polo players is the only complete example of Mamluk glasswork featuring a frieze of riders galloping to the right-hand side, one of whom is holding a polo stick. Polo was much-loved by the Mamluk rulers, uniting both military exercise and game. The bottle was made in Egypt or Syria, probably on commission for a Rasulid ruler in Yemen, as the red five-leaved rosettes on a white background on the frieze around the shoulder of the bottle appear also on metalwork which was produced on commission for these rulers.  
The bottle is made of nearly colourless, light-yellow glass. Its bulbous body, with its long cylindrical neck, is made of optically blown glass with vertical grooves and it sits on a circular base. The paint work, which is contoured in red and uses either the colours of enamel or just plain gold, is restrained. The principal frieze on this bottle consists of 12 riders galloping to the right. Above this frieze, over a tendril, there is another frieze in which animals (hares, a gazelle, a bear and hunting dogs) are running to the left. Three rosettes break up this frieze. The bottle’s shoulder part is adorned with three birds. The neck is covered by a colourful inscription over a gold background. The inscription consists of general words of praise, and cannot be used as a starting point from which to date the object.  
The bottle’s perfect condition never fails to provoke astonishment. Allegedly, the bottle made its way to China, and in the 19th century became part of the collection of Count F. von Pourtalès. Bottles, as other examples demonstrate, were often preserved because, filled with holy soil or other such relics, they became part of European church treasuries. This sort of painted receptacle must have been produced in large quantities, as the great number of fragments from different collections demonstrate – most of which were found in the rubble of Cairo’s old city. Obviously experienced artists created these small works of art in a short space of time.  
  
Click [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=py7pVIzmSuk&t=24s) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.
bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.short_description: Mamluk workshops produced elegant glass vessels such as this bottle, to which a glass painter has added a frieze with horsemen, one of whom has a polo mallet. The game of polo was extremely popular at the princely courts of the Mamluks. Enamel-painted glass vessels were much admired in Europe.
bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.initial_owner: Count F. von Pourtales, St. Petersburg.
bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.method_for_datation: Similar painted enamelled glassworks were created during the Mamluk period. Furthermore, the characteristic red rosettes over a white background enable it to be attributed to the Rasulid rulers of Yemen (626–858 / 1228–1454), who probably commissioned the creation of this type of vessel.
bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.method_for_provenance: Its form and characteristic enamel paintwork classify it as glasswork from the Mamluk period in Syria or Egypt. A more precise place of origin cannot be determined.
bdd605c9-b2d9-57fb-8063-869eda526bd5.obtention: Purchased by Count F. von Pourtalès, St. Petersburg, 1913.

bdffba7b-75ec-59cc-ba4d-4dfca567f089.name: *Porrón* (*porró*)
bdffba7b-75ec-59cc-ba4d-4dfca567f089.description:
Piriform vessel with conical umbo at its base. Long, conical spout extending from near the base, and neck with trilobed opening. Decorated with white, spiralling threads embedded in the paste.  
  
Vessel for holding and consuming liquids, especially wine. Along with the *botijo* (*càntir*) and the *almorraja* (*almorratxa*), it is among the most typical of Catalonian glass forms. The filigrana style of decoration–achieved by embedding glass threads in the vitreous paste–originated in Murano (Venice) and from there spread widely. Pieces inspired by this type of production were referred to as “a la façon de Venise”.
bdffba7b-75ec-59cc-ba4d-4dfca567f089.obtention: Purchase, 1935. From the José Sánchez Garrigos collection (most likely).

keywords: Blown glass; filigrana; Catalonia

be5014f2-b4bb-570b-94a8-c7b05ca72a9f.name: Untitled
be5014f2-b4bb-570b-94a8-c7b05ca72a9f.description:
Sculpture of two blocks, designed for assembly and composed of horizontally-overlapping glass sheets. A signature of “TE85” appears on the upper part of the piece. Torres Esteban’s work is often characterized by this use of green, cut and cold-glued industrial plate glass. The form of the piece is also typical of the artist’s style. Here we see an interest in volume, with luminescent and kinetic effects that show the influence of Eusebio Sempere.  
  
The work of Joaquín Torres Esteban is associated with the Studio Glass Movement, which originated in the United States and spread internationally. Torres Esteban is one of the pioneers of laminated glass sculpture in Spain. Throughout his glassmaking career, he participated in numerous international events and organized VICOINTER’83, an international contemporary glass exhibition in Valencia.  
  
In 1986, the National Museum of Decorative Arts dedicated a monographic exhibition to Torres Esteban, after which the artist donated this piece.

bf2d1e63-7381-51a0-93c7-f275d473108c.name: Glass tumbler.
bf2d1e63-7381-51a0-93c7-f275d473108c.description:
A white, translucent glass tumbler that was found in Palace B, where an inscription was found on the wall plaster thus associating the palace with the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tasim Billah. The glass is decorated with five vertically arranged lines of Arabic inscription that read: “drink and be filled with delight” and “made in Damascus.” It is, therefore, likely that the piece was made in Damascus and then transported to the Raqqa region. The spaces in between the inscriptions are decorated with a floral design. The object's decorative arrangement is executed in an applied coating of brown metallic lustre. It is believed that this type of lustre coating was used on glass before the technique was adapted for use on ceramics.  
Raqqa, a region that lies between the Euphrates and Balikh rivers, flourished during the Abbasid period. A group of Abbasid palaces, parts of which were excavated during the 1950s and labelled with the letters A, B, C and D, are found in the region.
bf2d1e63-7381-51a0-93c7-f275d473108c.short_description: The application of metallic lustre was first used on glass, as evidenced by this Damascene tumbler dating to the 'Abbasid period, before it was famously applied on pottery.
bf2d1e63-7381-51a0-93c7-f275d473108c.method_for_datation: The tumbler is believed to be contemporary to Palace B, which has been dated to the period of Caliph al-Mu'tasim Billah (r. 218–27 / 833–42).
bf2d1e63-7381-51a0-93c7-f275d473108c.method_for_provenance: The inscription on the tumbler specifies that it was made in Damascus.
bf2d1e63-7381-51a0-93c7-f275d473108c.obtention: The tumbler was found during archaeological excavations during the 1950s undertaken by the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities under the direction of Nasib Salibi.

c0244871-45bb-595e-94f1-b3c8fd4920b7.name: Stem cup.
c0244871-45bb-595e-94f1-b3c8fd4920b7.description: An enamelled and gilded glass cup with a tall stem. Enamel decoration in blue, green, red and white is concentrated around the shoulder of the cup, comprising round medallions alternating with Arabic inscriptions that repeat the word 'al-alim', the learned. This was a common title for both Mamluk sultans and of high-standing officers of state. Two further bands of pseudo inscriptions in green appear at either end of the stem. A sketchy design of phoenixes with flowers and foliage in red enamel fills the upper surface of the foot. This is one of a group of Mamluk glass objects that reached Europe from China. Active trade relations between China and the Islamic world date back to the AH 2nd/ AD 8th century. However, the absence of plain or marvered glass in China suggests that the enamelled glass arrived there as diplomatic gifts or luxury merchandise. A number of examples of this type of cup survive but their exact function is unknown.
c0244871-45bb-595e-94f1-b3c8fd4920b7.short_description: A cup with a tall stem of enamelled and gilded glass, techniques typical of the Mamluk period. The decoration comprises Arabic inscriptions, foliage, floral motifs and phoenixes. This cup was found in China, where it was probably imported shortly after production.
c0244871-45bb-595e-94f1-b3c8fd4920b7.dates: Hegira early 8th century / AD early 14th century.
c0244871-45bb-595e-94f1-b3c8fd4920b7.method_for_datation: The style and technique of this cup resemble certain Mamluk glass objects of the early 8th / 14th century.
c0244871-45bb-595e-94f1-b3c8fd4920b7.method_for_provenance: This is one of a number of Mamluk glasses found in China. However, it is clearly made by a Muslim craftsman in Egypt or Syria and, therefore, it was probably exported to China soon after it was made. Later it would have been brought to Europe through trade; it was donated to the Museum by Mrs Julius Spier, whose husband ran a trading company which had weekly auctions of imports from China.
c0244871-45bb-595e-94f1-b3c8fd4920b7.obtention: Donated in 1924 by Mrs Julius Spier in memory of her husband, through the National Art Collections Fund.

c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.name: Three
c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.short_description: These water pipes, or *araghil* (sing. *arghile*), is made of translucent glass painted with floral patterns in pale colours. The *araghil* have three main parts: first, you have a bowl for the coals sitting on top of a metal plate. Under this is the body of the *arghile*, which can come in a variety of shapes and sizes, and consists of a gasket and water jar. Connected to the main body is a pipe for smoking. The *arghile* originated in Persia and later became popular in 17th century Turkey, used by the Ottoman elite as a status symbol. The water pipe became hugely popular, and in 1841 even sparked a diplomatic crisis between France and the Ottoman Empire. However, although it remains popular in the modern Middle East, it was largely replaced by cigarettes in the 20th century. The *arghile* woks by vaporizing a flavoured tobacco called *shisha*, which is passed through water and then inhaled. Depending on their placement, the coals can either be used to boil the water and thus create water vapour, or to produce smoke by burning the tobacco. These *araghil* were used by Ottoman officials in 19th century Lebanon.
c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
keywords: Glass; Water pipe; Smoking

c12a5f6b-f5a7-56b3-a7ab-764076a23016.name: Base of globular waterpipe (hookah)
c12a5f6b-f5a7-56b3-a7ab-764076a23016.description: This globular hookah base has a short cylindrical neck that flares at the top.  Plant and floral decorations are distributed on the body and separated vertically by cords in relief. At its base, the neck is marke by two rings: the first has a triangular section and the latter - decorated with a chevron pattern - has a cylindrical section. The upper part of the neck is decorated by arches filled with ornamental plant motifs.
c12a5f6b-f5a7-56b3-a7ab-764076a23016.dates: Hegira 12th century / AD 18th century, first half

c1c21018-70eb-5e4f-93fb-c53b4de7b9a0.name: Glass vessel (*cista*) with *fenicio* ('Phoenician') decoration
c1c21018-70eb-5e4f-93fb-c53b4de7b9a0.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The massive emigrations of Murano's glass workers to Spain during the 1600s spurred the building of many kilns that fused formal training with the strong local glass tradition. The *cista* is part of a series of objects made in Murano in the second half of the 19th century, mainly by the Murano Venetian Glass Society, and inspired to Spanish models called "Façon de Venise", showing a Phoenician decoration. The *cista*, or vessel, has a lid with a pinnacle in aquamarine glass.

c2156823-ed9a-51e3-8767-c9347fdd1977.name: *Cluny* vase
c2156823-ed9a-51e3-8767-c9347fdd1977.short_description: This vase is of blown and moulded smoked glass. The handles are of coloured glass which have been moulded, pressed and applied to the vase, and from which there project on either side metal handles in the shape of serpents. In 1925, Lalique achieved public acclaim at the International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts in Paris, where he presented his new works in glass, which he described as a "wonderful material". In this way, the artist created an answer to the aspirations of a new era, represented by the Art Deco style, and contributed to a major shift in the art of glassmaking.

c27a36c0-c043-5311-9e26-1ac05ca21b70.short_description: There is a small group of *huqqa*s made of emerald-green glass with a related decoration. On some, the motif was painted direct on the glass. c2dbebc1-c7d1-5f4d-8937-c5042a5ea0d2.name: Cup
c2dbebc1-c7d1-5f4d-8937-c5042a5ea0d2.short_description: This refined cup made of greenish tinged glass with slightly curved sides, was initially blown as a thick vessel. Its flowing decoration was then masterfully wheel-cut in relief. This work was carried out in the so-called bevelled technique, where the slanted profile of the decoration blurs the distinction between the pattern and the background. This technique is first seen in profusion in the stucco decoration of the second and third century AH / ninth century AD palace city of Samarra in Iraq, before its spread across the Islamic empire. The manufacture of glass was highly developed in pre-Islamic times in both Iran and Syria, and production continued to develop under Islam. Cut glass was the most luxurious of all, requiring separate skills of hot glass working and wheel-cutting the finished products.

c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.name: Mosque lamp.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.description: An enamelled glass and gilt mosque lamp with a wide funnel-shaped neck and a rounded rim. The lamp has a squat body, steeply sloping shoulder and a flattened base, and a tall pedestal foot with a pronounced pontil mark on the underside. Six trailed suspension loops are placed around the body at regular intervals. The lamp is decorated comprehensively with enamel decoration executed in red, blue and light-green, embellished with gilding. Around the neck is a wide band of *thuluth* script executed in blue enamel, surrounded by a floral border. An excerpt from the Qur’an (*Sura* 2; verse 256), the inscription is interrupted by decorative roundels rendered in gold, red and green, each of which contain a little cup in the centre. The lower neck and upper body are decorated with floral bands interrupted by roundels with individual floral motifs. On the main body, another inscription in *thuluth* script gives the titles of the official who commissioned the lamp: Zain al-Din Mubarak who, according to the blazon above, was cupbearer to the sultan, al-Malik al-Salih, who is also named in the inscription. There were two rulers with the same titulature, both of whom were the sons of Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun: the first, al-Malik al-Salih Isma’il (r. AH 742–5 / AD 1342–5); the second, al-Malik al-Salih Salih (r. AH 751–4 / AD 1351–4).
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.short_description: Glass mosque lamps with enamelled decoration were commissioned in large numbers by the Mamluk elite in Egypt and Syria. Decorated with Qur’anic inscriptions and the titles of the patron, they were destined for the numerous mosques and *madrasas* endowed by the Mamluks throughout Cairo and the empire.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.method_for_datation: The appearance of the name of al-Malik al-Salih on this mosque lamp assigns the piece to the reign of either al-Malik al-Salih Isma’il (r. 742–5 / 1342–5) or to al-Malik al-Salih Salih (r. 751–4 / 1351–4).
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.method_for_provenance: Mosque lamps of this type were made in large numbers in both Egypt and Syria during the 8th / 14th century.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.obtention: Purchased by NMS from the Major W. J. Myers Collection in 1900.

c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.name: Stucco stained-glass window.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.description:
A stucco stained-glass window divided into 21 decorative units of vegetal and geometric motifs and inscriptions. The first unit is composed of a circular “flower” that complements and forms the arch, and which is adorned with a colourful geometric decoration in yellow, turquoise and dark-red glass. Adjacent to this area is a rectangular zone which contains the only inscription on the window. This is a verse from the Qur'an \[“al-Tawba”\] (“the Repentance”, 9: 18), which reads: “In the Cause of Allah, They are not comparable in the sight of Allah.” The inscription is carved in an interlaced script of white glass. The surrounding space is filled with simple squares of light-blue glass. Adjacent to the inscription are three squares of equal size. The two side squares are identical, and in the middle of each of them there is an eight-sided star. Both are divided into small pieces of dark-red, green and yellow glass. The middle square contains two polygons of yellow and blue glass; the decorative component transfers thereafter to three long rectangles. The two side rectangles are identical and are decorated with intertwining zigzag lines of blue, yellow and dark-red glass. The middle rectangle takes the form of a flower, out of which emerges an intertwining plant that wraps around three times to resemble a circle, and which is topped by a crown formed from vegetal motifs. The window terminates with three squares that are identical in size, and which resemble those mentioned earlier.  
The manufacture of stucco windows inset with stained glass requires a number of stages. The first stage is the preparation of a solid wooden frame to contain the finished window. Liquid plaster is then poured into the frame and left to dry completely. The window is then placed on an iron mount where an imprint of the decoration is made on the surface of the plaster. This can be done by transferring the design from a sheet of tracing paper with the use of a needle and lead filings, and then using a cutting tool. The carving is done directly on to the plaster by hand with the use of precision tools. The work is extremely exacting as the plaster is fragile, making the window vulnerable to damage. The carving is done at a level of deflection of 45 per cent, allowing light to fall at the centre of the mosque hall. The glass is slotted into the empty spaces from the back. Finally, the window is transferred from the workshop to the site where it is mounted. To produce a window such as this would take between nine and 12 months.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.short_description: This stucco window from al-Aqsa Mosque is divided into 11 decorative elements derived from vegetal, geometric and epigraphic forms. The independent elements appear as a collective unit within a wooden frame, which gathers a multiplicity of decorative forms in a number of colours.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by comparison of its style, decoration and form of production with other dated pieces, which are still *in situ*.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of the production of this piece in view of the presence of a permanent workshop for the production of such windows in the Haram al-Sharif. This workshop is still active at the Haram today and was re-established following a fire at al-Aqsa Mosque in 1969.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.obtention: The piece was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum in around 1929 during renovation works that took place following an earthquake which struck Jerusalem in 1927.

c68b60b7-1672-58bb-b263-57a293555eb1.name: Long Neck Cylindrical Bottle
c68b60b7-1672-58bb-b263-57a293555eb1.short_description: Cylindrical bottle made of thin, colourless, transparent glass. The neck of the bottle is cylindrical and very long. The rim is of an irregular, round shape made by the application of glass thread. The neck, shoulder and most recipients are decorated with spiral flutes, turned to the right. The bottom is extremely concave. The bottle is almost completely coated with a layer of milky white irridation. Presumed to be part of the tableware, these were found in the remainder of a building with more recent ceramic and one metal, partly recognizable object. According to Millica Križanac's research based upon excavated archaeological material, the building is dated as of the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Sremska Mitrovica came under Austrian control after almost two centuries of Turkish rule during the war of 1710–1718. As a trading centre on Sava, it attracted primarily residents of the surrounding area. Modest trade existed between Sremska Mitrovica and other towns, as well as with Belgrade, Vienna and Budapest.

c8458565-1997-5a79-84aa-df4f4a1e15ae.name: Perfume Bottle
c8458565-1997-5a79-84aa-df4f4a1e15ae.description:
This little toilette/perfume bottle was produced by using the free-blowing technique which was discovered by the glass-makers along the Syro-Palestinian coast possibly around in the middle of the 1st century BC. It has an opaque white decoration on the purple body. Its rim is folded out rolled up and over; with bevelled outer lip and flattened into side of mouth. It has a cylindrical neck; a globular body and a flat bottom. The trail wound around shoulder and body is also seen, ending in a thick marvered spiral on the bottom. The bottle is almost in an intact situation, except for the fugitive sections of the trail decoration, a small hole and a crack in the side. It is hard to determine the quality of the glass due to the patches of black, enamel-like weathering and iridescence around the bottle. The vessel is still full of dry and compacted earth.  
The invention of ‘free-blowing’ technique revolutionized the glass industry. It allowed vessels to be mass-produced thus rendering them less expensive and available to a wider market so that by the end of the 1st century AD free blown glass vessels were used widely throughout the Roman Empire. The majority were undecorated utilitarian pieces, used for storage and transport, and tablewares, like beakers and plates, but others were embellished with applied decoration. While still hot their bodies were rolled over loose glass chips of contrasting colours and then marvered flush with the wall of the vessel. Next, the pieces where reheated and further inflated and manipulated, so that when their necks were pulled out of their bodies the splashes also became elongated.  
Allowed thinning of the walls and the construction of larger and transparent closed forms.

c908951d-fa7b-502e-b55b-a25cd13ae231.name: Carafe
c908951d-fa7b-502e-b55b-a25cd13ae231.description:
This carafe is made of thin, transparent green glass with a ball-shaped body, slightly wavy walls, an elongated neck and an attached handle. The carafe has a stopper with an irregular circular base and a cruciform indent at the top. The decoration consists of a hand-painted blossoming garland floral decoration along the body and a thin gilding strip that follows the base and the opening rim, with traces appearing on the stopper.  
According to historical data the carafe was created in the Nacko Janković & Son manufactory. It is the second glasshouse to operate in Serbia, from 1882 to 1906. The focus of Nacko Janković & Son production was utility glass, manufactured in far more technologically advanced conditions than those of Avram Petronijević manufacture, as evidenced by this carafe that emerged at the end of the 19th century, shaped under the influence of modern stylistic movements, the greatest being Art Nouveau.

cabd4425-58c1-543a-89b1-b0d9502935eb.description: This small rectangular box belongs to a group of similar glass boxes said to have come from Egypt as well as Iran. It consists of two equal rectangular parts that have rounded edges and are secured together by original bronze hinges. Two hinges have been fixed on the exterior and terminate in hooked ram’s horn motifs on the upper side of the box. A third identical mount serves as a clasp and was used as a lock.

cb356315-ca0a-54b0-8955-18daba1b09c6.name: Glass Model
cb356315-ca0a-54b0-8955-18daba1b09c6.short_description: In 1863, the Bohemian-based glassmaker Leopold Blaschka started making models of sea invertebrates at the instigation of an admirer of his glass botanicals. These initial models were based on the illustrations of Philip Henry Gosse published in his treaty ‘A History of the British Sea-Anemones and Corals’, later observations were taken from live specimens shipped directly to the studio and kept in aquariums on site. Around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and over the years they produced models of anemones, cephalopods, mollusca, nudibranchs, and protozoans as well as the vast collection of botanicals held by Harvard University. In 1866, the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art was one of the first UK institutions to order invertebrate models from Leopold Blaschka after its Director Thomas Archer had viewed the then Natural History section of the British Museum’s collection. A set of actinia arrived in 1866, followed by a batch of 58 medusae and mollusks in 1868. In 1910, Ewen Kennedy, a private collector, donated his collection of 123 Blaschka models. The Blaschka models are now highly regarded for their beauty and realism and are still considered ‘an artistic marvel in the field of science and a scientific marvel in the field of art’.
cb356315-ca0a-54b0-8955-18daba1b09c6.method_for_datation: In the mid-1860s Leopold started selling models, around 1880, Rudolf began to assist his father, and then in 1890 the Blaschkas signed an exclusive contract to produce glass flowers for Harvard University, and stopped producing any other zoological models.
cb356315-ca0a-54b0-8955-18daba1b09c6.obtention: Donated to the Museum on the death of Mr Kennedy in 1910
cb356315-ca0a-54b0-8955-18daba1b09c6.bibliography: Swinney, G.N., "Enchanted invertebrates: Blaschka models and other simulacra in National Museums Scotland", *Historical Biology*, 20 : 1 (2008): 39-50.

cb356315-ca0a-54b0-8955-18daba1b09c6.author: Sarah Rothwell
keywords: Blaschka; lampworked glass; glass models

cbf22324-acdb-5d38-a8c2-0750b5f920f6.name: Bottle
cbf22324-acdb-5d38-a8c2-0750b5f920f6.short_description: This pale green bottle is of an inverted drop form with a long and slightly flaring cylindrical neck. It is decorated with wheel-cut facets in round honeycomb-like formations which vary in size according to the curvature of the body. A row of vertical rectangular facets is cut around its neck with the base elegantly finished into a single circular disc. The decoration of wheel-cut or wheel-engraved glass was executed with an abrasive tool after the glass had cooled. The use of honeycomb-cut facets, which dates back to a Roman practice, was very common on Sasanian models in Iran and Mesopotamia and was revived by glass cutters during the early Islamic period. This vessel was likely used by elite members of the society as a container to store precious liquids or ointments.
keywords: Glass; Bottle; Free-blown; Cut; Abbasid

d1137f79-cb15-57e4-a241-e0970c4e0ee4.name: A collection of beads, curios and pendants from the Galloway Hoard
d1137f79-cb15-57e4-a241-e0970c4e0ee4.short_description: This collection of glass beads, curios, and heirloom objects were bundled and strung together and placed at the top of carefully packed lidded vessel within the Galloway Hoard. Everything at the top of the vessel was wrapped, but the evidence has only partly survived, with some textiles preserved in corrosion on the silver brooch-hoop this collection of beads rested on. This collection consists of: a rattlestone, a rock crystal ball in a broken silver pendent frame, five glass beads, and a ‘relic’ bead pendent capped with a perforated coin. The rattlestone and the rock crystal ball may have been used as charms or amulets. The rock crystal ball and the coloured and decorated beads are more normally found in furnished Anglo-Saxon graves from several centuries earlier than when the Galloway Hoard was buried circa AD900. Several of the larger ‘melon’ beads are heavily worn from use. The clearest clue that this unusual collection was handed down as heirlooms comes from a ‘relic’ pendant made from a damaged bead enclosed in a silver frame and capped with a perforated coin. The coin was minted for Coenwulf, the King of Anglo-Saxon Mercia (died AD821). It is likely the coin was minted several generations before the Hoard was buried. Old and well-worn, it seems that all these objects were valued for their age or past ownership.
d1137f79-cb15-57e4-a241-e0970c4e0ee4.method_for_datation: Through comparison with similar beads used as grave-goods in early medieval furnished burials
d1137f79-cb15-57e4-a241-e0970c4e0ee4.obtention: Acquired from the Crown through Treasure Trove in 2017

d85f8421-f6df-5863-aed3-55b5bd21dcff.name: Scent bottle
d85f8421-f6df-5863-aed3-55b5bd21dcff.short_description: James Giles was responsible for a large output of sophisticated decoration on both glass and porcelain in London during the period 1749-1776. His workshop's gilding and enamelling is distinctive for its quality and fashionable designs, and notable for its large output and number of quality painters. This scent bottle shows an elaborate chinoiserie scene depicting a heron on a lake with buildings in the background, and a colourful array of flora and fauna. Giles was particularly specialised in painting imaginary birds, but it now very difficult to firmly attribute pieces directly to his studio as the workshop decorated pieces from a number of different glass factories and they were never signed.

d9191a66-c86d-5c20-beb8-0f08718ae5a7.name: Carafe and Glass - Part of a Service for Drink
d9191a66-c86d-5c20-beb8-0f08718ae5a7.description:
This preserved part of a beverage set consists of a high-stemmed glass and carafe with a stopper. The mould-blown, colourless, thin-glass bottle with pear-shaped body and a handle is raised on a low stem and base. Both items display identical decoration, each painted with white and yellow stylized floral ornaments and a blue ribbon carrying white painted ornaments. A thin gilding strip separates the decorated fields, encircling the upper and lower body of the carafe and glass, the rims and the stems.  
This part of the set was made using a mould-blowing technique at the factory of Nacko Janković & Son in Jagodina. Preserved data and objects from the Museum of Applied Art collections testify to the higher technological level of production and application of various glass decorating techniques in this factory. The attention paid to decoration is further evidenced by participation by the factory on several occasions in world exhibitions. Nacko Janković & Son Manufactury received a bronze medal for decoration in 1900.

d9a8677b-3869-5fcc-91d3-50b6d8a59c46.name: Mosque lamp
d9a8677b-3869-5fcc-91d3-50b6d8a59c46.short_description: Mosque lamp with a cursive inscription reading: “This was made for our Lord the Sultan al-Malik al-Kujuk, may God protect him with his Grace and illuminate his mausoleum”. This lamp was made for the tomb of the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Ala` ad-Din Kujuk, ibn al-Nasir, ibn Qalawun, who reigned as a child for six months in AH 746 (AD 1341-42). In September 1345 he was murdered by his younger brother Sha`ban and his mausoleum was erected in Cairo in 1346-1347.

d9bc604a-632e-5b67-a98e-6e1c1d0aea7f.name: Reverse painting on glass: Tattoo template with Christian motifs
d9bc604a-632e-5b67-a98e-6e1c1d0aea7f.short_description: In Cairo, the most famous saints have their weekly visiting day. For Imam Shafi’i it is Friday. The mausoleum of the legal scholar, who died in 820, is one of the most popular sites for Muslim pilgrimages in the city. In the mid-1970s a wandering tattoo artist set up his reverse glass paintings every week on the market place in front of the Shafi’i Mausoleum and waited for customers: Muslims as well as Copts. One of the reverse glass paintings acquired from him shows two images of the Virgin Mary, once as the *Mother of God*, and again as *Our Lady of Sorrows*. The latter image served as a model for the *Mater Dolorosa* of the Florentine 17th century master Carlo Dolci, as it attained cult status from Alexandria to Aswan among Christians. It is said that, in a church on the west bank of the Nile, a coloured print of Dolci's *Our Lady of Sorrows* "cried tears of blood" from her right eye for the persecuted Copts.
d9bc604a-632e-5b67-a98e-6e1c1d0aea7f.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.

db88f030-40ca-5244-a657-163f6b4ab60a.name: Small Ewer
db88f030-40ca-5244-a657-163f6b4ab60a.description:
This ewer demonstrates different techniques that would require artisans skilled in working with hot glass, likely in a glasshouse used to produce daily commodities. The overlapping disks on its surface form a variation of the “concentric omphalos” pattern that consists of the continuous use of disks with a central projection in high relief. Sometimes called a “ring-and-dot” motif, this variation creates the impression that two discs are arranged one on top of the other and that, in the middle of the top disc, there is a protrusion.  
In the Iranian region this exchange technique with pattern was used among wheel-cut glass during the 9th and 10th centuries. In later centuries the pattern was more common in the mould-blown technique.

materials: Glass, green, intense weathering; mould-blown, applied, tooled, worked on the pontil

ddfbe2bf-75cf-508a-af85-5d9ab86020a7.name: Enamelled flask
ddfbe2bf-75cf-508a-af85-5d9ab86020a7.short_description:
The finely decorated flask has a tall neck decorated with a fleur-de-lis band with enamel highlights, a plaited guilloche band and a row of male standing figures wearing church vestments. Two of the figures hold open books, perhaps missals. The body bears a band of seated figures, drinkers and musicians. Between the figures are beakers, a wine flask or footed dishes. On the shoulders of the flask rosettes alternate with large birds, evidently pelicans – in medieval Western Europe a symbol of Christ and the institution of the Eucharist.  
The robbed figures and the pelicans may suggest that the flask was ordered for a European, perhaps a pilgrim, as a memento of a visit to the Holy Land or as a gift to a Christian church or monastery.  
The flask is a superb specimen of the skills of Ayyubid glassworkers. The application of enamel to the glass indicates that this flask was made at an early stage in the development of enamelling, which would be consistent with an Ayyubid date.

de5e05a4-b9f2-55ba-bb00-29aa5da66e88.name: Bottle.
de5e05a4-b9f2-55ba-bb00-29aa5da66e88.description: A large long-necked bottle with flared foot and neck-ring. Most of the surface is decorated with enamelling and gilding. The neck of the bottle has interlacing bands of blue enamelling which create compartments filled with floral decoration. Around the base of the neck are roundels featuring phoenixes in heraldic poses which alternate with striding griffins. The most prominent part of the decoration is the calligraphic inscription around the body. Written in tall blue script against a background of coiled white arabesques with highlights in red, green, and yellow, the text is a dedication to an unnamed ruler: 'Glory to our lord, the Sultan, the wise, the just, the religious warrior, the king'. The first part of this phrase is repeated above the bottle's neck-ring. The elaborate all-over decoration of this bottle recalls the heyday of glass production in Syria and Egypt in the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods. An object clearly intended for a secular purpose, it may have been used to serve drinks at court.
de5e05a4-b9f2-55ba-bb00-29aa5da66e88.short_description: A large, long-necked glass bottle lavishly decorated with enamelling in several colours and gilding. The inscriptions, though prominent, are anonymous. The bottle was clearly made for a secular purpose and may have been used to serve wine and other drinks at court.
de5e05a4-b9f2-55ba-bb00-29aa5da66e88.dates: First half of the hegira 8th / AD 14th century.
de5e05a4-b9f2-55ba-bb00-29aa5da66e88.method_for_datation: The style of gilding and enamelling is typical of the glass industry in the late Ayyubid and early Mamluk periods. The figural decoration which characterises Mamluk art of the late 7th / 13th century, though, has here been reduced to a group of small roundels with phoenixes in heraldic poses. The calligraphic inscription to a (nameless) Sultan has taken over as the primary decorative motif, a focus on epigraphy which would soon characterise Mamluk art.
de5e05a4-b9f2-55ba-bb00-29aa5da66e88.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.

dee7a1c5-0f05-5ce0-876c-8ed539e6d7f9.name: Virginal
dee7a1c5-0f05-5ce0-876c-8ed539e6d7f9.short_description:
The maker of this glass-covered virginal is still unknown, and it has no known parallel among keyboard instruments, making it highly unique.  
  
The majority of the faces of the instrument are either enamelled or adorned with lamp-worked rods (tooled and fused in the open flame of a lamp or torch), whorls and florets. However, the inner lid is set with 18 panels which depict scenes from the Roman poet Ovid's work *Metamorphoses*. These intricately and exquisitely detailed scenes are framed within scrolling borders and each is labelled with the name of the characters who appear in the 25 books that constitute the poem. Included are Acteon, the hunter who, after catching sight of the goddess Diana bathing was transformed into a stag and killed by his own hounds.  
  
The uniqueness of the virginal has meant it has been associated with a glass virginal that was described as in the possession of Elizabeth I at Hampton Court. A German traveller named Paul Hentzner wrote in 1598 of 'a musical instrument made all of glass except the strings'. However, other contemporary descriptions of instruments at Hampton Court describe them being encrusted with jewels and inscribed with the Queen's cypher, which this instrument is unfortunately lacking.

df497ccb-7aa2-50fd-8a56-d90ab003137c.name: Pelican
df497ccb-7aa2-50fd-8a56-d90ab003137c.short_description: During the Middle Ages, a pelican pecking at its breast to feed its young with its own blood was considered a symbol of Christ’s Crucifixion.

e16fb843-5cf8-5b34-a3ef-a7749d418ec7.name: Lithyalinbecher
e16fb843-5cf8-5b34-a3ef-a7749d418ec7.description: At the beginning of the 18th century AD, the Harrach estate included the settlements of Seifenbach (Ryzoviste), Neuwelt (Novy Svet) and Harrachsdorf (Harrachov). All these settlements eventually merged into one, carrying the name Harrachov. This settlement is the birthplace of one of the most famous glass factories in Bohemia, known under the name of Harrach Glassworks. Among the workers and trainees in this factory we find many great names in glasswork such as Dominik Biemann, Johann Pohl and Elias Müller. Under the governance of Johann Pohl, this glassworking reached its peak. Furthermore, this period witnessed the production of two particular types of glass, named Hyalith and Lithyalin glass. Hyalith, opaque, usually black or red marbled glass, was already patented by Jiri von Burquoy and Harrach Glassworks manufactured this type of glass under the patent. Lithyalin was discovered by Friederich Egermann at his workshop in Blottendorf (Polevsko) and is unique for its process of creation. The glass is cut, then painted with metal oxides and finally fired to produce a marble effect. Pohl adapted this technique, combining it with the already established rothwelsch (Italian red) opaque glass that Harrach Glassworks had been producing since the middle of the 18th century AD, beautifully presented on this AD 1830 example with clear cuts and an oxidised reflection. Eventually, these techniques became specialties of the Harrach Glassworks, along with being the first to produce overlay glass in multiple colours in Bohemia.
e16fb843-5cf8-5b34-a3ef-a7749d418ec7.provenance: Nový Svět / Neuwelt; Polevsko / Blottendorf bei Haida
