e29c9462-222f-54d1-8d11-b1a1a1e9ee01.name: Bowl
e29c9462-222f-54d1-8d11-b1a1a1e9ee01.description: Glassmakers from Europe started travelling to the capital of China in the beginning of the 18th century AD. This progress was made possible through means of commercial and diplomatic interactions between China and the West, the latter being significantly represented by Venetian glassmakers from Murano. This alliance provided the Chinese with, on a practical level, novel mirrors, lenses, windowpanes and production skills. But also, in artistic terms, the alliance provided them with Aventurine glass and enamel materials, which would soon enough become their own productions. The Western glassmakers were invited to produce glassware mainly in the Chinese style, often copying ceramic forms. Normally glass was used for small snuff bottles and bowls were rare. Therefore, these types of bowls are esteemed for their beautiful form and colour, presenting signature techniques and shapes of Murano glassmaking.

e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.name: Mosque lamp.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.description: A large glass mosque lamp with a flaring mouth, flattened lower section, and low folded foot. Six glass rings are attached for suspension chains. The lamp is decorated with gilding and enamelling which forms a design in several registers. The top section of the neck features a large inscription in bold blue letters. The inscription, which is divided into three sections by circular medallions praising the sultan, includes the beginning of the famous Light Verse from the Qur'an (24: 35): 'God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His Light is as a wick-holder wherein is a light …'. This verse was a popular inclusion on lighting implements such as mosque lamps. The lower part of the neck has a band of sketchy decoration in red, punctuated by small blue medallions. The main part of the lamp's body features a dramatic network of fine interlacing patterns outlined in red against a blue background with floral elements. The interlacing is left clear, so that when the lamp was lit the patterns would have glowed. The bottom section of the lamp, the area above the foot, repeats the circular medallions from the neck.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.short_description: A mosque lamp of typical Mamluk shape, decorated with a bold inscription around the neck and a complex interlace pattern on the body. The interlace pattern is in outline, so when the lamp was lit – supposedly in the mosque of Sultan Hasan in Cairo – the interlacing bands would have glowed.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.initial_owner: Thought to have been made for the mosque and *madrasa* of Sultan Hasan (r. 748–52 / 1347–51 and 755–62 / 1354–61).
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.dates: Probably between hegira 757 / AD 1356 and AH 762 / AD 1361.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.method_for_datation: The lamp is said to have come from the mosque and *madrasa* of Sultan Hasan, which was built between 757 / 1356 and 762 / 1361.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that glass lamps like this were made in Cairo, as it would have been easier and safer than making them elsewhere and then transporting them.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., *Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East*, London, 2004, p.28 and plate 14.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.author: Barry Wood
keywords: religious object; Mosque interior decoration; calligraphy; inscription; floral decoration

e37256b2-67bf-5ba9-9652-b34bc0ac56d2.name: Ranftbecher Domkirche zu St. Stephan in Wien
e37256b2-67bf-5ba9-9652-b34bc0ac56d2.description: Anton Kothgasser spent most of his life working for the Vienna Porcelain Factory, yet he is mostly remembered for a series of beakers, usually signed and dated, that he painted with genre and topographic scenes. The specific technique used not only in this example, but almost all Kothgasser’s work, is translucent enamelling. Usually implemented on colourless, clear glass, it produces more delicate effects and is quicker that the previously practiced, original method of cutting out shapes in glass of different colours and leading them together. Standing on a star-cut base, the beaker is decorated with gold and a colourful veduta depicting St. Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna, which is also inscribed on the glass.

e3f716f9-a1ca-5994-b95e-0a12713c1e30.name: Glass vessel with handles and snake-thread trails
e3f716f9-a1ca-5994-b95e-0a12713c1e30.short_description: This basket-shaped object is made out of a mixture of clear, iridescent, and white-tinged glass with a yellow cast which has weathered over time. It is presumed that the shape was initially round but has been compressed over time. The basket stands on four feet and two bow handles topped with pinched crowns are placed on either side of the basket. This form may have been inspired by 3rd-century Roman glass designs.

e5cf5903-11e0-5580-a901-bee49dd2c87d.name: Flask
e5cf5903-11e0-5580-a901-bee49dd2c87d.description:
This pale green vessel is a flask which was made by using the free-blowing technique. The flask is irregular due to the possible slipping while forming the internal volume. It has a conical neck, a globular body which has a pushed-in bottom and some pinched indents in the side of the neck below the rim. Its flaring rim is folded out, over and in again. It is broken due to unknown reasons and mended around the neck and the body while has some other cracks in the body and the bottom. Milky weathering, iridescence and dulling are also seen on the surface of the flask, as well as a few blowing striations and pin-prick bubbles.  
In the free blowing technique, the glass melt, which is taken to the end of the continuous rotating blowing rod, is formed by rolling on the processing table and then blowing. After the internal volume is formed, it is taken to the noble bar from the opposite direction of the blowing rod (usually from the bottom of the container) for operations such as cutting a portion and forming the opening. The forming rod is attached to the container by a drop of the glass melt. Then, in the other direction, the tip of the form is cut or broken to remove the blowing rod. Attachments such as mouth edge profile, base, and handle are also made with auxiliary rods if necessary and then the glass is allowed to cool. The use of the free-blowing technique allowed thinning of the walls and the construction of larger and transparent closed forms.

e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.name: Ewer.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.description: A ewer carved from a single piece of rock-crystal. It has a pear-shaped body, beaked rim, and slightly splayed foot; a handle, which originally had a vertical thumb-piece at its apex, joins the rim to the lower part of the body. The body of the ewer is decorated on either side with identical scenes of a bird of prey attacking a four-legged animal with horns (a gazelle?). These vignettes are framed by large, leafy arabesque motifs. The whole design is contained within a delicate raised band which goes around the neck and down the body of the ewer on either side of the handle. This band acts as a frame and gives the design the feel of a textile wrapped around the ewer’s body. All of the details are drilled and cut with great skill, including the texturing in the form of lines and dots covering the bird and animal and the leaves of the arabesque patterns. Objects like this ewer were among the thousands of precious items looted from the Fatimid treasury during the unrest of 450 AH / AD 1060. A number of these made their way to Europe, where they were used as reliquaries in church treasuries.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.short_description: A pear-shaped ewer carved from a single block of the clear, colourless quartz known as rock-crystal. It is one of a number of luxury wares carved from rock-crystal for the Fatimid court in Cairo. Many such objects made their way into European church treasuries, where they were used as reliquaries.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.method_for_datation: There is a clear relationship between this ewer and a group of others in European collections, one of which has an inscription naming the Fatimid Caliph al-‘Aziz (r. AH 365–86 / AD 975–96). The decoration on the V&A ewer, including the arabesque pattern, is more complex and mature than is that on the others, suggesting a later date. Finally, Fatimid rock-crystal production was severely disrupted when violent social upheavals began in AH 452 / AD 1061.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Fatimid capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.bibliography:

e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.author: Barry Wood
keywords: figurative decoration; floral decoration; rock-crystal; carving; incision; animal decoration; bird; arabesque; reliquary; sumptuary art

e6e59cb7-d88f-532f-b065-f8e8d69cfd27.name: Studio glass
e6e59cb7-d88f-532f-b065-f8e8d69cfd27.short_description: Diego Feurer ranks among the leading glass artists in Switzerland. In his studio in Tesserete since the 1990s, he has focused on the murrine technique, in which colourful tesserae are melted down to form glass plates. Still in a heated state, these plates are then rolled (or blown) into the shape of vessels and objects, sanded, polished, and their surfaces cold-worked. The murrine technique lends Feurer's works a distinct and rich optical and aesthetic quality. Their textures and colours are reminiscent of vessels made of polished marble or stone.

e750697b-0787-548a-a9e2-a530da438063.name: Mosque lamps
e750697b-0787-548a-a9e2-a530da438063.short_description: From 1356 to 1363, Sultan an-Nasir al-Hasan commissioned a mosque to be erected in Cairo. He decorated it most luxuriously with mosque lamps made of enamelled glass. The most magnificent of them were produced in the workshops of Aleppo and Damascus. In the mosque, they are suspended on fine bronze chains from the ceiling, reminiscent of the star-spangled heavens. They decorate the space more than they illuminate it. In accordance with the religious surroundings, their ornamentation is modest: some elegant arabesques, the initial lines of the famous verses of light from the Qur'an and a dedication to the renowned benefactor. Together with his crest, the mosque lamps announce his generosity and his wealth. In 1855, it is believed that two of these precious mosque lamps were brought out of Egypt by the Austrian archduke Ferdinand Max, the future Emperor of Mexico; he decorated one of the splendid halls of his pleasure palace near Trieste with them.

e8a4c998-be32-5e65-9171-42e3735f2591.name: Cosmetic Bottle
e8a4c998-be32-5e65-9171-42e3735f2591.short_description: Cosmetic glass bottles with animal figurines were popular vessels in the pre-Islamic and early Islamic world and have been discovered in excavations in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Egypt. These bottles were likely produced in Syria sometime from the 1st-2nd century AH / 7th-8th century AD. Each of these animal-shaped flasks is unique, as the shapes of the animal figurines carrying baskets with small containers were freely and imaginatively tooled by the glassmaker. The animals most often depicted in these vessels are camels, horses and donkeys. This free-blown animal flask is of a colourless glass with a brownish tinge. The zoomorphic base on which its four animal legs are attached supports the openwork structure supporting a small container surrounded by a cage built in two tiers of applied and trailed dark green glass. The chest and head of an animal appear in the front and back. Such vessels were probably used as containers for perfume, balsam or khol.

e918c2ab-31e1-5d30-a10e-dc11b5fe5e5f.name: Bowl.
e918c2ab-31e1-5d30-a10e-dc11b5fe5e5f.description: An intact aquamarine-coloured glass bowl with a short flared neck, stained with dark-brown silver that resembles lustre painting. Blown in a mould with 15 vertical ribs, the glass is thick with numerous small bubbles. The decoration consists of vertical lines radiating from the base and a frieze of curling motifs just below the neck, between two horizontal bands. A further band runs around the rim of the bowl. When viewed from below the ribs and rays create a solar design, suggesting that this object may have been used as a lamp, suspended from the neck. The radial pattern recalls earlier glassware, whereas the curling motif is a common type of decoration on stained-glass from this period. Glassmakers in Egypt were particularly prolific during the Fatimid period, using skills inherited from the glass workshops of the Roman period.
e918c2ab-31e1-5d30-a10e-dc11b5fe5e5f.short_description: This bowl is remarkable: despite being made of finely moulded glass some 900 yeas ago, it remains completely intact. Lustre-painted glass was one of the many luxury objects that were prized during the Fatimid era.
e918c2ab-31e1-5d30-a10e-dc11b5fe5e5f.method_for_datation: Restrained designs painted with stains are usually attributed to the Fatimid period.
e918c2ab-31e1-5d30-a10e-dc11b5fe5e5f.method_for_provenance: The technique and decoration resemble other Fatimid glassware produced in Egypt. Furthermore, the bowl was found in Atfih in Egypt.

e98373dd-6e4e-5ada-9719-c553fa2337f9.name: Glass vessel possibly for chemistry.
e98373dd-6e4e-5ada-9719-c553fa2337f9.description:
A plain, utilitarian glass vessel without ornamentation. Its unusual shape indicates specialised use, probably in a field such as chemistry. It has an oval-shaped body with a narrow and long pipe coming out of its side and curving upward almost perpendicularly. The pipe grows gradually wider near the tip and its outward-splayed lip is shaped like a little funnel. This vessel is made of thin, white, translucent glass. It is free from decoration, probably so that the progress of chemical reactions taking place within it could be observed.  
The Abbasid period witnessed a cultural and scientific renaissance and archaeologists have discovered many glass finds intended for practical uses.
e98373dd-6e4e-5ada-9719-c553fa2337f9.short_description: Skilled craftsmanship was required not just for luxury wares but for more utilitarian objects as well. This undecorated but highly sophisticated glass vessel was probably used for experiments in chemistry.
e98373dd-6e4e-5ada-9719-c553fa2337f9.method_for_datation: Glass production flourished in many Islamic centres in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Egypt, and throughout several eras. Similarly, shaped glass fragments have been attributed to the early 'Abbasid period. Numerous utilitarian, Abbasid-era glass objects have been found in the Raqqa region during archaeological excavations of the 'Abbasid palace complexes under the direction of Nasib Salibi during the 1950s and Michael Meinecke during the 1990s. It is possible that this vessel was produced in the early Abbasid period.
e98373dd-6e4e-5ada-9719-c553fa2337f9.method_for_provenance: Numerous finds of glass in archaeological excavations at Raqqa, together with knowledge that the area was a glass-making centre, make it possible that the object was manufactured in Raqqa, a large urban city complex that flourished under the Abbasids.

e98373dd-6e4e-5ada-9719-c553fa2337f9.author: Mona al-Moadin
keywords: Glass vessel; chemistry; Nasib Salibi; Michael Meinecke; Raqqa; science; blown glass

e9ac8bfe-e5a8-566c-836f-41ec7b0ff65e.name: Master weight (*mithqal*).
e9ac8bfe-e5a8-566c-836f-41ec7b0ff65e.description:
This master weight (*mithqal*) made of translucent green glass is broken into three pieces. A *kufic* inscription, faintly impressed, can be seen in two places on the upper surface. The inscription consists of five lines of *kufic* characters, which are difficult to read with the naked eye. However, by making a rubbing of the two stamps, G. Marçais was able to decipher them and transcribed them as the following: '*î Allah, mimma amara bihi / al amir Abd al-Rahman bin Habib / Masal bin Hammad wali Mila / ichroune ukiya, fi sanat / sabaa wa ichrine wa miaî*' (In the name of God. Among that which was provided/ by the governor Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib / to Masal ibn Hammad, chief administrator of Mila / 20 *ukiya*, in the year / hundred and twenty-seven).  
Thus, according to the inscription, the master weight weighs 20 *ukiya*, and this weight value is guaranteed by an official stamp. The *ukiya* (ounce) is equivalent to 69.338 grams; the standard therefore weighed 1,386.76 grams.  
It was the amir who fixed the weight value of standards of weight, and who imposed it on the population through the *wali* (provincial administrators); the name of the amir is mentioned; here it refers to 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib, grandson of 'Uqba ibn Nafi, the founder of Kairouan. The *wali*, Masal ibn Hammad, he remains a mystery in terms of the chroniclers, but he is probably Sanhadjian, because his name, Hammad, which he also shares with his father, is commonplace in Sanhadjian sources, particularly those of the Maghrebi and Andalusian Zirids.  
Pieced together, these three fragments of glass would constitute a disc with a hole in the centre. This master weight served as a unit of measure to control the weights used in commercial transactions.
e9ac8bfe-e5a8-566c-836f-41ec7b0ff65e.short_description: Master weight broken into three parts and bearing a *kufic* inscription stating its weight (20 *ukiya* or 1,386.76 g) and the name of the provincial administrator charged by the governor, whose name is also given, with determining weight. These master weights were used for controlling trade.
e9ac8bfe-e5a8-566c-836f-41ec7b0ff65e.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
e9ac8bfe-e5a8-566c-836f-41ec7b0ff65e.method_for_datation: A stamp on the master weight dates it to 127 / 745.
e9ac8bfe-e5a8-566c-836f-41ec7b0ff65e.method_for_provenance: This master weight was discovered during terracing work in the mining region of Boukadra, Tebessa.

eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.name: Kohl jar.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.description:
Small, lenticular rock-crystal bottle, broken at the top and the bottom. Its high-relief decoration is divided into different sections. At the top there is a strip inscribed in florid *kufic* script that reads 'Baraka min Allah / wa lahu al-afiya' (The blessing of God) on both sides. The next section depicts two birds of prey, presumably falcons, facing one another around a vegetal composition in the form of volutes.  
As is common in this type of piece, this jar has a 'bore' (central cylindrical hole) that would almost certainly have been used to keep kohl or antimony chloride, which was used as a cosmetic. This jar would have been mounted on some sort of support and would also have had a glass rod used to dip into the substances and apply it.  
The production of colourless quartz rock-crystal provided a level of transparency that medieval craftsmen had not yet achieved using glass. This, combined with the difficulty of the technique, meant that this craftwork was always sought after. Objects made of this material were sometimes offered as diplomatic gifts.  
There is no evidence of the production of such objects in al-Andalus, and their presence on the Iberian Peninsula in the AH 4th and 5th / AD 10th and 11th centuries was undoubtedly due to trade with Fatimid Egypt. Many of the Islamic rock-crystal pieces that came to the Caliphate of Córdoba from the East were dispersed subsequently around the Iberian Peninsula and reused during the Christian age, embellished with new and sumptuous precious-metal elements.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.short_description: Objects carved from rock-crystal from Fatimid Egypt were much sought after for their beauty and quality, and consequently they were imported, exchanged as diplomatic gifts and considered to be valuable booty. The small size of the inside of this pot suggests that it was used to hold essence.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.method_for_datation: The rock-crystal industry in Fatimid Egypt grew up a short time before 254 / 868 and survived until 452–4 / 1060–2. Most researchers agree on the Egyptian origin of the approximately 180 objects from this era that are held around the world, as well as on Kurt Erdman's method of classifying them purely on the basis of stylistic analysis.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.method_for_provenance: According to its file, this jar came from Alcalá de Henares. There are currently 40 rock-crystal pieces in Spain, including various different bottles and chess pieces (there is another Fatimid piece in this material in the general inventory of the National Archaeological  Museum). Most of them, having been acquired during the Reconquest in the form of taxes or war booty, were deposited in churches or monasteries in various different regions of Christian Spain as offerings.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.obtention: The piece was deposited with the National Archaeological Museum by the Artistic Recuperation Service on 21 November 1910.

eb1acf73-bb6d-5942-b161-7eaac54291ff.name: Glass
eb1acf73-bb6d-5942-b161-7eaac54291ff.description:
Inverted, truncated conical glass of transparent crystal. Engraved decoration, framed by two horizontal borders – the top one formed by a succession of simplified pairs of leaves and the bottom of waves. Three images of Asian-inspired structures, framed by oval medallions, are surrounded by an overlay of radiant circles and stylised vegetation.  
  
The production of this and similar examples has traditionally been attributed to the Real Fábrica de Cristales de La Granja (La Granja Royal Crystal Factory) in Segovia, Spain. However, distinctly similar pieces were found in the 1724 shipwreck of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe in Bahía de Samaná, Dominican Republic, a discovery which casts doubt on the association of such works with the Royal Factory, as the debacle occurred prior to the institution’s foundation.  
  
Among other theories on the origin of these glasses, it has been suggested that they may have been produced at the Fábrica de Nuevo Baztán (Nuevo Baztán Factory), active between 1720 and 1728. Carlos León Amores proposes the more plausible hypothesis, however, that these were Bohemian crystal pieces marketed in Spain.  
  
Both the technique and the chinoiserie motifs are indeed associated with Bohemian glass production, a style that later gained popularity in the catalogues of La Granja.
eb1acf73-bb6d-5942-b161-7eaac54291ff.method_for_datation: Analysis of style and technique and comparison with similar pieces recovered from the shipwreck of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe.

eb5033cb-f5e6-537a-88bb-7d6bf116bf69.name: Laledan
eb5033cb-f5e6-537a-88bb-7d6bf116bf69.short_description: It is known that there were workshops producing glass vessels around Beykoz in Istanbul in the 19th century. The first glass workshop was founded by Mevlevi Dervish Mehmed Dede during the reign of Selim III (1789-1807). There were European glass craftsmen working in those workshops as well. Cups, bottles, jugs etc. made of colourful, colourless and opal glass were among Beykoz' productions. This is a *laledan* made of dark blue opaline. On the body there are white vervain motives with green leaves. There are three circles with stars and crescents.

ed4ee165-2235-50df-a724-514e1ecbda10.name: Shallow Dish
ed4ee165-2235-50df-a724-514e1ecbda10.description: This dish has a shallow wall with a narrow everted rim and stands on a ring-like foot. Its decoration consists of an allover pattern. A five-pointed star with enclosed triangles around the base and the lower part of the wall continues with a row of large lozenges containing smaller lozenges. The pattern can be seen when viewed from the exterior as well as on the interior if seen against light. This decoration was produced by blowing the glass into a dip mould; taken out of the mould it was further blown and tooled with great accuracy. A large pontil mark (from a hot metal rod with some glass attached to it) in the exterior center of the foot remains from shaping and tooling the dish.
materials: Glass, deep blue, thin brownish weathering; mould-blown, tooled, worked on the pontil

edacacf2-f3eb-5399-8940-2ceeca47f4c1.name: *La Toilette de Vénus*
edacacf2-f3eb-5399-8940-2ceeca47f4c1.short_description:
Venus sits naked on a bench under opulent open draperies reminiscent of a theatrical stage, half-concealing a park with a pillar in the background. In front of her stands an oval mirror. A pitcher, an open shell, jewellery, ribbons and flowers are laid out on the ground for her toilette. Her gaze distracted, she hugs a white dove in her right arm and touches the daintily arranged fingers of her left hand to her ear pendant, while a further chained dove flutters at her feet.  
  
The reverse glass painting is bathed in grey-blue light and thus, albeit in reverse, faithfully reproduces the colours and composition of the 1783 colour print *La Toilette de Vénus* by Jean-François Janinet (1752–1814). The print, which precisely mirrors the original painting by François Boucher (1703–70), is dedicated to “Madame la Comtesse de Coastin, Née Mailly”, but many scholars have regarded the goddess of love as a portrait of the Marquise de Pompadour, for the painting by Boucher was part of her collection.  
  
The careful and precise painting technique with the characteristic shape of the trees and the eyes, but also the original safety paper, which today serves as the lining, place the origin of this reverse glass painting in China.
edacacf2-f3eb-5399-8940-2ceeca47f4c1.obtention: Donated by Ruth und Frieder Ryser in 2006

This complex vessel within a vessel demonstrates the high level of skill amongst craftspeople in antiquity. Examples have been found across the Roman Empire from Britain to Syria to Germany, suggesting the transmission of knowledge via contact between makers.

ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.name: Mosque lamp.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.description: A mosque lamp of typical size and shape for Mamluk lamps, with flaring neck, wide body and high foot. Thick glass loops are attached for the suspension cords. The body is decorated with a large inscription which reads, 'This is what was made a *waqf* by the servant yearning for God the Exalted, hoping for the pardon of his generous Lord, Qijlis, \[officer\] of al-Malik al-Nasir'. The neck carries a verse from the Qur'an (9:18) and three medallions with the Mamluk blazon indicating the owner's rank, in this case a sword telling us that Qijlis was *amir silah* (arms-bearer) to the sultan. The lamp is said to have come from a monastery in Seidnaya, a village near Damascus.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.short_description: A mosque lamp of typical Mamluk form, with bold inscriptions and three medallions with the patron’s blazon, a sword. The patron was one Amir Qijlis, arms-bearer to the sultan, who commissioned this lamp as a pious donation to an unknown mosque.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.initial_owner: Sayf al-Din Qijlis al-Nasiri, an officer of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad between AH 716–31 / AD 1317–31.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.method_for_datation: The inscription mentions Sayf al-Din Qijlis al-Nasiri, who was promoted to *amir silah* of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad in 716 / 1317 and died in 731 / 1331.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.

efdc37d8-ffc1-5935-bdda-63b30ac03495.name: Bottle
efdc37d8-ffc1-5935-bdda-63b30ac03495.description: The care with which this blue bottle has been made and decorated indicates it is an outstanding object. In fact, its quality suggests it could have been traded as a luxury commodity to other parts of the world. China imported similar examples of Islamic glass, and the discovery of such vessels in Chinese tombs and treasuries helps provide crucial dating information.
materials: Glass, dark blue, patchy grey and black weathering flaked-off, considerable abrasion; free-blown, relief-cut, tooled, worked on the pontil

f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.name: *Mashrabiyya* window.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.description: A stucco and coloured glass *mashrabiyya* window, which belongs to a set of openwork windows in the Kelvingrove Collection, each with a different design in the centre of the niche. This one shows a cypress tree surrounded by flower stems under a niche. The green, red, and yellow coloured-glass pieces have been imbedded in the stucco openwork from the back. During the Ottoman period in Cairo both mosques and private houses were adorned with such windows from as early as the AH 10th / AD 16th century. The tradition of setting coloured-glass in stucco has endured since its earliest days in the Abbasid capital of Samarra (AH mid-2nd / AD 9th century) to the present day.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.short_description: This stucco and coloured glass window is decorated with a cypress tree and floral arrangements, typical of AH 13th- / AD 19th-century Ottoman art. The cypress tree symbolises a true Muslim as it stands tall and bows in the wind gracefully. Windows such as this adorned both homes and mosques in Cairo.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the style and technique of this window resembles many 13th- / 19th-century stucco windows still in place in Cairo today.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.obtention: Purchased by Glasgow Museums / Kelvingrove Art Gallery in 1896.

f25154c9-a824-51ce-9166-15340ff659ca.name: Vase
f25154c9-a824-51ce-9166-15340ff659ca.description:
This colourless, blown glass vase was made in the Art Nouveau style in the First Serbian Glass Factory in Paraćin. The entire surface of the vase is wrapped in three stylized flowers with twigs and leaves made by grinding technique. Similar stylistic patterns appear on items manufactured in the Sankt Petersburg Imperial Glass Factory after 1911, with a slight difference in the manner of decoration.  
Art Nouveau was an enduring style in Serbia glass production. With minor changes in decoration, some models were produced in factories even until the mid-20th century. The First Serbian Glass Factory on several occasions, with minor changes in decoration, repeated popular forms. The vase shown here was created in 1921, during a period of the factory’s success when enviable quality and processing of utility glass was achieved and the factory strived to reach the level of glassmaking expertise of the Czech and German glasshouses. In addition to the Czechs, Germans and Slovenians, a large number of local craftsmen were profiled as master glassmakers. The finest examples from this period were glass items of thin walls and fine structure decorated primarily with Art Nouveau floral motifs.
f25154c9-a824-51ce-9166-15340ff659ca.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.
f25154c9-a824-51ce-9166-15340ff659ca.provenance: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, Paraćin
f25154c9-a824-51ce-9166-15340ff659ca.obtention: Donated by Kapetanović family from Belgrade in 1968

f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.name: Underglass painted calligraphic panel
f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.description:
This underglass-painted panel consists of inscriptions in black *jali thuluth* (calligraphic Arabic script) inside an oval frame of leaves in a chestnut shade of gold. At the top is the word "Allah", below that the word "Muhammad", and in the centre the phrase "Ya aman Ali", all written as symmetric mirror compositions (*müsenna*). Between the two "ya" letters is a picture of a Bektaşi headdress and below it the figure of a submission stone (*teslim taşı*). The lines of the two lams are extended upwards to form two halberds, and the letter "ya" in the word ‘Ali’ forms his double-pointed sword Zülfikar. Around the lower edge of the oval frame appears the signature of the artist written in *riq‘a* script: "Painted by Hafız Ahmed Feyzi from the Demirhan neighbourhood of Bursa." In the lower corners of the panel are medallions formed of leaves painted in chestnut brown tones of gold, and in the upper corners are compositions of leaves and flowers.  
The pictures and scripts under glass are products of folk art. Such works are applied to the back of a piece of glass in reverse. They are dependent on the glass because the work disappears if the glass is broken. Their subjects are mostly illustrations of folkloric myths, stories, beliefs and symbols. Such panels were seen in the homes, small mosques, meeting places of dervishes and tombs in the past.
f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.method_for_datation: It was determined through publications and expert opinion.

f37cfcce-b0a0-5a4d-a76e-e42800b88c6a.name: Ewer
f37cfcce-b0a0-5a4d-a76e-e42800b88c6a.short_description: This jug is a rare example of early Islamic glasswork that carried any form of inscription. It is a rich, deep turquoise, a spectacular colour which was extremely unusual for any glass of this period. Made of mould-blown glass, the ewer is a drop form with a short foot, a thistle mouth and an extruded spout. A simple bent handle links the mouth and the body. A broad band of moulded *kufic* inscription that consists of repetitions of the Arabic word *al-Malk* (ownership) runs around its body divided by palmettes. The technique of moulding *kufic* inscriptions is found on glass vessels from Mesopotamia and from northeast Iran.

f3bdac71-7cdf-5bc4-bccf-2c0e773d181e.name: Goblet with cover
f3bdac71-7cdf-5bc4-bccf-2c0e773d181e.short_description:
With the exception of a few square centimetres, the surface of this covered goblet is engraved and polished. On the front side, a small relief bust made of biscuit porcelain is glazed into an oval panel, i.e., covered by glass on both sides. It depicts a profile portrait of King Ludwig I of Bavaria, who held the throne from 1825 to 1848. A silver crown thaler from 1828 may have served as a model for the portrait; a small beard on the lower lip, which is typical for depictions of Ludwig I, is visible on the relief.  
  
In the first half of the 19th century, the Harrach glassworks in Neuwelt, on the Bohemian side of the Krkonoše Mountains, was one of the leading companies in this important glassworks region. It was praised for having produced the finest glassware with glazed inserts around 1830. The porcelain reliefs, like the one on this goblet, were ordered from elsewhere.  
  
The production of portraits of Ludwig for the period from 1830 to 1833 has been proven. Pieces with this kind of decoration were considered luxury objects and probably used exclusively for representational purposes.
f3bdac71-7cdf-5bc4-bccf-2c0e773d181e.method_for_datation: By historical evidence. The Harrach glassworks in Neuwelt was one of the leading companies of the region and experimenting with glazed inserts since 1821. Portraits of King Ludwig I of Bavaria are known to exist at the time as shown by a silver Kronentaler dated 1828. The high quality as well as the  ruler's portrait can only point to Neuwelt.

f4987d48-6c52-594a-a15b-12a3fe0431f8.name: Mosque lamp
f4987d48-6c52-594a-a15b-12a3fe0431f8.short_description: This mosque lamp belongs to a well-established group of glass lamps probably made for the Mamluk Sultan (al-Nasir Nasir al-Din) Hasan (AH 734-763/ AD 1334-1361). f49a881b-465e-552f-97b1-6bfcba915e82.name: Bottle or perfume sprinkler.
f49a881b-465e-552f-97b1-6bfcba915e82.description:
A disk shaped bi-coloured bottle with a concave base and a small neck decorated with a marbling pattern achieved by dragging a comb-like tool that forms the loops. The same pattern in dark purple and white has been used all over the vessel.  
  
The 'combing' and blowing technique used on this vessel became popular in Egypt and Syria during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods, but had been practiced in Syria since the Roman period. The marbling technique used here entailed winding opaque glass threads (usually green, blue or purple) around the blown bubble of glass while it was still hot. The threads were then pressed on to the surface by means of a stone rod and then combed to form a series of parallel festoons, or white trails, that were tooled into festoons or feather-like patterns.
f49a881b-465e-552f-97b1-6bfcba915e82.short_description: A glass perfume bottle from Ajlun Castle, with a marbling pattern achieved by dragging a comb-like tool to form the loops. This technique became popular in Egypt during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods, although it had been practised in Syria since the Roman period.
f49a881b-465e-552f-97b1-6bfcba915e82.dimensions: Height 11 cm, height (of neck) 3 cm, width 8 cm.
f49a881b-465e-552f-97b1-6bfcba915e82.method_for_datation: The bottle was dated by analysis of the stratigraphic context in which it was found and through stylistic analysis and comparison with other, similar bottles produced in Syria and in Adana in Anatolia, Turkey.
f49a881b-465e-552f-97b1-6bfcba915e82.method_for_provenance: The bottle was recovered during an archaeological excavation at the Castle of Ajlun. Its place of production is uncertain but it is possible that it was produced in Syria.
f49a881b-465e-552f-97b1-6bfcba915e82.obtention: The bottle was recovered in 1927 by G. Horsfield in the moat at the Castle of Ajlun during an archaeological excavation and clearing programme in the south-west corner of the moat.

f4eb4e11-e54d-5077-b65a-a9a797807e06.name: Sculpture of Dounreay Power Station
f4eb4e11-e54d-5077-b65a-a9a797807e06.short_description: Glass artist Kate Williams’s practice explores the scientific, cultural, and artistic elements of glass and light. In her collaborative Glass Nuclear Power Station Project with the artist John Lloyd, three real, and one fictional nuclear power station were memorialised in cast uranium glass. The use of uranium glass for these sculptures represents society’s complicated relationship with nuclear power. Lit from underneath with ultraviolet light, which excites the particles of uranium dioxide; they emit a bright acid lime green colour. The use of uranium has been used as a safe colorant in glass since the mid-19th Century. However, here it suggests the vitrification of nuclear waste as a way of dealing with the nuclear legacy. The Dounreay site was opened in 1955 for the development of fast reactors. Three reactors were built on the site, the Dounreay Fast Reactor (DFR), Prototype Fast Reactor (PFR) and the Dounreay Materials Test Reactor (DMTR). All three are now closed.

f5554c23-9f46-546a-a095-8b630a57e77f.name: Bowlegarnitur
f5554c23-9f46-546a-a095-8b630a57e77f.description: An essential association for the foundation and development of Czech modern art was the one of Artěl – an initiative that was founded by two men: Alois Dyk, an art enthusiast, and banker. and Vilem Štech, an art theoretician and art historian also responsible for endorsing young Czech modernism. Several artists joined in the beginning, such as Pavel Janak, Jan Konupek and Helena Johnova. The name of the association was taken from Tolstoy’s novel *Anna Karenina* and meant a merely verbally agreed-upon community of people who work together and jointly vouch for each other, as well as have an equal share of the income. Since they lacked the finances, the Artěl could not afford their own workshop, and therefore performed manufacturing in different factories, such as the Rydl and Thon Company in Svijany-Podoli in Northern Bohemia for ceramics and porcelain, and the Pryl glass factory in Růženin in Central Bohemia for glass. Among the various artists that participated in Artěl, Josef Rosipal, even though he was an architect, was of particular importance for the implementation of the association’s ideas in the medium of glass. Rosipal’s most famous pieces are his cut services, created in simple shapes, commonly overlayed in red or blue with cut geometric decorative motifs. Additionally, since the sentiment of the Artěl association was oriented more towards expressionism, and, even more, cubism, these tendencies can be seen most clearly in the decorative motifs of the glass. The lid presented is a part of a complete set, composed of a punch bowl with a spoon and this lid, along with a set of six glasses. The handle of the lid is overlaid with ruby red glass and serves as a central point for the triangular decorative motifs that spread across the surface of the lid. The triangular and other geometric decorative motifs demonstrate the tendencies of the Artěl association in the fields of glass art.

f672a566-07c0-5def-83e1-f7239ef4cf19.name: Cup with *merletto* ('lace') decoration
f672a566-07c0-5def-83e1-f7239ef4cf19.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The tendency of Murano's industries in using bizarre shapes, often of zoomorphic inspiration, gave life to manufacts not so much functional as decorative. It was very successful. The cylindrical cup in green glass with white glaze and “lace” decoration is the result of a combination of common design details in the second half of the 19th century: while it shows a Victorian decoration, the structure of the object recalls a late 14th century model.

f85a994c-93f5-5c2e-a133-5f14f1826395.name: Reverse painting on glass: Al-Malik az-Zahir Baibars
f85a994c-93f5-5c2e-a133-5f14f1826395.short_description: A famous heroic epic painted on glass is played out in Palestine in 1260. The great moment for the former slave, al-Malik az-Zahir Baibars, arrives when he inflicts the first defeat on the Mongols. In the same year, Baibars, by now Sultan of Egypt, begins to gradually shut down the final strongholds of the Christian crusaders in the Levant; not so much due to religious zeal, but rather to eradicate "the Franks" as a source of unrest. Essentially, this saviour of Islam would lend himself to religious warriors as an icon. In 2005 the television series *Az-Zahir Baybars* is broadcast in Syria. The programme avoids, however, any religious instrumentalisation of the material. Given the religious furore in the Arabic world and beyond, the television series transmits a remarkable message: Muslims and Christians, in spite of their chequered and difficult historical relationship, are supporters of the same civilisation; both are called upon to contribute together to its continued existence.

f87b1927-367b-54c3-b700-eea1b1e9442b.name: Tankard with lid
f87b1927-367b-54c3-b700-eea1b1e9442b.short_description:
This tankard is a typical example of a historicist object from the late 19th century. At that time, a renewal of artisanal craftsmanship was taking place with the aim, among others, of counteracting the mass production that arose with industrialisation. This movement was mainly inspired by objects from earlier periods, but it produced works with a strong claim to stylistic independence and a high level of craftsmanship.  
  
This example largely incorporates elements found in 16th-century pieces from archaeological excavations. It originates from the Rheinische Glashütte in Cologne-Ehrenfeld.  
  
Oskar Rauter, the company’s technical and commercial manager in the late 1800s, studied Roman, Venetian and Old German glassworks and recorded them in sketchbooks. These sketches were used to prepare glassware designs incorporating some reinterpretation of the original pieces.  
  
In 1881 and 1886, the company published commodity price currents containing drawings and descriptions of this glass piece, which is described as a “ring-shaped beaker with lid, with 30 grommet prunts and metal rings and pincered foot rim, antique green”. The description also highlights the resemblance to several Old German glass tankards, although these usually have no lids.
f87b1927-367b-54c3-b700-eea1b1e9442b.method_for_datation: By historical evidence and documents. The present piece originates from the Rheinische Glashütte in Cologne-Ehrenfeld and is listed in their “commodity price currents” of 1881 and 1886 among the glassware produced “in old German style”.
f87b1927-367b-54c3-b700-eea1b1e9442b.method_for_provenance: By historical evidence and documents. The present piece originates from the Rheinische Glashütte in Cologne-Ehrenfeld and is listed in their “commodity price currents” of 1881 and 1886 among the glassware produced “in old German style”.

f934a965-24ae-5b22-965c-17838c6cb895.name: Fragment of a glass vessel.
f934a965-24ae-5b22-965c-17838c6cb895.description:
Part of the base of a transparent glass vessel decorated with brown metallic lustre. Its ornamentation consists of the depiction of a mountain-goat or deer with two long horns. The animal is seen running towards the right, and carrying in its mouth a branch that ends in a heart-shaped leaf; branches similar to that being carried by the animal adorn the background. The depiction reveals details of the torso and the shanks of the animal in a naturalistic style.  
Glass decorated with metallic lustre is considered to have been an innovation known in Egypt since the AH 2nd / AD 8th century which flourished during the Fatimid period, where paintings of animals, birds and plants were produced on glass, in the same style as those used on ceramics with metallic lustre. At the Benaki Museum in Athens, there are pieces of glass, which carry the signature of 'Sa'ad', a Fatimid ceramist who was famous during the latter half of the AH 5th / AD 11th century and the beginning of the AH 6th / AD 12th century. Fatimid ceramists had, therefore, transferred styles of decoration in metallic lustre on ceramics to glass.  
In addition to decorating glass with metallic lustre, Egypt was known for other kinds of decoration on glass such as ornamentation with thin glass filaments, which were added and then pressed around the vessel; cut-glass decorations in high relief; stamped decoration and a method of glass-appliqué in high relief. Thick glass, which closely resembles rock-crystal, was also popular and was decorated by cutting the design into the glass in deep recesses.
f934a965-24ae-5b22-965c-17838c6cb895.short_description: A piece from the base of a transparent glass vessel decorated in metallic lustre, a new technique that became known in Egypt at the beginning of the Islamic era in imitation of lustre ceramics and which flourished under the Fatimids.
f934a965-24ae-5b22-965c-17838c6cb895.method_for_datation: This piece was dated by comparison of its decorative style with that used in the decoration of ceramics with metallic lustre during the Fatimid period.
f934a965-24ae-5b22-965c-17838c6cb895.method_for_provenance: An Egyptian provenance is certain as metallic-lustre glass is known to have flourished in Egypt during the Fatimid period.
f934a965-24ae-5b22-965c-17838c6cb895.obtention: The glass fragment was bought by the Museum from an antiquities dealer, Tano, in 1940.

f994be40-bb74-57d6-b8ef-58ebdb438852.name: Vase
f994be40-bb74-57d6-b8ef-58ebdb438852.description: In the complete course of art history, rarely has there been a movement in which the decorative arts played such an integral role as Art Nouveau. Among these arts, glass held the most important role by far. As a very flexible and mostly transparent material, glass provided an ideal medium in which artists of the movement could express their ideas that were inspired by nature and organic forms. The style, originating in England, spread throughout Europe; yet the most notable places it set its roots were Belgium, France, the Czech Republic, Germany and Austria. Known as Jugendstil in the German-speaking lands, the movement bared witness to divine glass creations from many, now world-famous, craftspeople who have truly earned honourable mentions in the history of the decorative and applied arts. An essential place for the birth and development of the Jugendstil in Vienna was the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshops), founded by Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser. The main aim of the workshops was to bring the artist or designer closer to the craftspeople and technicians entrusted with the execution of their designs, while also encouraging the designers to be their own crafters. The Wiener Werkstätte was host to a large number of Austrian craftspeople, such as Dagobert Peche, Otto Prutscher and Ludwig Heinrich Jungnickel. Designed by Otto Prutscher, this colourless, hexagonal vase serves as an ideal example of the implementation of sources and inspiration found in nature on the most delicate material of Art Nouveau.

f9c02b0e-988c-5ed8-84dc-f015f0a4d4f8.name: Wineglass
f9c02b0e-988c-5ed8-84dc-f015f0a4d4f8.description:
Clear, mould-blown glass with yellow casing and cut decoration. Disc-shaped foot; slender, stylised stem and conical cup. The piece was designed by the Viennese architect and designer Otto Prutscher and is a clear reflection of his architectural background and the style of the Vienna Secession milieu. Although Vienna Secession art initially coincided with the principles of Art Nouveau, it gradually adopted a more geometric and linear aesthetic, favouring a synthesis of architecture and decorative art. The organisation found inspiration in the Arts and Crafts movement, seeking to establish a connection between designer, artisan and public, and to create practical designs for daily living.  
  
Decorative squares and a preference for geometry are salient themes here, as well as in the general repertoire of the Vienna Secession, Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser. This piece was produced by Meyr’s Neffe Glassworks, in Adolfov, Czech Republic, and distributed by E. Bakalowits Söhne, in Vienna.

f9f0db9c-6034-5d02-b5c8-8b68a3f973f3.name: Beykoz glass - cup
f9f0db9c-6034-5d02-b5c8-8b68a3f973f3.short_description: Cup decorated with a stripped band, floral motifs and in the centre a circular medallion with a basket of fruits. It was made in the workshops of Istanbul on the Asian side. The basket with the fruit motif is a known motif of the 18th century as for example in the decoration of the private chambers of sultan Ahmed III (1703–1730) at the Topkapi Palace, and on the fountains of Istanbul. Ottoman glass of the 19th century was developed in order to compete with the imported glass from Venice and Bohemia. The technique is European but the decoration Ottoman.
f9f0db9c-6034-5d02-b5c8-8b68a3f973f3.author: Mina Moraitou
keywords: Beykoz glass

fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.name: Spa Glass
fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.description:
The 'Collection of Ceramics, Glass and Porcelain' at the Museum of Applied Arts houses a large number of spa glasses from Central Europe. Initially, water at spa resorts was drawn using vessels made of natural materials, but with the development of industry in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, glass cups began to be produced. Glass was considered a very suitable material, as it preserved the qualitative properties of mineral water. Patients would wait in line, and following doctors' recommendations, pour precisely the prescribed number of millilitres of healing water into their cup.  
  
This spa glass, from the Collection, features a depiction of the Church of St. George in Oplenac and represents a type of souvenir glass. It has a flat shape, made of moulded glass, with a hand-painted application and enamel detailing. It is dated to the 1930s, during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and was most likely produced by the Serbian Glass Factory in Paraćin. This is supported by stylistic features, as well as evidence from numerous factory catalogues of the period, in which spa glasses with painted motifs were part of the product range.  
The Cyrillic inscription on the application also points to a local and national identity, while the motif of Oplenac is associated with the Karađorđević dynasty, making this spa glass a piece of promotional memorabilia as well.
fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.
fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.obtention: Given by Biljana Crvenković from Belgrade in 2023
fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.author: Zeina Al Amad
keywords: spa glass, glass, Serbian Glass Factory, Paraćin

fabf4535-e263-529b-9b2c-f09555375400.name: Mosque Lamp
fabf4535-e263-529b-9b2c-f09555375400.short_description: Glass mosque lamps such as this splendid example were made in abundance during the Mamluk period in Egypt and Syria. Free blown, enamelled and gilded, these lamps contained oil and were suspended from the ceiling of mosques, madrasas and palace complexes, illuminating the buildings with their beautifully executed decoration, including Qur’anic verses, proverbs, sultanate titles, or geometric and floral patterns. This particular lamp, with a rounded body and long sloping curved shoulder with a flared, conical mouth and trumpeted foot, has six applied loop handles around its body from which it would have hung. The lamp’s body and mouth are both decorated entirely with blue floral medallions outlined with white strapwork, set against loosely drawn red floral motifs. This example, although comparatively small in height, relates to a known set of other mosque lamps attributed to the reign of the Mamluk Sultan Hasan (AH r. 747-762 / AD 1347-1361). These lamps were most probably made for the madrasa of Sultan Hasan in Cairo, which was completed in 763-764 AH / 1362-1363 AD. Like many other examples, this lamp remained in its original structure until the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries AH / nineteenth century AD, when many were sold and entered into museum collections worldwide.

fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.name: Watermelon-shaped bottle
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.short_description:
Glass vessels in the shape of fruits were made in Syria-Mesopotamia and Egypt as early as the mid 2nd millennium BC. With the introduction of glass-blowing in the Roman period, they became much cheaper and, by the 2nd century AD, flasks and jars in the form of bunches of grapes or dates were popular all over the empire, persisting into the 6th and 7th centuries.  
The deliberately matt surface of this bottle gives an added dimension of naturalism. There are, however, no known parallels for its shape and size.
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.type: Blown, tooled, wheel cut and polished glass
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.method_for_datation: There are no known parallels, but according to S. Goldstein, the thick walls and rim are reminiscent of Sasanian and early Islamic flasks, including some found at Jerash and Shiraz. The treatment of the surface and the cutting also suggest a late Sasanian date.

keywords: glass; wheel-cut; blown glass; Iran; Iraq; Sasanian art; glass-blowing
materials: Dark emerald-green glass, blown, tooled, wheel cut and polished

fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.name: Oil lamp.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.description: A glass lamp composed of three sections: base, body and the neck, and completely covered with vegetal decoration beautifully and skilfully executed. It is painted with a variety of colours, with enamel and with profuse gilding. In addition it is adorned with written inscriptions and the blazon of the endower. The neck of the lamp is wide and narrows as it moves in closer to the body, thus taking the form of a conic glass. The neck is adorned with both vegetal motifs that fill the surface, and with an inscription band in Mamluk *thuluth* script. The inscription, 8 cm high, rendered in dark-blue, includes part of a verse from the Qur'an, “al-Tauba” (“the Repentance” 9: 18): “The Mosques of Allah shall be visited and maintained by such as believe in Allah and the Last Day”.The verse is intercepted by three circular medallions with a red circle at the centre, within which is a gilded goblet, the blazon of Amir Tankaz al-Nasiri. A decorative band is located between the body of the lamp and its neck formed from eight consecutive lotus flowers. The body is decorated with a relatively large gilded inscription band, against a dark-blue background, it reads: “This has been ordered by the Sublime, our lord, the *amir*, al-Saifi Tankaz supporter of the honourable and protected Mamluks in al-Sham \[Syria\]”. The inscription is interrupted by six suspension loops that are used to attach the chains for hanging the lamp. There is decorative band below that containing the inscription this is adorned with vegetal motifs. The lower area of the body, before transferring to the base, contains six medallions, three of which contain blazons and the remaining three of which are filled with vegetal motifs. The base of the lamp is 4 cm high; it is wider at the bottom than the top. The base is adorned with three bands filled with gilded vegetal decoration.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.short_description: The glass lamp is completely covered with intricate and skilful vegetal decoration and is painted in a variety of colours, with enamel and gilding. The body bears a gilded inscription and the blazon of its endower, Amir Tankiz al-Nasiri, against a dark-blue background. The lamp has a number of decorative medallions.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.initial_owner: Amir Tankaz al-Nasiri who occupied the position of a representative of the Sultanate in al-Sham (Great Syria) region in AH 712–40 / AD 1312–40. This was during the rule of the Mamluk sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun (who ruled three times: AH 693–4, 698–708 and 709–41 / AD 1294–5, 1299–1309 and 1309–40).
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.method_for_datation: The lamp was dated based on the written inscriptions on it, which mention the name of its owner, Amir Tankaz al-Nasiri.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.method_for_provenance: Lamps, similar to that exhibited here, were renowned during the Mamluk period. They were typically produced in either Cairo or Damascus, so it is likely that this piece was made in Damascus in view of the fact that Amir Tankaz was a deputy there.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.obtention: The lamp was transferred from al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil) to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem in 1967.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.bibliography: Abu Khalaf, M., *Islamic Art Through the Ages: Masterpieces of the Islamic Museum of al-Haram al-Sharif,* Jerusalem, 1998.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Thuluth; gilded glass; painted glass; epigraphic decoration; vegetal decoration; lamp; mosque interior decoration

fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.name: El transparente Universo (The Transparent Universe)
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.description:
Originally from Segovia, Torres Esteban represents one of the first exponents who worked with studio glass in Spain. From the late 70s, his presence in international forums enabled him to contact sculptors from around the world and make propositions to the representatives of CEVIDER in Valencia, the organizer of the VICOINTER ‘83 exhibition.  
The glasswork by Torres Esteban is characterised by the construction of monumental geometric shapes, which is owed to both constructivism and kinetic art. His playfulness led him to work with geometry and the shapes he created, all of which were generally of a changeable nature. His works facilitate different arrangements that move away from the solidity of the closed to the open, the passive space that surrounded the cube, becomes dynamic and plays with the light that is projected on the interior surfaces of the piece, in which certain cuts in glass sheets that compose it have developed spherical cavities.
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.method_for_datation: Author archives and conversations with his son in order to create the exhibition: “Torres Esteban. A passion for glass”.
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.method_for_provenance: Temporary exhibition at the Royal Glass Factory. Museo Tecnológico del Vidrio, 1998

fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.name: ‘Eye of envy’ amulet.
fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.description:
A blue 'eye of envy' made of a moulded, blue glass disc decorated with a series of diminishing circles of yellow, then white, with a black spot at the centre. Probably a bead from a string of other similar beads, it has a hole though the side for threading. This type of glass 'eye' might also have been sewn on to garments and headdresses.  
  
Within Islamic popular belief blue eyes are thought to be envious eyes; the eye of envy is worn to repel such negative power by reflecting back to the perpetrator their own envy, thereby protecting the wearer from the effects of jealousy, thought to cause illness or disaster.  
  
Such eyes can be crudely made like this bead, or can be drawn with accuracy and quality of craftsmanship, as found in jewellery made of gold or silver; the quality does not affect the protective power. Plain blue beads are also thought to play a similar protective role, and are sometimes used in place of an eye of envy.
fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.short_description: In popular Middle Eastern Islamic belief blue eyes are thought to be both envious and to have the ability to repel envy. This blue glass eye is worn to protect the bearer from the effects of jealousy, which may cause the loss of what is being envied or illness or disaster.
fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.

fd21d364-fb99-5021-8bb2-b43f1e9c0ac6.name: Stream of flowers
fd21d364-fb99-5021-8bb2-b43f1e9c0ac6.description: Kyohei Fujita (1921-2004) was born in Tokyo in 1921 and joined the Department of Crafts at the Tokyo Fine Arts School (now known as Tokyo University of the Arts) to study metal engraving. After graduating he joined the Iwata Glass Company, but left shortly after to pursue a career as an independent glass artist. In 1964, he created the glasswork *Rainbow Colors*, which opened doors to international criticism. Later on, following many years of trial and error, he exhibited his *Ornament Boxes* in 1973, adapting the traditional Japanese aesthetic to suit a more contemporary style, using glass, which was very well received by the public. The following year, he continued to develop this series of ornament boxes, which have become so characteristic of Kyohei Fujita’s glasswork. They were very well received in the West as they fused the contemporary aesthetic with that of the traditional Rinpa School.
fd21d364-fb99-5021-8bb2-b43f1e9c0ac6.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja
fd21d364-fb99-5021-8bb2-b43f1e9c0ac6.method_for_datation: Personal files regarding VICOINTER, 83, belonging to Torres Esteban. Production by Ira Sapir. Doctoral Thesis by Mª Cristina Giménez Raurell: "Escultura y vidrio: España (1975-1995). New Glass Movement".

fd93bf8a-d085-595a-a14f-c616a5d43a58.name: Gülabdan (rose water bottle)
fd93bf8a-d085-595a-a14f-c616a5d43a58.short_description: It is known that there were workshops producing glass vessels around Beykoz in Istanbul in the 19th century. The first glass workshop was founded by Mevlevi Dervish Mehmed Dede during the reign of Selim III (1789-1807). There were European glass craftsmen working in those workshops as well. Cups, bottles, jugs etc. made of colourful, colourless and opal glass were among Beykoz' productions. This Beykoz-produced *gülabdan* (a small flask for sprinkling rose water) is made of green glass, in the shape of an ewer. There are cut floral decoration on the body. There are yellow, brown, blue, green and pink flower motifs.
keywords: Beykoz ceramic; Turkish decorative arts

fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.name: Carafe.
fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.description:
The shape of this carafe is asymmetrical, like most glass objects, but particularly harmonious. The belly of the vessel is about the same height as the neck. The belly is slightly rounded, widening a little towards the top. The shoulders curve in sharply and the neck narrows towards the mouth which opens out to a flat collar.  
The neck is decorated with vertical indentations. Two circular grooves surround the belly above a grid of diagonal lines. Each triangular or diamond-shaped section contains an indentation made with a barley-seed.  
This type of decoration is used, to great effect, as a background pattern in some Kairouanese book bindings dating from the AH 3rd, 4th and 5th centuries (AD 9th, 10th and 11th). A similar pattern is seen in a painting of Jawsaq al-Khaqani (the Emperor's Pavilion) at Samarra. The form, style and manufacturing technique come probably from classical and Sassanid traditions, indeed from methods used since ancient times. However, this carafe has certain similarities to vases found at Fustat and Samarra during the excavations undertaken by the American Research Centre in Egypt in 1965 and 1981. It bears an even more striking resemblance to some of the objects (probably Fatimid) from the Serce Limani wreck found off the Turkish coast. The decoration on these was engraved using small grindstones. To cut the geometric shapes, the grooves and the scalloped, braided and floral decorations, elongated chisels were used, some tapering and some curved.  
A kiln excavated on the site of this find at Sabra proves that glass-works in the Middle Ages were always relegated to the outskirts of the cities.
fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.short_description: The shape, style and manufacturing technique of this well-proportioned glass carafe are borrowed from the classical and Sassanid traditions of Antiquity. There are, however, even clearer similarities with items amongst the cargo of a Fatimid wreck found off the Turkish coast.
fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.dates: Hegira, end of the 4th–first half of the 5th centuries / AD 10th–11th centuries.
fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.method_for_datation: This carafe comes from Sabra al-Mansuriyya, built in 337 / 968. It bears a striking likeness to some of the objects found in the above-mentioned Serce Limani wreck cargo. We know that the ship sank in the second quarter of the 5th / 11th century and that the Sabra site was completely abandoned after the Hilalian invasions in 449 / 1057. We can, therefore, date this carafe with assurance to between the end of the 4th / 10th century and the first half of the 5th / 11th century.
fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.method_for_provenance: This carafe was discovered by chance in 1992 at the Sabra al-Mansuriyya site. Brick pickers broke open a large jar with a pick-axe and found contents of priceless value: carafes, goblets, flasks and cups, each demonstrating the great skills of the artisan glass-blowers of Sabra.
fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.provenance: Probably from the glass-works at Sabra al-Mansuriyya or from the glass-works at Kairouan.
fe5a75ec-3604-55c2-8c21-6b4f292e10cd.obtention: This piece was kept at the Bardo Museum. It was then acquired by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada, on its inauguration. It is currently on display there.

keywords: Geometric decoration

fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.name: Tumbler
fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.description:
Cylindrical, red tumbler whose walls on the outside are covered with red translucent paint. The painted decoration consists of the yellow coat of arms of the Principality of Serbia with crossed green oak branches. The opposite side of the tumbler displays a painted cornucopia, covered with a wide ribbon and a Cyrillic inscription, Споменъ (Memento).  
During the 19th century, along with the establishment of its state, Serbia sought to align with developed countries through modernization. One important component of this process was industrial production, and amidst challenges posed by the trade lobby and competing imports from Austro-Hungary one of the first steps made included establishment of the Glass Manufacture of Avram Petronijević. The owner himself had a flair for creating new processes and was very persistent, obtaining the exclusive right of production from the state, along with some benefits, including the ability to use raw materials from the environment where the factory was built and a twelve year tax exemption. The Manufacture did not operate for very long (1846-1852), but its work represented a significant shift, marking the beginning of Serbian industrialization. The largest number of the items preserved from this Manufacture originate from the period around 1850, consisting largely of glasses of simple shape and massive look, decorated with the heraldic motifs of the Principality of Serbia, including this tumbler from the Museum of Applied Arts collection. Whether painted with red or yellow translucent colours, they bear the image of the state coat of arms as decoration and a heraldic inscription in Cyrillic.
fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material and technique, and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.
fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.method_for_provenance: By stylistic analysis and historical documentation

fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.author: Biljana Crvenković
keywords: Coat of arms; Painted glass; Mould-blown; Manufacture; Serbia

feb4b0a1-063e-5d7c-b120-acf74338a57d.short_description: Glass produced in Bohemia in a European form but with a strong Middle Eastern influence. Acquired by Franks.

fefdb972-098b-576b-83f9-fe2d57f445d5.name: New Identity
fefdb972-098b-576b-83f9-fe2d57f445d5.short_description: The glass artist and educator Ray Flavell’s academic career and practice have run parallel with the origination and development of the studio glass movement since the late 1960s; of which he was a pioneer in Art Glass education in the UK. He taught Glass at the West Surrey College of Art & Design from 1978 to 1990 (now the University of the Creative Arts). In 1990, he moved to Edinburgh and was appointed the Head of the Glass Programme at Edinburgh College of Art; teaching there for 18 years, until his retirement in 2008. And is highly regarded for his work that explores the delicacy and precarious fragility of glass through the use of conventional glass artefacts like bowls and phials in combination with flat glass planes. In his work New Identity, Flavell looks to discuss his deep respect for glass and glass-working techniques, celebrating the tools and techniques employed in this ancient craft.

ffda1884-d458-52e1-ac48-a4c3e5cbd811.name: Flask
ffda1884-d458-52e1-ac48-a4c3e5cbd811.description:
In the middle of the 1st century BC glass-makers along the Syro-Palestinian coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated with air through a hollow blow-pipe. This invention of ‘free-blowing’ revolutionized the glass industry. It allowed vessels to be mass-produced thus rendering them less expensive and available to a wider market so that by the end of the 1st century AD free blown glass vessels were used widely throughout the Roman Empire. The majority were undecorated utilitarian pieces, used for storage and transport, and tablewares, like beakers and plates, but others were embellished with applied decoration. While still hot, their bodies were rolled over loose glass chips of contrasting colours and then marvered flush with the wall of the vessel. After that, the pieces where reheated and further inflated and manipulated, so that when their necks were pulled out of their bodies the splashes also became elongated. Attachments such as mouth edge profile, base, and handle are also made with auxiliary rods if necessary and then the glass is allowed to cool. The use of the free-blowing technique allowed thinning of the walls and the construction of larger and transparent closed forms.  
This tall slender flask has wheel-abraded horizontal lines; a band of three fine lines on the neck, another band of four lines around the body and it is in intact position. Although there is not any weathering on the exterior, there are some patches of internal staining, weathering, iridescence and a very few pin-prick bubbles. The pale blue-green flask also has a knocked-off, unworked rim, and a funnel-shaped neck; slight tooled constriction at its base. This kind of body shape is called piriform, meaning ‘pear shape’. The flask is tooled and cut; also has a tubular pushed-in base-ring and low kick in the bottom.
